t: Clean two kettlebells to the rack position: bells resting on your forearms, elbows tucked close to your ribcage, wrists neutral, and feet shoulder-width apart. | Take a short breath and brace your core firmly before each rep. | Perform the first dip: bend your knees slightly and drop your hips straight down a few inches, keeping your torso upright and heels flat. | Reverse the dip explosively, driving hard through your legs to generate upward momentum on the kettlebells. | As the bells float up from the rack, drop under them by performing a second shallow dip, catching both bells overhead with your arms fully locked out. | Stand fully upright with both kettlebells pressed overhead, elbows straight, biceps near your ears, and your core braced to protect your lower back. | Lower the kettlebells back to the rack position under control by absorbing the descent with a slight knee bend. | Reset your rack position and brace before initiating the next rep.

t: Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width, angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, and clean both kettlebells to the rack position. | Press one kettlebell overhead and lock the arm out fully, keeping your gaze fixed on the overhead bell throughout the movement. | Hold the second kettlebell in your lower hand, letting it hang at arm's length on the same side as your forward foot. | Push your hips back and toward the side of the overhead bell, initiating the hinge from the hip rather than bending the spine laterally. | Slide the lower kettlebell down the inside of your front leg as you hinge, maintaining a straight line from the overhead bell through your shoulder. | Continue lowering until the lower bell approaches the floor or your hip flexibility limit is reached, keeping both arms straight. | Drive your hips forward to return to the starting position, squeezing your obliques and glutes to power the ascent. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch the kettlebell positions and repeat on the opposite side.

t: Place two step boxes, weight plates, or platforms shoulder-width apart and stand on them with one foot on each, toes angled out at roughly 45 degrees. | Hold a kettlebell by the horns (the top of the handle) with both hands so it hangs straight down between your legs. | Stand tall, brace your core, pull your shoulders back, and take a breath in before you descend. | Push your knees out in line with your toes and lower your hips straight down, allowing the kettlebell to drop below the level of the platforms. | Descend until your thighs are at or below parallel, or until you reach the bottom of your comfortable range of motion without your lower back rounding. | From the bottom, drive through your heels and the balls of your feet, pressing the floor away to stand back up. | Squeeze your glutes and adductors at the top and fully extend your hips before beginning the next rep. | Lower the kettlebell to the floor under control when you have completed your set.

t: Place a weight plate or wedge flat on the floor. t: Set a kettlebell on the floor next to where your right shoulder will be, then lie down on your back beside it. | Roll onto your right side, grip the handle with both hands, and pull the kettlebell into your chest as you roll back flat. | Settle the kettlebell into a rack position with your upper arm pressed against your ribcage, plant both feet flat with knees bent, and lay your left arm out on the floor for stability. | Press the kettlebell to full arm extension directly above your right shoulder, rotating the palm to face your feet at the top. | Lower the kettlebell under control by bending the elbow, keeping it at roughly 45–60° from your torso, until your upper arm rests lightly on the floor. | Let the arm settle into the bottom position and feel the stretch across the chest and shoulder — control the descent rather than dropping into it. | Reverse the movement and press the kettlebell back to full arm extension, squeezing the chest and triceps at the top. | Complete all reps on one side, then roll the kettlebell down to the floor with both hands, switch sides, and repeat.

t: Stand with your feet hip-width apart, holding a kettlebell with both hands in front of your hips, arms straight. | Push your hips back and hinge forward at the waist, keeping your back flat and the kettlebell close to your legs as it lowers toward mid-shin level. | Pause when you feel a stretch through your hamstrings, maintaining a neutral spine throughout. | From the bottom of the hinge, bend your knees and shift your hips down and forward to transition into a squat position, keeping your chest up and the kettlebell between your legs. | Lower until your thighs are roughly parallel to the floor, or as deep as your mobility allows without rounding your lower back. | Drive through your heels to stand back up, extending your hips and knees simultaneously. | Return to the standing position with hips fully extended to complete one rep. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, maintaining control of the kettlebell throughout.

t: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and a kettlebell on the floor centered between your feet. | Push your hips back, hinge forward, and grip the kettlebell handle with both hands, keeping your spine long and your chest lifted. | Brace your core and squeeze your lats to create tension through your back before the lift begins. | Drive through your heels to extend your hips and knees, pulling the kettlebell off the floor until you are fully upright. | At the top, keep the kettlebell close to your body and your hips level. | Hinge back down under control, and as the kettlebell approaches the floor, rotate it to one side by pivoting at the hips and allowing the trailing knee to soften — do not twist your spine. | Set the kettlebell down lightly, reset your brace, then drive back to standing. | On the next rep, rotate to the opposite side to work both directions evenly. | Complete your set, then lower the kettlebell to the floor with a controlled hinge to finish.

Hold the kettlebell with both hands at chest height, gripping the sides of the handle. | Lean your torso back to roughly 45 degrees so your body forms a V-shape with your thighs. t: Sit upright on a bench or sturdy chair with your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. | Hold a kettlebell in each hand with a neutral grip, arms hanging straight down at your sides and palms facing inward. | Brace your core, pull your shoulders back and down, and maintain a tall, neutral spine throughout the set. | Inhale, then exhale as you raise both kettlebells out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with your elbows and keeping a very slight bend in them. | Lift until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor and your wrists are level with or just below your shoulders. | Pause briefly at the top, squeezing the lateral deltoids without shrugging your traps. | Slowly lower the kettlebells back to the starting position over 2–3 seconds under control. | Reset your posture if needed, then repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

t: Sit on a bench or box with your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart, and your spine tall. | Clean the kettlebell to the rack position on one side: wrist straight, elbow tucked close to your body, the bell resting on the back of your forearm at shoulder height. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and press your non-pressing hand against your thigh or knee for stability. | Take a deep breath, brace your torso, and press the kettlebell directly overhead in a straight vertical path. | Fully extend your arm at the top, locking out the elbow and shrugging your shoulder slightly to engage the serratus anterior. | Pause briefly at the top with the kettlebell directly over your shoulder joint. | Lower the kettlebell in a controlled manner back to the rack position at shoulder height. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch the kettlebell to the other hand and repeat.

t: Sit upright on a bench or box with your feet flat on the floor, hips at roughly 90°, and your core braced. | Clean the kettlebell to the racked position, or use both hands to lift it there: the handle rests diagonally across your palm, the bell sits on the back of your forearm, and your elbow points forward and slightly out at about 45° to your torso. | Set your shoulder blade down and back — packed, not shrugged — before you begin pressing. | Take a breath in, brace your core, and press the kettlebell straight up, finishing with your arm fully extended and your bicep close to your ear. | At the top, your forearm should be vertical and your wrist stacked directly over your elbow and shoulder. | Lower the kettlebell under control back to the racked position on your forearm, allowing your elbow to travel slightly forward as the bell descends. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch arms. Re-rack the kettlebell safely to the floor when the set is finished.

t: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a kettlebell in each hand at shoulder height in the rack position — elbows tucked, knuckles facing up, and bells resting on the back of each forearm. | Brace your core and glutes, and set a neutral spine before initiating any movement. | Press the right kettlebell overhead to full elbow lockout, turning the palm forward at the top, while simultaneously beginning to lower the left kettlebell back toward the rack position. | Time the two arms so the left bell settles into the rack at the same moment the right elbow locks out — that shared beat is the seesaw rhythm. | Without pausing at the top, begin pressing the left kettlebell overhead while the right arm descends in a controlled arc back to the rack position. | Keep your torso upright throughout; resist the urge to lean toward whichever arm is pressing. | Continue alternating in a smooth, fluid rhythm for the target number of reps per side. | To finish, lower both kettlebells to the rack simultaneously, then set them down with control.

t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointed slightly outward, holding one kettlebell with both hands in front of your hips. | Brace your core, pull your shoulder blades down and back, and hinge slightly at the hips to load your glutes and hamstrings. | Allow the kettlebell to swing laterally to one side — toward the outside of your hip — by initiating a controlled hip shift and rotation toward that side. | At the bottom of the arc, snap the hips back to center and use the momentum to drive the kettlebell across the body in a lateral arc to the opposite side. | Let your torso rotate slightly to follow the bell while keeping your spine neutral and your core braced — avoid bending sideways at the waist. | Control the bell at the apex of each side swing; do not let it pull your shoulders out of their packed position. | Continue alternating the lateral swing smoothly from side to side for the prescribed number of reps. | To finish, let the arc shorten until the bell settles in front of your hips, then hinge at the hips and set it down on the floor under control.

t: Stand with a kettlebell on the floor between your feet, which are roughly hip-width apart. Hinge at the hips and grip the handle with one hand, keeping your back flat and your shoulder packed down. | Swing the kettlebell back between your legs slightly, loading the hips and hamstrings. | Drive your hips forward explosively, extending your knees and hips together to generate upward momentum on the bell. | As the kettlebell rises, keep it close to your body and pull your elbow high and to the outside, guiding the bell upward. | At the top of the pull, rotate your wrist so your palm faces inward and allow the bell to wrap smoothly around your forearm into the rack position. | In the rack position, the bell rests on the back of your forearm and wrist, your elbow is tucked close to your ribs, and your fist is at about chin height. | Stand tall, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core at the top before reversing the movement. | Lower the bell with control by letting it swing back down between your legs, maintaining a hip hinge rather than rounding your lower back. | Complete all reps on one side before switching arms.

t: Kick up into a handstand with your heels resting against the wall, hands roughly shoulder-width apart and fingers spread, 6–12 inches from the wall. | Establish a tight, hollow body position — ribs down, core braced, glutes squeezed — with your body stacked vertically over your hands. | Begin the kip by bowing your hips toward the wall and bending at the knees to create an arched position, loading tension in your hips and shoulders. | Snap your hips back to a hollow body position explosively, driving your knees toward your chest to generate upward momentum through the torso. | Use that momentum to lower yourself quickly into the bottom of the press, letting your head descend toward the floor in a controlled dip. | As the momentum reverses, press forcefully through your palms, extending your arms and driving your body back up to a locked-out handstand. | At the top, reset your hollow body position and pause briefly before initiating the next kip cycle. | To dismount, carefully pike your hips, walk your feet down the wall, and step back to the floor.

t: Kneel on a mat with your knees hip-width apart and the tops of your feet flat on the floor. | Place your hands on your lower back or hips with fingers pointing downward to support the lumbar region. | Engage your core lightly and tuck your hips slightly forward to create a stable base. | Begin to lean back slowly, initiating the movement from the upper thoracic spine rather than collapsing into the lower back. | Allow your chest to lift and your shoulders to draw back as your torso arches into extension. | If comfortable, raise your arms overhead or reach them behind you to deepen the stretch along the front of the torso. | Breathe slowly and deeply into the belly, using each exhale to gently deepen the extension. | Hold the end position for 20 to 45 seconds while maintaining steady breathing. | To release, bring your hands back to your hips, contract your abdominals gently, and return upright in a controlled manner.

t: Position yourself beneath a fixed chin-up bar on a smooth floor or with a slider pad under your knees. Kneel upright with your knees hip-width apart and your shins resting on the surface. | Reach up and grip the bar with a supinated (palms-facing-you) grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Your arms should be fully extended and your body hanging in a near-vertical line from the bar. | Brace your core and pull your shoulder blades down and together to create tension across your back before you begin the pull. | Begin pulling yourself up by driving your elbows down toward your hips. As you pull, allow your knees to slide forward along the surface toward the bar, reducing the load on your arms. | Continue pulling until your chin clears the bar, keeping your chest tall and your elbows tracking close to your sides. | Pause briefly at the top with your chin above the bar, squeezing your lats and upper back. | Lower yourself under control by extending your arms and allowing your knees to slide back to the starting position as your body descends. | Once your arms are fully extended and your knees are back under your hips, reset your core tension and begin the next rep.

t: Anchor the ropes to a fixed point at ground level and lay them out straight in front of you. | Kneel facing the anchor, with knees hip-width apart and toes pointed behind you or tucked under — whichever allows a stable base. | Sit tall through the hips, brace the core, and keep the spine neutral from tailbone to crown. | Grip one rope end in each hand with an overhand grip, arms slightly bent and elbows close to the body. | To begin alternating waves, drive one arm down forcefully toward the floor while lifting the other, then switch rapidly to produce a continuous wave toward the anchor. | To perform simultaneous waves, drive both arms down and up together in unison, generating a double-wave pattern. | Maintain a steady rhythm throughout the set — focus on consistent wave amplitude rather than maximum speed. | Breathe continuously; exhale on each downward drive and inhale on the upward phase, or breathe in short rhythmic bursts if the pace demands it. | At the end of the set, slow the ropes gradually to a stop, set them down, and release the grip before standing.

t: Start on all fours with your knees hip-width apart and your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, directly under your shoulders. | Extend your hips so your body forms a straight line from knees to head — this is your kneeling plank starting position. | Brace your core lightly and squeeze your glutes to keep your hips aligned with your torso. | Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor, keeping your elbows at roughly a 45° angle to your torso. | Allow your hips to descend as your chest nears the floor, so your body is close to lying flat. | Press through your hands to push your chest up and forward, beginning the cobra portion of the movement. | Continue pressing until your arms are nearly straight, allowing your lower back to arch and your hips to drop toward the floor — squeeze your glutes and erector spinae at the top. | Reverse the motion by tucking your hips back under, re-engaging your core, and returning to the kneeling plank position. | Reset your alignment and repeat for the desired number of reps.

t: Start on all fours on a mat with your hands directly under your shoulders and your knees directly under your hips. | Slowly slide both knees apart, moving them as wide as is comfortable while keeping the inside edges of your feet and lower legs flat on the mat. | Keep your hips level and parallel to the floor as you widen your knees — do not allow one hip to hike or rotate. | Maintain a neutral spine with a flat back; avoid letting your lower back sag or round. | Lower your hips toward the floor by sinking your pelvis down and slightly back until you feel a stretch along the inner thighs and groin. | Rest your forearms on the mat in front of you for support if needed, keeping your torso relaxed. | Breathe deeply and steadily — inhale to prepare, exhale to relax further into the stretch without forcing the range. | Hold the position for 20 to 60 seconds, breathing continuously and letting the inner thighs release gradually. | To exit, walk your knees back in toward each other slowly before returning to the starting position.

t: Lay an agility ladder flat on the ground in a clear, open area with enough room to run through it completely. | Stand at one end of the ladder with your feet hip-width apart, knees slightly bent, and weight balanced on the balls of your feet. | Drive your right foot into the first square, followed immediately by your left foot so both feet land inside the same square. | Step your right foot out to the right side of the ladder, then your left foot into the next square, continuing the two-in, two-out pattern down the length of the ladder. | Pump your arms in opposition to your legs — right arm forward when left leg steps, left arm forward when right leg steps — to maintain rhythm and balance. | Keep your eyes forward and your chest upright throughout; resist the urge to look down at the ladder. | Land on the balls of your feet with each contact, minimizing the time each foot spends on the ground. | Walk back to the start after completing the full length of the ladder, rest 30–60 seconds, then repeat for the desired number of sets.

t: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing inward — this is your starting position for both the wrong and right demonstrations. | WRONG: Shrug your shoulders upward and swing the dumbbells up using momentum, allowing your torso to lean back and your elbows to drop below your wrists at the top. | WRONG: Raise the dumbbells overhead or past shoulder height, and turn your palms to face upward (like pouring water), which shifts tension away from the side delts. | Lower the dumbbells back to the starting position and reset. | RIGHT: Keep your shoulders down and back, and initiate the movement by driving your elbows outward — not by lifting your hands. | RIGHT: Raise the dumbbells in a smooth, controlled arc until your arms are parallel to the floor (no higher), keeping a slight bend in your elbows and your wrists level with or slightly below your elbows. | RIGHT: Pause briefly at the top, then lower the dumbbells slowly back to your sides over 2–3 seconds, maintaining tension throughout. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, keeping your torso upright and still on every repetition.

t: Begin in a high push-up position with your hands shoulder-width apart, arms straight, and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to keep your hips level throughout the movement. | Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows outward at roughly a 45-degree angle from your torso. | Press back up to the starting position in one controlled movement, fully extending your arms. | Step your right hand and right foot one step to the right, then follow with your left hand and left foot so you return to shoulder-width stance. | Perform another push-up in the new position. | Continue walking in the same direction for the desired number of reps or distance, then reverse and walk back to the left. | Complete the set by finishing with a final push-up in your ending position.

t: Stand in a boxing stance with your left foot slightly forward, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, knees soft, and weight balanced evenly on the balls of your feet. | Raise your hands to guard position — fists near your cheekbones, elbows tucked close to your ribcage. | Shift your weight slightly onto your left foot and dip your left shoulder a few inches downward to load the punch. | Drive explosively off your left foot while rotating your hips and torso upward and to the right. | Simultaneously thrust your left fist in a tight upward arc — palm facing you — aiming to strike at chin height in front of you. | Keep your right hand at guard throughout the motion to protect your head. | Snap your left fist back to guard position immediately after the punch lands, using the same rotational path in reverse. | Reset your stance and repeat for the desired number of repetitions or rounds.

t: Find a firm, flat surface such as a treatment table or exercise mat and lie face-up with your legs fully extended. | Slide both heels together so your legs are parallel and touching, with your toes pointing toward the ceiling. | Relax your hips, legs, and lower back completely — avoid actively pulling or pushing either leg. | Flex your hips and knees to bring both knees up to your chest, hugging them briefly to reset any pelvic tilt. | Slowly lower both legs back to a fully extended position, letting them settle naturally without adjusting. | Look down at your ankles from above, or have a partner observe at foot level to compare the position of the medial malleoli (inner ankle bones). | Note any visible difference between the height or position of the two ankles — a discrepancy may suggest a functional or structural leg length difference. | Repeat the reset-and-lower sequence two to three times to confirm the finding is consistent.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs straight and your arms at your sides, palms pressing lightly into the floor. | Curl your head and shoulder blades off the mat into a partial crunch position and hold them there for the entire set — do not rest your head down between reps. | Press your lower back into the mat by engaging your core before you begin moving your legs. | Keeping both legs straight and together, exhale and raise them until they are perpendicular to the floor at approximately 90 degrees. | At the top of the leg raise, contract your lower abdominals and curl your hips off the mat by tilting your pelvis posteriorly, lifting your tailbone 2–4 inches from the floor. | Hold the hip lift for one count, ensuring the effort comes from your abs rather than momentum. | Slowly reverse the movement: lower your hips back to the mat first, then begin descending your legs in a controlled manner. | Lower your legs until they are just above the floor without letting them touch, keeping tension in the core throughout. | Inhale as you lower your legs and prepare for the next repetition, maintaining the head-up position the entire time.

t: Lie on your side on a mat with your body in a straight line, legs stacked on top of each other and your bottom arm extended along the floor to support your head. | Place your top hand lightly behind your head or rest it on the floor in front of your chest for balance. | Brace your core and press your waist gently toward the mat to keep your spine neutral. | In one coordinated movement, raise your top leg upward and simultaneously crunch your torso laterally, bringing your elbow and hip toward each other. | Pause briefly at the top when you feel a contraction through the obliques and a stretch in the gluteus medius. | Slowly lower your leg and return your torso to the starting position with control, avoiding letting either the leg or torso drop passively. | Complete all reps on one side, then roll over and repeat on the opposite side.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs extended, a slight (15–20 degree) bend in both knees, and your arms at your sides with palms facing down. | Press your lower back gently into the mat by engaging your core before initiating any movement. | Maintain the same slight knee bend throughout — this is the fixed position for the entire set, not a dynamic flex. | Exhale and raise both legs together in a controlled arc until your thighs are perpendicular to the floor, or as close to vertical as your flexibility allows. | Pause briefly at the top and squeeze your lower abdominals, ensuring your lower back remains in contact with the mat. | Inhale and slowly lower your legs back toward the floor in a controlled manner, resisting gravity the entire way down. | Stop the descent just before your feet touch the floor to keep continuous tension on the core. | Reset your breath and repeat for the target number of repetitions.

t: Place your mat perpendicular to a clear section of wall so that the short edge nearly touches the baseboard. | Sit sideways with one hip touching the wall, then swing your legs up the wall as you lower your torso onto the mat so you end up lying on your back with your legs extended vertically. | Scoot your hips as close to the wall as is comfortable, or allow a small gap if that feels better for your lower back. | Straighten your legs and let them rest passively against the wall, feet relaxed and hip-width apart. | Rest your arms on the floor beside you, palms facing up, and allow your shoulders and upper back to fully release into the mat. | Close your eyes, breathe slowly and evenly, and let your whole body become heavy against the floor. | Hold the position for 2–10 minutes, adjusting your distance from the wall if you feel any discomfort in the hamstrings or lower back. | To exit, bend your knees and bring them toward your chest, then roll gently onto one side and pause before pressing yourself up to seated.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with both legs extended and your arms resting at your sides, palms facing down. | Press your lower back gently into the mat to establish a stable, neutral spine. | Inhale to prepare, then on the exhale slowly slide your right leg out to the side along the floor, keeping your foot flexed and your toes pointing up toward the ceiling. | Move the leg only as far as you can while both hips remain in contact with the mat — do not allow the opposite hip to lift. | Hold the end position for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing steadily and relaxing into the stretch with each exhale. | To deepen the stretch, gently press your inner thigh toward the midline for about 5 seconds as if drawing the leg back to center, then release and let the leg settle a few degrees wider on the exhale. | After the hold, slowly slide the leg back to the center on an inhale, keeping the movement controlled. | Repeat on the left side, holding for the same duration. | Complete 2 to 3 rounds per side, allowing the range of motion to increase naturally over successive repetitions.

t: Adjust the seat height so your hips are aligned with the pivot point of the machine's track — most Ab Coaster machines have a height pin or knob for this. | Kneel on the padded knee rest and grip the handles firmly with both hands, keeping your arms slightly bent and your shoulders relaxed. | Brace your core before moving — draw your navel gently inward and squeeze your abs to create tension. | Exhale and contract your abs to drive your knees upward along the curved track toward your chest in a smooth, controlled arc. | Continue until your knees reach the top of the arc and your abs are fully contracted — avoid jerking or using momentum to reach the peak. | Pause briefly at the top and squeeze your abdominals hard for one count. | Inhale and lower your knees back down the track slowly and under control, resisting gravity rather than letting the carriage drop. | Stop just short of the fully extended bottom position to keep tension on the abs, then begin the next rep. | Complete all reps, then carefully step off the knee rest.

t: Set the lever arm or cable attachment on the abduction machine to a height that aligns with your ankle or lower shin. | Stand next to the machine with the working leg closest to the attachment point, and secure the cuff around your ankle. | Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, holding the machine frame lightly for balance — do not lean into it. | Brace your core by drawing your navel gently inward, keeping your torso upright throughout the movement. | Exhale and raise the working leg out to the side and slightly forward in a controlled arc, combining abduction with a moderate hip flexion angle. | Lift until you feel a firm contraction in the outer hip (gluteus medius) and the hip flexor — typically 45 to 60 degrees — without tilting your pelvis. | Pause briefly at the top of the range, then inhale and lower the leg back to the starting position under control over two to three seconds. | Complete all reps on one side before switching legs, keeping the motion smooth and avoiding momentum. | Adjust the machine weight so you can maintain full control throughout — avoid using a load that forces you to hitch your hip or lean sideways.

t: Load the desired weight plates onto the machine's horns and secure them with collars. | Sit in the seat and place both feet on the platform at roughly hip-width apart, with toes pointed slightly outward. | Disengage the safety handles and hold the machine's side handles firmly to stabilize your torso. | Press the platform out fully with both legs to establish your starting position, then allow one foot to remain on the platform while lifting the opposite foot a few inches away. | Lower the platform by bending the working knee in a controlled manner until your knee reaches approximately 90 degrees, keeping your lower back flat against the pad. | Press the platform back to full extension through your hip and thigh without locking the knee aggressively at the top. | Complete all reps on the first leg, then switch so the other foot is the working leg and repeat. | Once all reps are done, engage the safety handles before removing your feet from the platform. | Lower the platform gently back to the rest position and re-rack safely.

t: Load the plate-loaded leverage machine and adjust the chest pad (if present) or seat height so that the handles are at approximately mid-chest level when you sit upright. | Sit facing the machine and plant your feet firmly on the footrests or floor. Grip both handles with a close, neutral (palms facing each other) or parallel grip, arms fully extended and a slight tension already on the weight stack. | Sit tall with your chest up, core braced, and shoulders pulled down and back. Keep your torso stationary throughout the set. | Begin with your weaker or non-dominant arm: pull that handle toward your lower ribs, leading with your elbow and driving it straight back past your side. | As your pulling arm reaches the fully contracted position — shoulder blade squeezed in and elbow behind your torso — begin extending it back out under control. | Simultaneously initiate the pull with your other arm so that one arm is pulling while the other is extending. t: Set the seat back and safety catches to a depth where your knees reach roughly 90 degrees when the sled is lowered. Adjust the backrest angle if the machine allows. | Sit down and position your feet shoulder-width apart on the footplate, toes turned out slightly. Keep your entire foot flat against the plate. | Disengage the safety catches by rotating or pressing them outward, then hold the sled under control with your legs near full extension. | Brace your core, press your lower back firmly into the seat pad, and keep your head neutral against the headrest. | Lower the sled in a controlled manner until your knees reach approximately 90 degrees — or the point just before your hips begin to tuck under. | Drive the footplate away from you by pushing evenly through the whole foot, extending your knees and hips together until your legs are almost fully straight. Do not lock out hard at the top. | Pause briefly at the top, then begin the next rep without bouncing at the bottom. | After your final rep, re-engage both safety catches before releasing the weight fully.

t: Adjust the seat back position so that when seated, your knees form approximately a 90-degree angle with your feet flat on the footplate. | Sit firmly in the seat with your back flush against the pad and your head resting naturally against the headrest. | Place your feet shoulder-width apart on the footplate, toes pointing slightly outward (about 15–30 degrees). | Grip the handles on either side of the seat to stabilize your upper body throughout the movement. | Press through your heels and the balls of your feet to extend your legs, pushing the footplate away until your legs are nearly straight — do not lock out your knees at the top. | Pause briefly at the top of the movement, keeping a slight bend in the knees. | Slowly lower the footplate back toward you in a controlled manner until your knees return to approximately 90 degrees, or until you feel a comfortable stretch in the hips and thighs. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining steady breathing — exhale on the press, inhale on the lowering phase. | To finish, press to the top position and engage any safety latches or pegs before releasing your feet from the footplate.

t: Adjust the lever machine so the pad sits across your lower thighs, just above the knees, and your hips are free to hinge over the edge of the platform. | Step onto the footrests and hook your feet securely under the anchor, keeping them hip-width apart. | Fold at the hips and lower your torso toward the floor until your body forms roughly a 90° angle — or as far as your flexibility allows without rounding your lower back. | Cross your arms over your chest or place your hands lightly behind your head; avoid pulling on your neck. | Brace your core and squeeze your glutes, then drive your hips forward and raise your torso by extending through your lower back and hips. | Continue rising until your body forms a straight line from head to heels — do not hyperextend past neutral. | Pause briefly at the top to feel peak contraction in your erector spinae and glutes. | Lower your torso back down slowly and under control to the starting position. | Complete all reps, then step off the machine safely.

t: Set the leverage machine to a height appropriate for attaching the belt around your hips, and position a bench or platform behind you at knee height. | Step into the belt attachment and secure it snugly around your hips so the machine supports the load through your pelvis. | Stand facing away from the machine and place the top of your rear foot on the bench behind you, finding a stance width where your front foot is roughly one shin-length ahead of the bench. | Stand tall with your torso upright, core braced, and shoulders pulled back before initiating the movement. | Lower your body by bending your front knee, allowing your rear knee to descend toward the floor while keeping your front foot flat and your knee tracking over your toes. | Descend until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor or your rear knee lightly grazes the ground, whichever comes first. | Drive through the heel and mid-foot of your front leg to push yourself back up to the starting position. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch legs and repeat.

t: Load the machine with an appropriate amount of weight — start light, as even modest loads create significant stretch tension on the calves. | Sit or stand in the machine according to its design, and position the balls of your feet on the edge of the footplate with your heels hanging freely off the bottom. | Extend your legs so the machine is supporting the load, then allow your ankles to dorsiflex fully — heels dropping as far down as your range of motion allows. | Keep your knees straight (to emphasize the gastrocnemius) or slightly bent (to emphasize the soleus), depending on which part of the calf you want to target. | Maintain a neutral spine and a relaxed upper body throughout the hold — do not grip or brace aggressively. | Hold the stretched position for the desired duration, typically 20–60 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the muscles to relax into the stretch. | When the hold is complete, plantarflex slightly to release the tension before unloading the machine and stepping off safely.

t: Load the leverage machine with the appropriate weight and position yourself under the shoulder pads, standing with feet hip- to shoulder-width apart and toes angled out 15–30 degrees. | Stand tall to take the load on the shoulder pads, then rotate the handles to unrack the weight. | Brace your core, take a deep breath in, and keep your chest tall and gaze forward. | Initiate the descent by simultaneously pushing your knees out in line with your toes and sitting your hips back and down. | Lower yourself until your thighs are at or below parallel to the floor — achieving full depth with hips below knees. | Keep your heels flat on the platform throughout the descent; do not allow them to rise. | At the bottom, pause briefly, then drive through your entire foot to push the floor away and return to standing. | Exhale as you push through the concentric phase; fully extend your hips and knees at the top without locking out aggressively. | Complete all reps, stand fully upright, then rotate the handles to re-rack the weight before stepping out from under the pads.

t: Step into the hack squat machine facing away from the sled. Position your shoulders under the shoulder pads and your feet hip-width apart, roughly at the center of the platform. | Straighten your legs to lift the sled off the safety stoppers, then release the handles. Keep your chest up and your core braced. | Begin the descent by pushing your hips backward while hinging at the hips, not by rounding your lower back. t: Start in a high plank position with your hands shoulder-width apart and your body in a straight line. | Step your right foot forward and place it on the outside of your right hand, so your foot is flat on the floor and your knee is stacked directly above your ankle. | Lower your left knee to the mat and let the top of your left foot rest on the ground behind you. | Press your hands into the mat and lengthen your spine, avoiding rounding through the upper back. | On an exhale, sink your hips forward and down toward the floor, deepening the stretch in the front hip and groin. | Hold the position for 30–60 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing your hips to relax a little further with each exhale. | To deepen the stretch, lower onto your forearms if your flexibility allows, keeping your spine long and your hips level. | Press back through your hands to return to high plank and repeat on the opposite side by stepping your left foot forward.

t: Lie face down on a mat with your legs extended straight behind you, feet together or hip-width apart, and your arms resting alongside your body with palms facing down. | Rest your forehead lightly on the mat and take a slow breath in to prepare. | On an exhale, engage your core gently and press your pubic bone into the mat to stabilize your pelvis. | As you inhale, simultaneously lift your head, chest, and arms off the mat, reaching your fingertips back toward your feet. | Squeeze your glutes and lift your legs off the mat, keeping them straight and internally rotated so your big toes point toward each other. | Hold the top position for 3–5 breaths, keeping your gaze directed slightly downward to keep the neck long. | On an exhale, slowly lower your chest, arms, and legs back to the mat with control. | Rest briefly with your cheek to one side before repeating.

t: Lie on your back on the floor and grip a fixed anchor directly behind your head — a heavy rack base, the legs of a sturdy sofa, or a partner's ankles — with both hands shoulder-width apart. | Press your shoulders into the floor and keep your arms straight throughout the set; they act only as an anchor, not a pull. | Drive your legs up and brace your entire body — core tight, glutes squeezed, legs together and toes pointed — so your body forms a single rigid plank from shoulders to feet. | This raised position, with your hips and legs vertical or just past vertical, is your starting point for every rep. | Begin the descent by resisting gravity: slowly lower your legs and hips toward the floor while keeping your body completely straight, avoiding any bend at the hips. | Control the speed of descent with your core and hip flexors; aim for 3–5 seconds to reach the floor. | Keep your lower back from sagging — if your hips drop faster than your legs, your midsection has broken and the rep has ended. | Allow your body to make contact with the floor, then reset: bring your legs back to the raised starting position using whatever assistance you need (partner, momentum, or a straight-leg crunch), and repeat for the target number of reps. | After your final rep, lower yourself fully and release the anchor.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs extended and your arms resting at your sides. Allow your head to rest fully supported on the surface. | Establish a neutral spine by making sure your lower back has a slight natural arch and your chin is gently tucked — neck packed — rather than jutting forward. | Take a slow breath in to prepare. On the exhale, gently tilt your head toward your right shoulder in a pure lateral flexion movement, keeping your face pointing straight up at the ceiling. | Move only 5–10 degrees — the range should be small and deliberate. You should feel a mild activation along the left side of your neck, where the scalenes are lengthening and engaging against gravity. | Optional: place your right hand lightly against your right temple and press your head into your hand with about 20–30% effort to add gentle isometric resistance. Your head should not actually move when resistance is applied. | Hold the position for 2–3 seconds while breathing normally. Do not hold your breath. | Slowly return your head to the center starting position and pause for a moment before switching sides. | Repeat the lateral tilt toward your left shoulder, applying the same controlled range and optional hand resistance on the left side. | Complete 8–12 repetitions per side for 2–3 sets, resting 30–60 seconds between sets.

t: Stand facing a wall or sturdy surface, roughly one arm's length away, and place both hands on it at about shoulder height for balance. | Step one foot forward so the toes are a few inches from the base of the wall, keeping both feet pointing straight ahead. | Bend the front knee and push it slowly toward the wall while keeping the heel of that foot flat on the floor. | Keep the back leg straight and press its heel firmly into the floor to anchor the stretch. | Shift your weight gently forward until you feel a distinct stretch through the calf and ankle of the front leg. | Hold the position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and steadily without bouncing. | Release, return to the starting position, and switch legs. | Complete 2–3 holds per side, moving your foot slightly farther from the wall to increase the stretch intensity as your mobility improves.

t: Start in a push-up position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart and your hips raised so your body forms an inverted V, similar to a downward-dog. | Keep your arms and legs straight and your heels pressing toward the floor at the top of the arc. | Begin the movement by bending your elbows and lowering your chin toward the floor, initiating the forward sweep. | Scoop your chest forward and down in a smooth arc, keeping your hips lower than at the start as your body sweeps through the bottom position. | Press through your hands and extend your elbows as you continue the arc, pushing your chest upward and forward into an upward-dog position with hips near the floor. | At the top of the press, your arms should be straight, your chest open, and your gaze forward or slightly upward — feel the stretch across the pectoralis major and through the front of the torso. | Reverse the arc by pushing your hips back and upward, returning to the inverted-V starting position. | Control the return so you feel the rectus abdominis engage as the hips rise. | Repeat for the prescribed number of reps, maintaining a smooth, continuous motion throughout each cycle.

t: Start in a standard push-up position with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms straight, body in a straight line from head to heels. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and keep your hips level so your spine stays neutral throughout the movement. | Lower your right forearm to the floor, placing it where your right hand was, then lower your left forearm so both forearms are flat on the ground. | Hold the forearm plank position for a moment, keeping your hips from rising or sagging. | Press your right hand back to the floor, followed by your left hand, returning to the push-up position. | Alternate the leading arm each rep to balance the workload evenly on both sides. | Complete the target number of transitions, then lower your knees to the floor to rest.

t: Stand with feet hip-width apart and place your hands on your hips or extend them forward for balance. | Adopt a quarter-squat position by pushing your hips back slightly and bending your knees, keeping your chest tall and core braced. | Shift your weight onto your right foot and step your left foot diagonally forward and to the left, landing softly on the ball of your foot. | Follow with your right foot, stepping only far enough to return to a hip-width stance without letting your feet touch, and keep the squat depth as you step. | Continue stepping in the same diagonal direction for the prescribed number of steps or distance. | Reverse the pattern by stepping diagonally backward and to the right, leading with the right foot, to travel back to your starting position. | Finish the set by bringing your feet back to hip-width and standing tall out of the quarter-squat.

t: Begin in a high plank position with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms straight, and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Brace your core and keep your hips level — they should not pike up or sag toward the floor. | Drive your right knee diagonally toward your left elbow, rotating your hip slightly to complete the cross-body movement. | Without pausing, kick your right leg out to the right side, extending it roughly parallel to the floor. | Return your right foot to the starting position under control. | Immediately repeat the sequence on the opposite side — drive the left knee toward the right elbow, then kick the left leg out to the left. | Continue alternating sides at a brisk, controlled pace, maintaining plank alignment throughout. | Complete the prescribed number of repetitions or time interval, then lower your knees to the floor to rest.

t: Start in a high plank position with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms fully extended, and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Engage your core and keep your hips level — do not let them rise or sag. | Drive your right knee toward your chest as explosively as possible. | Before that foot returns to the ground, simultaneously drive your left knee forward in a switching motion. | As both feet leave the ground during the switch, add a small explosive hop so both feet are briefly airborne at the same time. | Land softly with one knee drawn in and the opposite leg extended, absorbing impact through the balls of your feet. | Continue alternating legs in a rapid, rhythmic cadence for the target duration or repetitions. | To finish, bring both feet back to the starting plank position and hold briefly to stabilise.

t: Start in a high plank with your hands flat on the floor directly under your shoulders, arms straight, and body in a straight line from head to heels. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and ensure your hips are level — neither piked up nor sagging toward the floor. | Drive your right knee forward and bring your right foot all the way up beside your right hand, landing in a low lunge position with your heel flat or close to flat on the floor. | Pause briefly in the lunge to feel the stretch at the front of your left hip, keeping both hands planted and your right knee tracking in line with your right foot. | Step your right foot back to the starting plank position with control, re-establishing a neutral spine before the next rep. | Drive your left knee forward in the same way, bringing your left foot up beside your left hand into the low lunge position. | Pause, then return the left foot to the plank. | Continue alternating sides for the prescribed number of reps or time, maintaining steady breathing throughout.

t: Place a folded towel on a smooth, hard floor — hardwood, tile, or laminate works best. | Get into a high-plank position with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms straight, and both feet resting on the towel. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and set a neutral spine — your body should form a straight line from head to heels. | Slide your right foot forward along the floor, drawing your right knee toward your chest without raising your hips. | Slide the right foot back to the starting position, fully extending the hip before the next rep. | Immediately slide your left foot forward in the same controlled manner, keeping your hips level throughout. | Continue alternating legs at a steady pace, maintaining shoulder position directly over your wrists for the duration of the set. | To finish, press back through your shoulders, step off the towel, and release the plank position.

t: Place your hands flat on the floor, slightly wider than shoulder-width, and extend both legs behind you into a high-plank position with your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Engage your core by bracing your abs and squeezing your glutes so your hips stay level with your shoulders throughout the set. | Lift your right foot and drive your right knee diagonally across your body toward your left elbow, rotating your hip slightly to allow full range of motion. | Pause for a brief moment at the top of the drive, feeling the contraction in your obliques and hip flexors. | Return your right foot to the starting position with control, keeping your hips from rising or dropping as the leg extends back. | Immediately drive your left knee diagonally toward your right elbow, mirroring the movement on the opposite side. | Continue alternating legs in a smooth, rhythmic pattern for the target number of repetitions or duration. | Keep your breathing steady throughout — exhale as each knee drives across, inhale as the foot returns.

t: Stand with your feet together or hip-width apart, toes pointing straight forward and the outer edges of your feet parallel. | Press all four corners of each foot — the ball of the big toe, the ball of the little toe, and both sides of the heel — evenly into the floor. | Engage your thighs lightly so the kneecaps lift, but do not lock your knees; keep a very slight, natural bend. | Tuck your tailbone just enough to neutralize the lower back — avoid an exaggerated arch or a full posterior tuck. | Lengthen through the entire spine, drawing the crown of your head upward as if a thread were pulling it toward the ceiling. | Roll your shoulders up, back, and down so your shoulder blades settle onto your upper back and your chest opens without your ribcage flaring forward. | Let your arms hang at your sides with palms facing your thighs or slightly forward; keep your fingers long and relaxed. | Soften your jaw and face, breathe steadily through your nose, and hold the pose for five to ten slow breaths. | Release by taking one deep breath, then step your feet together if they were apart and allow your body to relax.

t: Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width with an overhand grip, arms fully extended and body hanging straight. | Engage your core and retract your scapulae to create tension through your lats and upper back. | Initiate an explosive pull by driving your elbows down and back, pulling the bar toward your lower chest rather than your chin. | As the bar reaches chest height, lean forward aggressively and begin rotating your wrists so your hands transition from below to above the bar. | Use the momentum of the pull to drive your torso up and over the bar, keeping the bar close to your body throughout the transition. | Once your hips are level with the bar and your chest is above it, press your hands down into the bar to straighten your arms into the dip lockout position. | Pause briefly at the top with arms fully extended and body supported above the bar. | Lower yourself in a controlled manner back through the transition and into a full hang to complete the repetition.

t: Place a Bosu ball dome-side up on the floor and sit on the center of the dome. | Walk your feet forward and lower your lower back onto the top of the dome so it sits roughly at the level of your lumbar spine. | Let your torso arch back over the dome until your abs feel a full stretch, with your head, upper back, and arms hanging below the level of your hips. | Place your fingertips lightly at the sides of your head or cross your arms over your chest — do not pull on your neck. | Brace your core and exhale as you curl your torso upward, lifting your shoulders and upper back off the dome. | Continue curling until your abs are fully contracted and your torso has reached roughly a 30–45° angle above horizontal. | Hold the contracted position for one count, then inhale and slowly lower your torso back over the dome to the starting stretched position. | Control the descent fully — let the dome support your arch without bouncing off it. | Complete your reps, then carefully sit upright before stepping off the Bosu ball.

t: Stand with your feet slightly wider than hip-width apart and your toes angled out at roughly 45 degrees. | Lower your hips down into a deep squat, keeping your heels flat on the floor if possible; if your heels rise, place a folded mat or small wedge under them. | Allow your thighs to open wider than your torso so your knees track over your toes. | Bring your palms together at the center of your chest in a prayer position, thumbs lightly touching your sternum. | Press your elbows firmly against the inner surfaces of your knees, using this contact to encourage the knees to widen and the hips to open further. | Lengthen your spine upward, lifting the crown of your head toward the ceiling and drawing your shoulder blades slightly together to avoid rounding the upper back. | Breathe steadily, holding the position for five to ten slow breaths or as directed by your practice. | To exit, press through your feet, engage your legs, and rise back to standing in a controlled manner.

t: Place a flat bench behind you and sit on the floor in front of it, facing away. | Lean back and position both heels on top of the bench with your feet together or no more than a few inches apart — this narrow stance is the key challenge of the movement. | Plant your hands flat on the floor beside your hips for initial stability. | Brace your core, press through your heels, and lift your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to heels. | Lift your hands off the floor and extend your arms alongside your torso or hold them slightly out to the sides for balance, engaging the deltoid anterior and serratus anterior. | Hold the top position with your glutes lightly squeezed, but focus on drawing your lower ribs toward your hips to keep the rectus abdominis under tension. | Keep your hips level — resist any rotation caused by the narrow foot placement. | Lower your hips back to the floor under control to complete one repetition, or hold the top position for the prescribed time if performing an isometric variation.

t: Sit or stand beneath a chin-up bar and take a close, shoulder-width or narrower supinated (palms-facing-you) grip on the bar. | Hang at full arm extension, cross your feet if needed, and pull your shoulder blades down and back to activate the lats before you begin pulling. | Brace your core and depress your shoulders away from your ears to create a stable base. | Pull yourself upward by driving your elbows straight down toward your hips, keeping them close to your sides throughout the movement. | Continue pulling until your chin clears the bar or your upper chest approaches it, squeezing the lats and mid-back at the top. | Lower yourself in a controlled, slow manner back to full arm extension, resisting gravity on the way down. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, maintaining tension in the back and avoiding swinging.

t: Place a stable raised surface — weight plates, a low step, or a sturdy block — on the floor and stand on top of it with your feet hip-width apart or closer, toes pointing slightly outward. | Stand tall with your chest up, shoulders back, and arms extended in front of you or crossed at your chest for counterbalance. | Brace your core and shift your weight evenly through both feet, making sure your heels are fully supported by the platform. | Begin the descent by simultaneously pushing your hips back and bending your knees, allowing them to track over your toes. | Lower yourself as deep as your mobility allows — ideally until your thighs go below parallel — letting your heels drop toward the floor below the platform level to exploit the full deficit range. | Pause briefly at the bottom without collapsing your torso or rounding your lower back. | Drive through your entire foot to press the floor away, extending your hips and knees together as you return to standing. | Lock out at the top by squeezing your glutes and fully extending your legs before beginning the next rep.

t: Grip a pull-up bar with your hands placed 4–6 inches apart, palms facing away from you. Your thumbs should wrap fully around the bar. | Jump or step up so your chin is above the bar and your arms are bent, starting in the top position of a pull-up. | Brace your core, depress your shoulder blades, and avoid letting your body swing. | Lower yourself in a controlled manner until your elbows reach roughly 90 degrees — this is the halfway point. | Pause briefly at the bottom of this range, keeping tension in your back. | Pull yourself back up until your chin clears the bar and your elbows are fully bent. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, then lower yourself fully to a dead hang to dismount safely.

t: Lie face-down on an exercise mat with your legs extended and the balls of your feet on the floor, hip-width apart. | Place your hands flat on the floor beside your chest, fingers pointing forward, to support yourself during setup. | Tuck your chin slightly and place your forehead, just below the hairline, flat on the mat — do not roll back onto the crown of your head. | Brace your neck muscles and press through your forehead and the balls of your feet to lift your torso and thighs off the mat. | At the top, your body should form a gentle arc from feet to head with your hips at roughly the same height as your shoulders — avoid letting the hips rise much higher than the head. | Keep your hands lightly hovering near the floor or cross them over your lower back once you feel stable, but keep them within reach for safety. | Hold the position for the prescribed duration, breathing steadily through your nose — do not hold your breath. | To finish a repetition, lower your torso back to the mat under control, leading with your chest, and remove your head last.

t: Stand or sit tall with your spine neutral, shoulders relaxed, and feet hip-width apart. | Gently drop your chin toward your chest, feeling a mild stretch along the back of your neck. | Slowly roll your head to the right, bringing your right ear toward your right shoulder without lifting the shoulder. | Continue the arc by tilting your head back slightly — only as far as is comfortable with no sharp pain. | Keep rolling to the left, bringing your left ear toward your left shoulder in a smooth, continuous motion. | Return to the chin-down position to complete one full circle. | Perform the desired number of slow circles in this direction, then reverse and repeat the same number of circles in the opposite direction.

t: Sit or stand tall with your spine neutral, shoulders relaxed, and feet hip-width apart on the floor. | Relax your jaw and let your mouth close gently so your neck muscles are not braced. | Place your hands loosely in your lap or at your sides — do not use your hands to push or pull your head. | Slowly lift your chin up and away from your chest and begin to tilt your head backward, leading with the top of your skull moving toward the back wall. | Continue the movement until you feel a gentle stretch across the front of your throat and along both sides of your neck — stop well before any point of discomfort or dizziness. | Hold this position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and evenly, allowing the anterior neck muscles to gradually release. | To release, gently bring your head back to neutral by lifting your chin and returning your gaze forward — do not let your head drop forward quickly. | Rest for a breath or two, then repeat for 2–3 rounds as needed.

t: Sit or stand tall with your spine neutral, shoulders relaxed, and chin level with the floor. | Slowly drop your chin toward your chest, letting the weight of your head gently stretch the back of your neck. | From that flexed position, begin to rotate your head slowly to the right, bringing your chin toward your right collarbone. | Pause for 2–3 seconds when you feel a comfortable stretch along the left side and back of your neck. | Slowly rotate back through center — chin still lowered — and continue rotating to the left, bringing your chin toward your left collarbone. | Pause again for 2–3 seconds to feel the stretch along the right side and back of your neck. | Return to center and gently lift your head back to the neutral starting position. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions or hold each end position for a longer duration as needed.

t: Sit or stand tall with your spine long and your shoulders relaxed away from your ears. | Look straight ahead to establish a neutral starting position. | Slowly lower your chin toward your chest, allowing the weight of your head to guide the movement without forcing it. | Place both hands lightly on the back of your head and allow the gentle weight of your arms — not active pressure — to deepen the stretch. | Hold this position and breathe steadily, exhaling to relax further into the stretch. | Hold for 20–30 seconds, feeling the stretch along the back of your neck and upper back. | To release, remove your hands first, then slowly raise your head back to neutral. | Repeat 2–3 times per session, resting a few seconds between each hold.

t: Sit or stand tall with your spine neutral, shoulders relaxed, and feet flat on the floor. | Lower your chin slowly toward your chest until you feel a mild stretch along the back of your neck — hold for two to three seconds. | Return your head to the neutral position. | Gently rotate your chin toward your right shoulder as far as comfortable without straining, feeling the stretch along the left side of your neck. | Hold the rotated position for two to three seconds, breathing steadily. | Return your head to center, then repeat the rotation toward your left shoulder. | Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions, keeping all movements slow and controlled throughout.

t: Sit or stand tall with your spine in a neutral position, shoulders relaxed and pulled slightly back and down. | Begin with a chin tuck: gently draw your chin straight back, as if making a slight double chin, to align your head over your spine. | From the tucked position, slowly tilt your head back by lifting your chin toward the ceiling, allowing your neck to extend gently. | Stop as soon as you feel a mild stretch along the front and sides of your neck — do not force further range of motion. | Keep your mouth closed and your jaw relaxed throughout; avoid letting your mouth drop open as you extend. | Hold the stretched position for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing slowly and allowing the anterior neck muscles to release. | To exit, bring your chin back to neutral slowly and with control — do not let your head drop forward. | Repeat 2 to 3 times per session, resting briefly between holds.

t: Sit upright in a chair or stand with your feet hip-width apart, keeping your spine long and your shoulders relaxed. | Look straight ahead so your ears are roughly stacked over your shoulders as your starting position. | Slowly slide your head forward — as if pushing your chin toward an imaginary wall in front of you — without tilting your chin up or down. Your head should translate forward, not tilt. | Hold the protracted position for 2–3 seconds and notice the gentle stretch along the back of your neck. | Reverse the movement by drawing your head straight back and tucking your chin slightly until your ears are again stacked over your shoulders — you should feel the stretch shift up to the base of your skull. This is the retraction phase. | Hold the retracted position for 2–3 seconds, then return to neutral. | Repeat the forward-and-back cycle for the prescribed number of repetitions, moving slowly and deliberately throughout.

t: Set the reformer to a light or medium spring tension — heavier springs make the return easier, lighter springs increase the challenge on the adductors. | Stand sideways on the reformer with one foot flat on the stationary footbar platform and the other foot flat on the carriage, feet parallel and hip-width apart. | Engage your core, stand tall, and soften the knees slightly so neither leg is locked out. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale as you press the carriage foot outward, sliding your leg away from your body in a controlled arc — stop before your hips begin to tip to one side. | Keep your pelvis level and square throughout the slide; resist any temptation to hike the hip on the moving side. | At the end of the range, pause briefly, then inhale and use your inner thigh of the moving leg to draw the carriage back to the starting position with control. | Complete all reps on one side, then step off carefully and switch sides. | Perform 8–12 repetitions per side for mobility and strength, or 5–8 slow, controlled reps when focusing on balance and stability.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides, and your weight evenly balanced across both feet. | Shift your weight onto your left foot and drive your right knee upward to roughly hip height, flexing the foot so the toes point up. | As your right foot descends, simultaneously drive your left knee upward, mimicking the alternating leg action of running. | Keep a soft bend in the landing knee each time your foot touches down — never lock the knee on contact. | Pump your arms in opposition to your legs: when the right knee rises, the left arm swings forward with the elbow bent at roughly 90 degrees, and vice versa. | Land lightly on the balls of your feet rather than crashing down on your heels, keeping contact time with the floor brief. | Maintain an upright posture with your chest lifted, core gently braced, and gaze forward throughout the movement. | Continue at a steady, sustainable rhythm for the target duration or rep count, breathing rhythmically through your nose and mouth.

t: Set the parallel bars to a width slightly wider than your shoulders. Mount the bars and lock your arms out fully, holding your body upright above them. | Lean your torso forward aggressively, pushing your shoulders into protraction (rounding them forward) and shifting your hips in front of your hands. Your body should form a near-horizontal angle to the floor. | Brace your core and waist hard to hold the forward-tilted position. Keep your legs together and either straight or slightly tucked — do not let your hips sag or pike. | With control, bend your elbows and lower your body downward while maintaining the same forward lean throughout the descent. Your elbows will flare slightly outward. | Lower until your elbows reach roughly 90°, or as deep as your shoulder mobility and strength allow, without losing the planche lean. | Press firmly through the bars to extend your arms back to the starting locked-out position, keeping the forward lean intact throughout the push. | Complete your reps, then carefully return to an upright seated position on the bars before dismounting.

t: Begin from a solid full planche hold: hands flat on the floor shoulder-width apart, arms fully extended, body parallel to the ground with no leg contact. | Engage your core, glutes, and legs to form a single rigid plank; do not allow your hips to rise or sag before initiating the press. | Protract your shoulder blades fully and push the floor away to create maximum scapular spread. | Initiate the press by driving force through your palms and extending through the anterior deltoids, allowing your hips and torso to begin rising while maintaining horizontal body alignment as long as possible. | Continue pressing as your body pivots upward; your shoulders travel back from ahead of your hands until they finish stacked over them. | Finish in a balanced handstand with arms fully locked, body vertical, and shoulders stacked directly over your wrists. | To lower, reverse the movement under control: shift your shoulders forward, allow your body to descend in a slow arc, and resist with your anterior deltoids and triceps the entire way down. | Land back in the full planche position with arms straight and body parallel to the floor, absorbing the load through shoulder protraction rather than elbow bend.

t: Place a stability ball on the floor and kneel behind it. | Walk your hands onto the ball so your forearms or palms rest on top, and extend your legs behind you into a full plank position. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and align your body in a straight line from head to heels. | Keeping your hips level, lift your right hand off the ball and tap the side of the ball firmly. | Return your right hand to the top of the ball and immediately lift your left hand to tap the opposite side. | Continue alternating sides in a controlled rhythm, resisting any rotation or sagging of the hips with each tap. | Breathe steadily throughout — exhale as you tap, inhale as you return. | Complete your target number of reps per side, then step your feet in and return to a kneeling position to finish.

t: Get into a high plank with your hands directly under your shoulders and your feet hip-width apart. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and make your body form a straight line from head to heels. | Shift your weight slightly onto your right hand without letting your hips rotate or drop. | Lift your left arm off the floor, extending it straight in front of you at shoulder height. | Hold for one to two seconds while keeping your hips square to the floor and your spine neutral. | Lower your left hand back to the starting position with control. | Repeat the lift on the right arm, again resisting any rotation through the hips or shoulders. | Continue alternating arms for your target number of reps per side.

t: Set up in a forearm plank: elbows directly under your shoulders, forearms flat on the floor, legs extended behind you, weight on your toes. | WRONG — Pike: Deliberately raise your hips toward the ceiling until your body forms an inverted V. Hold for a moment and notice how tension shifts off your core and onto your shoulders. | WRONG — Sag: Lower your hips until they drop toward the floor. Hold briefly and notice the excessive arch in your lower back and the loss of abdominal tension. | RIGHT — Neutral spine: Return your hips to a level position so your head, shoulders, hips, and heels form a single straight line parallel to the floor. | Brace your core as if preparing to absorb a punch to the stomach, squeeze your glutes lightly, and press your forearms into the floor. | Hold the correct position for 20–60 seconds, breathing steadily without allowing your hips to drift upward or downward. | Finish by dropping your knees to the floor and resting briefly in a child's pose before your next set.

t: Set up in a high plank with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms fully extended, and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and set your hips level — they should not rise or sag at any point during the exercise. | Keep your upper body completely still and your gaze on the floor a few inches ahead of your hands so your neck stays neutral. | Jump both feet out to the sides simultaneously, landing softly on the balls of your feet with a slight bend at the knees. | Immediately jump both feet back together to the starting position, maintaining the same hip height and core brace. | Continue the out-and-in leg movement for the target number of repetitions or time interval. | To finish, step your feet together, hold the plank briefly, then lower to the floor with control or press back into a rest position.

t: Place a folded towel on a smooth, hard floor (hardwood, tile, or laminate). Get into a high plank: hands directly under your shoulders, body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Step both feet onto the towel so they rest side by side and can slide freely across the surface. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and set your spine in a neutral position — no sagging at the hips and no piking upward. | Press actively through your palms and spread your fingers wide to engage the serratus anterior and keep your shoulder blades flat against your rib cage. | Slide both feet out to the sides simultaneously, as far as comfortable, while keeping your torso completely still and your hips level. | Pause briefly at the wide position, feeling tension through the outer hips and obliques. | Slide both feet back together with control, maintaining the rigid plank position throughout. | Repeat the out-and-in motion for the desired number of reps, breathing steadily — exhale as you slide out, inhale as you return.

t: Start on all fours with your hands directly under your shoulders, fingers spread wide and pressing firmly into the floor. | Step your feet back one at a time until your body forms a straight line from head to heels, resting on the balls of your feet. | Lock your elbows fully and push the floor away so your shoulder blades spread slightly apart, engaging the serratus anterior. | Brace your core hard as if bracing for a punch, drawing your navel gently toward your spine without holding your breath. | Squeeze your glutes and press your heels back to keep your hips level — neither sagging toward the floor nor piking up toward the ceiling. | Keep your head in a neutral position, gaze at a spot on the floor about 30 cm in front of your hands. | Breathe steadily in and out while maintaining full-body tension throughout the hold. | When the set is complete, lower your knees to the floor with control.

t: Place a folded towel on a smooth, low-friction surface such as hardwood, tile, or laminate flooring. | Get into a high plank with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms straight, and feet hip-width apart resting on the towel. | Brace your core and squeeze your glutes so your body forms a straight line from head to heels. | Exhale and slide your feet toward your hands by driving your hips up and back, forming an inverted-V shape as your hips rise. | Continue the slide until your hips are as high as your flexibility comfortably allows and your heels are close to your hands. | Pause briefly at the top with your core engaged, arms straight, and head resting between your arms. | Inhale and slide your feet back to the starting plank position under control, resisting the urge to let your hips drop suddenly. | Re-establish the straight-line body position with your core braced before beginning the next rep.

t: Place two dumbbells on the floor shoulder-width apart and get into a high plank position with each hand gripping a dumbbell, wrists neutral, and feet hip-width apart so your body forms a straight line from head to heels. | Brace your core firmly, squeeze your glutes, and set your shoulder blades — this position must stay rigid throughout every rep. | Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor, keeping your elbows at roughly 45° to your torso, until your chest nearly reaches the dumbbells. | Press back up to the starting plank position by fully extending your arms. | Without allowing your hips to rotate or rise, drive one dumbbell up toward your hip by pulling your elbow straight back and squeezing your back at the top of the row. | Lower the dumbbell under control until your arm is fully extended and the dumbbell is back on the floor. | Perform another push-up, then row the opposite arm in the same controlled manner. | Continue alternating the row after each push-up for the target number of reps, then lower both dumbbells to the floor to finish.

t: Place your hands directly under your shoulders and extend your legs behind you into a high plank position, forming a straight line from head to heels. | Engage your core and squeeze your glutes to stabilize the spine before you begin moving. | Jump both feet simultaneously to the right, landing softly with your feet outside your right hand. | Pause for a brief moment to control the landing, keeping your hips level and your shoulders stacked over your wrists. | Jump both feet back to the starting plank position, re-establishing the straight-body alignment. | Immediately jump both feet to the left, landing softly outside your left hand. | Return both feet to center plank to complete one full repetition. | Continue alternating sides for the prescribed number of repetitions or time interval. | Finish by stepping one foot at a time back to center and lowering your knees to the floor to exit the position safely.
