t: Start in a forearm plank: elbows directly under shoulders, forearms flat on the floor, body in a straight line from head to heels. | Brace your core and squeeze your glutes so your hips stay level throughout the movement. | Plant your right hand on the floor where your right elbow was and press your torso up. | Follow with your left hand so you arrive in a high plank (push-up position) with arms fully extended. | Hold the high plank for one count, keeping hips level and core tight. | Lower your right elbow back to the floor, then your left elbow, returning to the forearm plank. | That is one rep. On the next rep, lead with the left hand going up and the left elbow going down. | Continue alternating the leading arm for the desired number of reps or time.

t: Kneel on a soft surface with your knees hip-width apart and the tops of your feet flat on the floor, toes pointing straight back. | Sit your hips back toward your heels so your body weight gently presses the ankles and feet into plantar flexion. | Place your hands on your thighs or the floor beside you for balance and to control how much pressure you apply. | Keep your spine tall and your torso upright rather than hunching forward. | Hold the stretched position for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the front of the shin and ankle to relax. | To deepen the stretch slightly, shift a small amount of additional body weight toward your heels; back off immediately if you feel sharp discomfort in the knee or ankle. | Release by lifting your hips and returning to an upright kneeling position before switching sides if working one leg at a time.

nE: Plantar Flexor And Foot Everter Stretch
nR: Plantar Flexor And Foot Everter Stretch
nH: Plantar Flexor And Foot Everter Stretch
t: Sit on the floor with your legs extended in front of you, or on a chair with the foot to be stretched resting on the opposite knee. | Grasp the top of your foot and toes with both hands, or loop a towel or resistance band around the ball of your foot. | Gently pull your foot toward your shin (dorsiflexion) until you feel a stretch along the back of your calf. | While maintaining that dorsiflexion, slowly turn the sole of your foot inward (inversion) so it faces slightly toward the midline of your body. | Hold the combined dorsiflexion and inversion position until you feel a stretch along the outer lower leg and lateral ankle — the peroneal muscles. | Breathe steadily and relax the foot and ankle muscles throughout the hold. | Hold for 20–30 seconds, then slowly release the foot back to a neutral position. | Repeat on the other side, performing 2–3 holds per foot.

t: Sit on the floor with your legs extended in front of you, or sit on a chair with your feet flat on the ground and your working leg crossed over your opposite knee. | Take hold of your foot with both hands — wrap one hand around the heel and place the other across the top of the foot. | Gently pull your toes and forefoot upward toward your shin to dorsiflex the ankle, feeling a stretch along the back of the calf. | While maintaining that dorsiflexion, slowly rotate the sole of your foot outward (eversion) so the bottom of your foot faces away from your body. | Hold the combined position — ankle dorsiflexed and foot everted — for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and letting the muscles relax with each exhale. | Release the stretch gradually, return the foot to a neutral position, and repeat on the same side for 2–3 rounds before switching feet.

t: Set up the Roman chair so the pad sits just below your hip bones, leaving your upper body free to hinge forward without restriction. | Hook your ankles under the foot pads and stand upright, spine neutral, core braced, and gaze directed slightly forward. | Hold a weight plate against your chest with both hands, pressing it close to your sternum and keeping it there throughout the movement. | Hinge at the hips and lower your torso slowly toward the floor until your body is roughly perpendicular to the ground. | Pause briefly at the bottom without rounding your lower back, keeping tension in the posterior chain. | Squeeze your glutes and drive your hips into the pad as you raise your torso back to the starting position. | Stop when your body forms a straight line from head to heels — do not hyperextend past neutral at the top. | Complete your reps under control, resetting your brace between reps if needed.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your arms alongside your torso, palms pressing down into the floor. | Engage your core and exhale as you lift both legs off the floor, bringing them to a 90-degree angle above your hips. | Continue to press your palms into the floor and slowly lower your legs over your head, reaching your feet toward the floor behind your head. | Keep your legs as straight as possible, using your quadriceps to hold the knees extended while the hamstrings lengthen. | Once your toes touch or approach the floor, interlace your fingers behind your back and press your arms into the mat to create stability. | Keep your neck long and your gaze toward your chest, and hold the pose, breathing steadily for 5–10 slow breaths. | To exit, unclasp your hands, place your palms back on the mat, and slowly roll your spine back down to the floor one vertebra at a time. | Lower your legs with control back to the starting position and rest briefly in a neutral supine position.

t: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and hands on your hips or clasped in front of your chest. | Step your right foot wide to the side — roughly two to three feet from your left foot — keeping both feet pointing forward. | Shift your weight to the right, bend your right knee, and push your hips back to lower into a side lunge. t: Stand with your back flat against a wall and your feet shoulder-width apart, positioned about 60–70 cm from the wall. | Slide your back down the wall until your hips and knees are both at roughly 90 degrees, entering a wall-sit position. | Keep your chest up, core braced, and both feet fully planted on the floor. | Hold the bottom position for 1–2 seconds to establish stability. | Drive explosively through your heels and the balls of your feet, pushing off the ground to jump straight up. | Extend your knees and ankles fully at the peak of the jump, letting your back slide up the wall rather than pushing your hips away from it. | Land softly with slightly bent knees and immediately slide back down the wall into the squat position. | Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions without losing contact with the wall between reps.

t: Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees fully extended, and arms relaxed at your sides. | Place a piece of tape or a reference marker at the base of your feet so you have a consistent measurement point. | Take a slow, deep breath in to lengthen the spine before beginning the movement. | Exhale gradually and hinge forward at the hips, lowering both hands toward the floor without bending your knees. | Reach as far as possible in a controlled manner — do not bounce or force the stretch. | Hold the lowest position for two to three seconds and note where your fingertips reach relative to the floor or reference line. | Return slowly to the upright position by engaging your core and stacking the spine vertebra by vertebra. | Rest for thirty seconds, then repeat the movement two more times. | Record the best of three attempts as your flexibility score, measured in centimeters above or below the floor reference.

t: Sit tall in a chair or stand upright with your spine neutral and shoulders relaxed. | Interlace your fingers and place both palms flat against the back of your head. | Keep your chin level and your gaze forward so your neck stays in a neutral position. | Gently press the back of your head into your hands as if you are trying to extend your neck backward. | Resist firmly with your hands so that your head does not actually move — this is the isometric contraction. | Apply only moderate, controlled force; the neck should feel working tension, never sharp pain. | Hold the contraction for 5–10 seconds while breathing steadily — do not hold your breath. | Release the pressure gradually, rest a few seconds, then repeat for the desired number of sets.

t: Sit on the floor with both legs extended straight in front of you. | Loop the rope around the ball of one foot, holding one end of the rope in each hand. | Sit tall with your back straight and your target leg fully extended. | Gently pull both ends of the rope toward you to dorsiflex your foot, drawing your toes back toward your shin. | Hold the stretched position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and avoiding any jerking or bouncing. | Slowly release the tension on the rope and allow your foot to return to a neutral position. | Repeat for the desired number of holds, then switch to the opposite foot.

t: Stand with feet hip-width apart, barbell over mid-foot. Grip the bar just outside your legs with a double-overhand grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart. | Hinge at the hips and bend your knees forward until your shins touch the bar, chest up, back flat, and shoulders positioned slightly in front of the bar. This is your starting position. | Begin the first pull by pressing the floor away with your legs, keeping your hips and shoulders rising at the same rate and the bar moving in a straight, close path up your shins. | As the bar passes your knees, sweep it back into your hips by extending your knees slightly and shifting your torso toward vertical — this loads the hips for the explosive second pull. | Drive the second pull by violently extending your hips, knees, and ankles simultaneously. Shrug your shoulders hard and allow your elbows to pull high and wide as the bar travels upward. | Once the bar reaches chest height and you have generated maximum upward momentum, pull yourself under the bar by bending your knees into a quarter-squat and rotating your elbows forward rapidly. | Receive the bar on your front deltoids and upper chest in the front rack position — elbows high, upper arms parallel to the floor, wrists extended. Your feet may move slightly outward as you catch. | Stabilize in the quarter-squat with the bar under control, then stand fully upright to complete the rep. | Lower the bar back to the floor under control — either by reversing through the rack and hinge positions or by a controlled drop if bumper plates and appropriate flooring are in use.

t: Stand facing a fixed horizontal bar set at roughly hip to waist height, or set up rings or a suspension trainer at the same height. | Grip the bar with both hands shoulder-width apart, palms facing down, and walk your feet back until your body forms a straight diagonal line from heels to head with arms extended. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and keep your body rigid — this position is your starting plank. | Initiate the movement by pushing the bar away from your torso while simultaneously hinging slightly at the hips, driving your chest toward the floor in a controlled arc. | Allow your elbows to bend naturally and your shoulder blades to protract as you reach the bottom of the arc, feeling a stretch across your lats and chest. | Reverse the motion by pulling the bar back toward your hips and pressing your body back up to the starting diagonal, engaging the lats and pecs together through the return arc. | At the top, fully extend your arms and re-establish the rigid plank position before beginning the next repetition. | Complete the set, then step your feet forward to safely release tension and return to standing.

t: Load the power sled to an appropriate weight and attach a single handle or strap to one side of the sled's upright post. | Stand behind the sled and grip the handle with both hands on the same side, keeping your arms extended in front of your torso. | Adopt a hip-width athletic stance and hinge forward slightly at the hips so your torso is angled toward the sled. | Brace your core firmly to resist the rotational pull created by the off-center attachment point. | Drive through the balls of your feet, extending your hips to push the sled forward with your first step. | Walk forward with short, powerful strides, maintaining consistent foot contact and pushing through each step. | Keep your chest up, shoulders square, and resist any twisting of the torso throughout the movement. | Continue for the prescribed distance or time, then stop, reposition, and repeat with the handle on the opposite side to balance the anti-rotation stimulus.

t: Load the power sled with the desired weight and position it on a turf or smooth surface. | Face away from the sled and place both hands on the upright handles at hip height, gripping firmly. | Step backward until your arms are nearly fully extended and you feel light tension against the sled. | Adopt a slight forward lean through your torso, keeping your spine neutral and your chest up. | Drive one foot back into the ground, fully extending the knee and pushing through the ball of that foot. | Step the opposite foot back and repeat in a smooth, alternating walking pattern, maintaining constant sled movement. | Keep each stride short and controlled — approximately hip-width apart — to preserve knee tracking over the toes. | Breathe steadily throughout: exhale as each foot pushes, inhale during the recovery step. | At the end of the set, bring both feet together and ease the sled to a stop before releasing the handles.

t: Load the sled with an appropriate weight and attach a waist harness or hand straps so the sled trails directly behind you. | Face away from the sled and step into a wide, batwing stance with your feet 1.5–2 times hip-width apart and toes turned out 30–45°. | Brace your core and hinge slightly at the hips so your torso leans forward 15–30°, keeping your chest up and your spine neutral throughout. | Sink your hips into a quarter- to half-squat position, ensuring your knees track over your toes in line with the wide stance. | Drive powerfully through the balls of your feet to push the ground away and drag the sled forward, maintaining the batwing leg position as you step. | Take short, controlled steps and reset the wide stance after each stride to keep the thighs under continuous load. | Continue driving forward for the programmed distance, then stand tall, step out of the harness, and allow the sled to come to rest.

t: Attach a pulling harness or waist belt to the power sled's tow strap and load the sled with an appropriate weight. | Put the harness on and step far enough away from the sled so the strap is taut but not pulling you backward when you stand upright. | Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, core braced, and shoulders back. | Step one foot backward, placing the ball of that foot on the ground approximately two to three feet behind you. | Lower your rear knee toward the floor by bending both knees simultaneously, stopping when the rear knee is just above or lightly touches the ground. | Keep your front shin as vertical as possible and your torso upright throughout the descent. | Drive through the heel of your front foot to stand back up, pulling against the sled's resistance as you return to the starting position. | Complete all reps on one leg before switching, or alternate legs each rep depending on the protocol. | At the end of the set, step forward toward the sled to release strap tension before removing the harness.

t: Attach a hip harness around your waist or grip the sled handles, then position yourself facing away from the loaded power sled with the straps or handles taut. | Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, shoulders back, and core braced to create a stable base before the first step. | Step one foot backward — far enough that when your back knee descends, your front shin stays close to vertical. | Lower your back knee toward the ground in a controlled descent, stopping 1–2 inches above the floor as your body weight pulls the sled forward. | Drive through your front heel to return to a standing position, bringing your feet back to hip-width apart. | Alternate legs each rep, or complete all reps on one side before switching — follow your program's prescribed pattern. | Maintain an upright torso and level hips throughout; avoid twisting toward the stepping leg. | After your final rep, step toward the sled to release tension before setting down the handles or unclipping the harness.

t: Attach long straps or handles to the power sled's harness point and load the sled with an appropriate amount of weight plates. | Stand facing the sled at the far end of the straps with your feet hip-width apart, arms extended in front of you holding the handles with a neutral or overhand grip. | Take up the slack in the straps so there is light tension on the sled before you begin. | Brace your core, keep your chest tall, and step one foot back into a reverse lunge, lowering your rear knee toward the floor. | As you descend into the lunge, simultaneously row both handles toward your hips or lower chest by driving your elbows back behind you. | Pause at the bottom of the lunge with your front thigh roughly parallel to the floor and the handles pulled fully in, squeezing your shoulder blades together. | Push through your front foot to stand back up, straightening the knee and hip, while returning your arms to the extended starting position under control. | Alternate legs each rep or complete all reps on one side before switching, depending on your training goal. | Set the handles down safely once the set is complete and step away from the sled.

t: Attach two handles or loops to the sled's strap anchors so you have one grip point for each hand. | Load the sled with an appropriate amount of weight and position yourself facing the sled at the far end of the straps. | Hinge forward slightly at the hips — roughly 15–30 degrees — so your torso is angled toward the sled and your upper arms are close to your sides. | Grip both handles with a neutral or overhand grip, elbows bent and hands near your chest at the start of each rep. | Brace your core and keep your spine neutral throughout the set. | Drive your hands back and downward by straightening your elbows fully, pushing against the strap tension and drawing the sled toward you. | Pause briefly at full elbow extension to maximise triceps activation. | Return your hands to the starting position under control, allowing the sled to settle before the next rep. | Complete all reps for the set, then release the handles and step clear of the sled safely.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides, and your core lightly braced. | Begin jogging in place, then exaggerate the knee lift so each thigh rises to at least parallel with the floor on every stride. | As one knee drives up, swing the opposite arm forward to shoulder height to maintain balance and rhythm. | Land each foot on the ball of your foot rather than your heel, allowing the ankle to absorb impact softly before your heel briefly kisses the floor. | Keep the contact time short: spring back off the ground immediately, aiming for a light, bouncy feel rather than heavy stomping. | Maintain an upright torso — do not lean back or hunch forward; keep your chest open and gaze forward. | Control your breathing by matching your inhale and exhale to the rhythm of your strides. | Continue for the target duration or rep count, then slow gradually to a jog-in-place and return to standing.

t: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and a slight bend in the knees, or sit upright on a bench with feet flat on the floor. | Bring both palms together in front of your chest at sternum height, fingers pointing upward and elbows bent and angled down. | Press your palms firmly against each other to create isometric tension through the shoulders and chest. | Brace your core and keep your spine neutral so your lower back does not arch. | While maintaining palm-to-palm pressure, push your hands upward and forward in a controlled arc until your arms are fully extended overhead. | Hold the top position for one count with palms still pressed together and arms straight. | Lower your hands back down along the same arc, keeping continuous palm pressure throughout the descent. | Return to the starting position at chest height and pause briefly before the next repetition. | Complete the desired number of reps, then relax the arms and release the palm pressure.

t: Stand with your feet slightly wider than shoulder-width apart and toes turned out at roughly 45 degrees. | Bring your palms together at chest height in a prayer position (thumbs lightly touching your sternum). | Take a breath in, then on the exhale begin to lower your hips straight down toward the floor, keeping your chest tall and spine neutral. | Continue descending until your hips drop below knee level and your elbows are inside your knees. | Press your elbows gently outward against the inner thighs to encourage the knees to track over the toes and open the hips wider. | Keep your heels flat on the floor; if they rise, widen your stance slightly or place a folded mat under your heels for support. | Lift your chest, lengthen through the crown of your head, and breathe deeply, relaxing deeper into the stretch on each exhale. | Hold the position for 30–60 seconds, continuing to breathe slowly and evenly. | To exit, press through your heels, engage your glutes, and slowly rise back to standing.

t: Set the preacher bench to a height where the upper arms rest flat on the pad with the armpits just clearing the top edge. | Load the EZ barbell with a light-to-moderate weight and grip the inner angled grips with an underhand (supinated) hold. | Rest both upper arms on the pad, let the bar hang at arm's length, and feel what the wrong position is: allow your wrists to bend backward (extend) under the bar's weight so the knuckles point toward the floor — notice the strain this creates. | Now actively correct your wrists: flex them very slightly or hold them neutral so they stay in line with your forearms and the bar sits across the base of your fingers rather than your palm. | Brace your core, keep your shoulders down, and maintain this neutral wrist position throughout the set. | Curl the bar upward by bending at the elbows, driving your forearms toward your upper arms while keeping the wrists locked in the neutral position — do not let them collapse back into extension as the weight increases. | Pause briefly at the top when your forearms are near vertical and confirm that your wrists are still neutral. | Lower the bar slowly and under control back to full elbow extension, continuing to hold the wrists neutral during the descent. | Complete the set, then re-check your wrist position on the last few reps, as fatigue is when the wrists are most likely to drift back into the wrong position.

t: Stand with your feet at hip-width, toes turned out slightly — the same foot position you use for your clean or snatch receiving stance. | Raise both arms directly overhead into your receiving position: shoulder-width apart for the snatch, or just outside shoulder-width for the clean and jerk. | Actively push your hands upward, engaging your deltoids, upper back, and triceps so your arms are under tension — not just held up passively. | Begin to lower yourself into a quarter to half squat, keeping your torso as upright as possible and your heels flat on the floor. | As you descend, drive your hands harder upward — press yourself under the imaginary bar rather than letting yourself fall. Think: push the ceiling while the floor pushes back. | Reach the bottom of your squat with both elbows fully locked out, wrists neutral, and shoulder blades actively engaged upward. | Hold the locked-out overhead position for 1–2 seconds, reinforcing proprioception and stability in the receiving position. | Stand back up while maintaining the overhead lockout, then lower your arms in a controlled manner before resetting for the next rep.

t: Lie on your right side on a flat surface with your hips and knees bent to roughly 90 degrees. | Stack your knees and keep your head resting on your right arm or a folded towel. | Bring your left knee forward toward the floor in front of you, letting it drop as far as is comfortable without lifting your right hip. | Reach your left arm straight up toward the ceiling. | Slowly rotate your left shoulder back toward the floor behind you, allowing your thoracic spine to rotate while your hips stay as stable as possible. | Let your left arm rest on the floor behind you, or as close to the floor as your range of motion allows. | Hold the position for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the gluteus medius and obliques to release with each exhale. | Return to the starting position, then repeat on the opposite side. | Perform 2 to 3 holds per side.

t: Kneel upright on a mat with your knees hip-width apart and your toes pointing behind you. Interlace your fingers and place both hands behind your head (prisoner position). Keep your chest tall and core braced throughout. | Step your right foot forward, planting it flat on the floor so your right knee is directly above your right ankle — you are now in a half-kneeling position. | Drive through your right heel and left toes to push your hips forward and upward, bringing your left foot up beside your right foot so you are standing fully upright. | Pause briefly at the top with hips extended, glutes squeezed, and hands still behind your head. | Reverse the movement by stepping your left foot back and lowering your left knee to the floor with control. | Then step your right foot back and lower your right knee to the floor, returning to the starting kneeling position. | That is one repetition. On the next rep, lead with the opposite foot (left foot steps forward first) to train both sides equally. | Continue alternating the leading leg for the desired number of repetitions or complete all reps on one side before switching.

t: Lie on your back with your knees bent at roughly 90° and your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. | Interlace your fingers and place your hands behind your head, with your elbows flared wide and pointing toward the ceiling — this is the prisoner position. | Brace your core by drawing your navel gently toward your spine, and press your lower back lightly into the floor. | Exhale and curl your head and shoulders off the floor, leading with your chest rather than your chin. | Continue raising your torso until it is at roughly 30–45° from the floor — do not sit all the way up. | Hold the top position for one count, keeping your elbows wide and your chin neutral (not tucked hard or jutting forward). | Inhale and lower your torso back to the floor under control, vertebra by vertebra, until your shoulder blades touch the floor. | Reset your brace and repeat for the target number of reps.

t: Position two sturdy, heavy chairs back-to-back or side by side with a gap between them wide enough to fit your torso. The chair backs or seats you grip must be at a height that allows your arms to be fully extended when you hang below them with bent knees. | Stand between the chairs and grip the top of each chair back (or the seat edges) with an overhand grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart. Test that both chairs are stable and will not slide before loading your full bodyweight. | Lower yourself until your arms are fully extended and lift your feet off the floor by bending your knees to roughly 90 degrees, crossing your ankles if that helps keep your legs tucked. | Brace your core, depress your shoulder blades, and pull yourself upward by driving your elbows down and back toward your hips. | Continue pulling until your chin clears the level of your hands or your chest approaches the grip point — whichever range your shoulder mobility and chair height allow. | Pause briefly at the top with your shoulder blades fully retracted and depressed. | Lower yourself with control over 2–3 seconds until your arms are fully extended again. | That is one repetition. Keep your knees bent and feet off the floor for the entire set. | Complete the desired number of repetitions, then carefully place your feet back on the floor before releasing the chairs.

t: Place two dumbbells side by side on the floor with their handles parallel and close together — roughly 6–10 inches apart, well inside shoulder-width — hex dumbbells are ideal because they will not roll. | Kneel behind the dumbbells, grip both handles firmly with a neutral (palms facing each other) wrist position, and step your feet back into a high plank so your body forms a straight line from head to heels. | Position yourself so the handles sit under your upper chest with your wrists stacked over them, hands roughly 6–10 inches apart and just inside your shoulder line. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and tuck your elbows so they point back toward your hips rather than flaring to the sides. | Inhale and lower your chest in a controlled manner toward the dumbbells, keeping your elbows tracking close to your torso throughout the descent. | Descend until your chest is just above or lightly touches the handles, feeling a stretch through the triceps and chest at the bottom. | Press forcefully through both dumbbell handles to drive your body back to the starting position, exhaling as you push. | Fully extend the elbows at the top without locking them aggressively, and reset your brace before the next repetition. | Complete the desired number of repetitions, then lower your knees to the floor in a controlled manner to dismount safely.

t: Place a stability ball on the floor and kneel behind it to set your starting position. | Place one hand flat on top of the stability ball and the other hand on the floor, spacing your hands roughly shoulder-width apart so one arm is elevated. | Step your feet back into a full push-up position, forming a straight line from head to heels with your core braced. | Squeeze your glutes and engage your abs to prevent your hips from sagging or rotating toward the ball side. | Lower your chest toward the floor by bending both elbows, keeping the elbow of the hand on the ball tucked at roughly a 45° angle to your torso. | Descend until your chest is roughly level with the hand on the ball, or until you reach your full comfortable range of motion. | Press firmly through both hands to extend your arms and return to the starting position. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch so your other hand is on the stability ball and repeat.

t: Start in a high plank position with your hands shoulder-width apart, arms fully extended, and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows at roughly a 45° angle to your torso. | Press explosively back up to the high plank position, fully extending your arms. | Immediately push your hips up and back, forming an inverted V (pike position) while keeping your arms and legs as straight as possible. | At the top of the pike, lift your right hand off the floor and reach across to touch your left foot or left ankle. | Return your hand to the floor, lower your hips back to the high plank position, and brace your core. | Perform another push-up, pike again, and this time reach your left hand to touch your right foot. | Continue alternating sides for the desired number of reps or time.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your arms at your sides. | Hinge at the hips, bend your knees, and place both hands on the floor just outside your feet. | Jump or step your feet back simultaneously so you land in a high plank — hands directly under your shoulders, body in a straight line from head to heels. | Perform one push-up: lower your chest to the floor by bending your elbows, then press back up to the high plank position. | From the top of the push-up, jump both feet out wide (like the bottom of a jumping jack) and then immediately jump them back together — this is the plank jack. | Jump or step your feet forward toward your hands, returning to the low squat position. | Drive through your legs and swing your arms overhead to explode into a vertical jump, fully extending your body at the top. | Land softly with bent knees to absorb the impact, and immediately lower back into the starting position for the next rep.

t: Stand behind your mat and decide on your hand-placement width — directly under your shoulders, fingers pointing forward or slightly outward. | Place your hands on the floor at the chosen width, then step both feet back until your body forms a straight line from head to heel — this is the correct plank start. | Check that your hips are neither sagging toward the floor nor piked up toward the ceiling; your spine should be neutral throughout. | Squeeze your glutes and brace your core as if bracing for a punch, locking the trunk into a single rigid unit. | Press the floor away with your palms so your shoulders are slightly protracted (pushed apart) rather than collapsing between your shoulder blades. | Align your head with your spine — chin slightly tucked, gaze directed a few inches in front of your hands, not straight down or craned upward. | Verify your elbows are fully extended but not hyperextended, with arms vertical when viewed from the side. | Take a breath in through the nose, hold it to reinforce spinal stiffness (Valsalva), and you are in the correct start position — ready to lower into the push-up. | For the WRONG position contrast: notice how a sagging lower back, flared elbows, raised hips, or a forward-jutting chin each compromise alignment — consciously avoid these before beginning any set.

t: Set up in a high plank position with your hands flat on the floor, slightly wider than shoulder-width, wrists under your shoulders, and feet hip-width apart. | Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line from head to heels before beginning any movement. | Inhale and lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows at roughly a 45-degree angle to your torso. | Lower until your chest nearly touches the floor, pausing briefly without collapsing your hips or arching your lower back. | Exhale and press explosively through your hands to return to the top of the push-up position. | Without pausing, use that momentum to pike your hips upward, shifting your weight onto one hand while lifting the other arm across your body toward the opposite foot. | Touch or reach as close as possible to your opposite foot, keeping both legs as straight as you can through the pike. | Return your hand to the floor and lower your hips back to a straight plank position — this is one rep. | Perform the next rep and reach with the other hand, alternating the toe touch side each rep.

t: Place the push-up handles shoulder-width apart on a firm, non-slip surface with the grips parallel or angled slightly outward. | Grip the handles firmly and step into a high plank position: arms fully extended, hands under your shoulders, body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Squeeze your glutes, brace your core, and tuck your hips slightly to prevent your lower back from sagging. | Inhale and lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows at roughly a 45° angle to your torso — not flared straight out to the sides. | Continue lowering until your chest passes the level of the handles, taking advantage of the increased range of motion the bars provide. | Pause briefly at the bottom without resting your chest on the floor, keeping tension in your chest and shoulders. | Exhale and press through the handles, driving the floor away until your arms are fully extended at the top. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, maintaining a rigid plank position throughout every rep.

t: Place a sturdy, non-rolling chair on a flat surface and position yourself in front of it. | Place both hands on the front edge of the chair seat, slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, with fingers pointing forward. | Walk your feet back until your body forms a straight line from head to heels, with arms fully extended and core braced. | Squeeze your glutes and tighten your core to keep your hips level and your spine neutral throughout the movement. | Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the chair seat in a controlled manner, keeping your elbows at roughly a 45-degree angle to your torso. | Lower until your chest nearly touches the edge of the chair, then pause briefly at the bottom. | Press through your palms to push your body back up to the starting position, fully extending your arms without locking your elbows. | Complete the desired number of repetitions while maintaining a rigid, plank-like body position throughout.

t: Stand upright with your feet shoulder-width apart and hold a PVC pipe horizontally behind your back with both hands, palms facing away from your body. | Position your arms so the pipe rests across the back of your hips, with your elbows slightly bent and your grip about shoulder-width or slightly wider. | Brace your core lightly and keep your chest up and your shoulder blades gently retracted throughout the movement. | Slowly pull the pipe upward and away from your body by externally rotating both shoulders simultaneously, keeping your elbows close to your sides. | Continue lifting the pipe as high as your mobility allows without forcing the movement or shrugging your shoulders toward your ears. | Hold the top position for one to two seconds, feeling the contraction in your rotator cuff muscles. | Lower the pipe back down to the starting position in a controlled manner. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, moving smoothly through your full pain-free range of motion.

t: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and hold a PVC pipe with a grip slightly wider than shoulder-width. | Bring the pipe to the front rack position: elbows raised to shoulder height, pipe resting across the front of your shoulders and upper chest. | Push your elbows up as high as possible while keeping the pipe in contact with your shoulders — do not let it drift forward. | With elbows raised, gently pull the ends of the pipe apart as if trying to widen it, creating outward tension. | Begin to squat or hinge slightly at the hips to load the stretch, keeping your chest up and your upper back engaged. | Hold the end position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the shoulder and thoracic tissues to relax into the stretch. | Lower your elbows slowly to release tension, then return to the starting position. | Repeat for 2–3 sets, focusing on progressively raising the elbows higher with each hold.

t: Stand with your feet hip-width apart, toes pointing forward or slightly out, and place the stick across your upper traps — not your neck. | Grip the stick with both hands at a comfortable width outside your shoulders to keep it stable throughout the movement. | Brace your core lightly, maintain a neutral spine, and unlock your knees with a soft bend of about 15–20°. | Initiate the movement by pushing your hips straight back, not by bending your knees or rounding your lower back. | Hinge forward until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor, or until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings — whichever comes first. | Pause for a moment at the bottom, keeping your back flat and the stick level across your shoulders. | Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return to the upright starting position. | Reset your brace and repeat for the target number of reps.

t: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and toes pointing straight ahead or slightly out. | Hold a PVC stick (or dowel) vertically behind your back, gripping it with one hand at your lower back and the other behind your head. | Position the stick so it maintains three points of contact: the back of your head, between your shoulder blades, and your tailbone (sacrum). | Brace your core lightly, set your shoulders back and down, and keep your chest up before you move. | Initiate the movement by pushing your hips back — not by bending your knees — while keeping both feet flat on the floor. | Continue hinging until your torso approaches parallel to the floor, or until your hamstrings pull tight, whichever comes first. | Throughout the descent, verify that all three contact points remain on the stick and that your shins stay close to vertical. | Pause briefly at the bottom, then drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return to a tall standing position. | Reset the stick contact points between reps before beginning the next repetition.

t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart or slightly wider, toes turned out 15–30 degrees. | Hold the PVC pipe with a wide snatch-width grip — hands well outside shoulder-width — and press it overhead until your arms are fully extended. | Rotate your shoulders outward to engage your upper back and pull the pipe apart slightly to create tension, keeping it directly above or just behind the crown of your head. | Brace your core, take a breath, and keep your chest tall before beginning the descent. | Push your knees out in line with your toes and sit your hips back and down simultaneously, descending into a full squat until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor. | Keep the pipe locked out overhead throughout the descent — do not let your arms drift forward or your elbows bend. | At the bottom, pause briefly to confirm your heels are flat, your chest is upright, and the pipe remains stacked above your feet. | Drive through your full foot to stand, keeping your knees tracking over your toes and the pipe locked out until you reach full hip and knee extension. | Reset your breath and brace before each rep.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and hold a PVC pipe in front of your thighs using a wide overhand grip — hands spaced well outside shoulder width. | Brace your core lightly and keep your elbows soft but not deeply bent throughout the movement. | Begin the forward pass by raising the pipe upward in a smooth arc, keeping your arms as straight as comfortably possible. | Continue the arc overhead, allowing your shoulders to rotate naturally as the pipe passes above your head. | Lower the pipe behind your back until it rests against your glutes or upper hamstrings, maintaining control throughout. | Pause briefly at the bottom of the behind-back position, then reverse the arc to bring the pipe back overhead and down to the starting position in front of your thighs. | That is one repetition. Perform 8–15 controlled reps, adjusting grip width as needed to complete the full range of motion.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, then step your right foot forward about 3–4 feet and your left foot back, keeping both feet flat on the floor. | Angle your back (left) foot out to roughly 45° to give your hips a stable base, and square your hips as much as possible toward the front of the mat. | Place your hands on your hips and draw your shoulder blades down and back to lengthen your spine. | On an inhale, grow tall through the crown of your head, creating as much length in the torso as possible. | On an exhale, hinge at the hips — not the waist — and fold your torso forward over your front (right) leg, keeping your back flat. | Lower as far as your hamstring flexibility allows: rest your hands on your shin, ankle, the floor beside your foot, or on blocks for support. | Hold the position for 5–10 slow, steady breaths, relaxing deeper into the stretch with each exhale. | To come out, engage your core, press through both feet, and rise back up on an inhale with a flat back. | Step your feet together, then repeat on the opposite side with the left foot forward.

t: Lie face-down on a flat surface with your legs extended and your forehead resting on your free hand or a folded towel. | Keep your hips pressed evenly into the floor and your core lightly engaged so your lower back stays neutral. | Bend your right knee, bringing your right heel toward your right glute. | Reach back with your right hand and grasp the top of your right foot or your ankle. | Gently pull your heel closer to your glute until you feel a firm stretch along the front of your right thigh — do not force the movement. | Hold the position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and allowing the muscle to relax into the stretch. | Release your foot, straighten your right leg, and return to the starting position. | Repeat on the left side: bend the left knee, grasp the left foot or ankle with the left hand, and hold for 20–30 seconds. | Complete 2–3 rounds per side, resting briefly between rounds.

t: Anchor the resistance band at a low point — a door anchor near the floor, a rack post, or a sturdy fixed object. | Face the anchor, stand roughly 2–3 feet away, and grip one end of the band in each hand with a neutral grip (palms facing each other). | Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is at roughly 45 degrees, keeping your back flat and core braced. | Let your arms hang straight toward the anchor point with light tension already in the band at the start. | Drive both arms back simultaneously, pulling the band alongside your hips in a sweeping arc — like the arm push of a cross-country skier. | Squeeze your lats and rear deltoids at the end range, with your arms fully extended behind your hips. | Slowly return your arms to the start position over 2–3 seconds, maintaining hip hinge and spine neutrality. | Complete all reps, then stand upright. Adjust your distance from the anchor to increase or decrease resistance.

t: Loop a resistance band around both ankles or just above both knees, depending on where you want to feel the most tension. | Stand with your feet slightly wider than hip-width apart so the band is already under mild tension. | Sink into an athletic position: soft knees, hips pushed slightly back, chest tall, and core braced. | Initiate the drill by stepping laterally with your lead foot, moving it out about shoulder-width. | Quickly follow with your trail foot, bringing your feet back to the starting width — do not let your feet come together completely, as this releases band tension. | Continue stepping rapidly in the same direction for the target number of steps or distance. | Keep your weight centered and low throughout; avoid bouncing upright between steps. | After completing reps or distance in one direction, reset and repeat leading with the opposite foot. | Maintain control on the final step, returning to a stable athletic stance before resting.

t: Anchor a resistance band securely at a low point in front of you, such as a door anchor near the floor or a sturdy post. | Lie face down in a prone position with your arms extended forward, holding the band with both hands shoulder-width apart. | Press your toes into the floor and brace your core to create a stable body position, keeping your hips level throughout. | Retract your shoulder blades and lift your chest slightly off the floor, maintaining a neutral spine. | Walk your right hand outward to the side against the band's resistance, keeping your elbow soft and arm relatively straight. | Follow immediately by walking your left hand outward in the same direction, advancing your hand position like a spider crawling. | Continue crawling your hands for the prescribed number of steps or distance, feeling the band tension increase as you move. | Reverse the motion by walking your hands back toward center in a controlled manner, resisting the band as it pulls you forward. | Return to the starting position and reset before beginning the next repetition.

nR: Resistance Band Split Jump with Single Arm Row
nH: Resistance Band Split Jump with Single Arm Row
t: Anchor a resistance band at hip-to-chest height to a stable post or rack. Stand facing the anchor, feet together, and grasp the band in one hand with your arm fully extended and light tension already in the band. | Set your distance from the anchor so the band is taut but not pulling you forward. This is your starting position. | Explosively jump upward, scissoring your legs in the air, and land in a split stance — one foot forward, one back — with both knees soft and bent to absorb impact. | At the moment your feet contact the ground, drive your elbow straight back and row the band toward your lower chest, squeezing your back at the end of the pull. | Hold the row for one count at the bottom of the split, keeping your torso upright and chest tall. | Push off both feet explosively to jump again, simultaneously straightening your rowing arm back to full extension as you leave the ground. | While airborne, switch your legs so the opposite foot lands forward. Land again with soft, bent knees in the new split stance. | Row again as you land, completing one rep on each side. Continue alternating legs and rowing for the prescribed time or rep count, keeping a steady rhythm throughout.

nE: Resistance Band Split Squat with Horizontal Pallof Hold
nR: Resistance Band Split Squat with Horizontal Pallof Hold
nH: Resistance Band Split Squat with Horizontal Pallof Hold
t: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to a stable post, rack upright, or cable column. Stand perpendicular to the anchor point — the anchor should be directly to one side of you. | Grasp the band with both hands and step laterally away from the anchor until there is firm tension in the band. This is your starting position for setting up the Pallof hold. | Step one foot forward and one foot back into a split squat stance, keeping your feet roughly hip-width apart side to side for balance. The front foot should be flat; the back foot balanced on the ball. | Press both arms straight out in front of your chest at shoulder height, elbows fully extended and hands together — this is the horizontal Pallof hold position. The band will pull you toward the anchor; brace your waist to resist it. | Keeping your arms extended and your torso upright and square, inhale and slowly lower your back knee toward the floor, descending in a controlled split squat. | Stop just before your back knee touches the ground, then press through your front foot to drive back up to the starting position. Keep your arms extended and resist any rotation throughout the movement. | Complete all reps on this side while maintaining the Pallof hold, then lower your arms and rest briefly. | Switch sides — reposition so the anchor is on your opposite side and the opposite leg leads — and repeat the same number of reps to balance the work.

t: Place a folded towel on a smooth, low-friction floor surface and lie flat on your back with your arms at your sides for stability. | Bend your knees to roughly 90 degrees and position both heels on the center of the towel, hip-width apart. | Press through your heels and brace your core to lift your hips off the floor, forming a straight line from shoulders to knees. | Keeping your hips elevated, slowly slide both heels outward along the floor, allowing your legs to extend and your hips to lower in a controlled descent. | Stop the slide when your legs are nearly fully extended and your hips are just above or lightly touching the floor. | Dig your heels into the towel and contract your hamstrings to curl both heels back toward your glutes, simultaneously driving your hips back up. | Return to the starting bridge position with hips fully elevated and knees at 90 degrees. | Pause briefly at the top, squeeze your glutes and hamstrings, then begin the next repetition. | Complete all reps in a controlled manner, maintaining tension throughout the movement rather than using momentum.

t: Stand with your feet wide apart, roughly 3–4 feet, turning your right foot out 90 degrees and your left foot in about 15 degrees. | Bend your right knee until your thigh is approximately parallel to the floor, stacking the knee directly over the ankle. | Extend both arms out to the sides at shoulder height, parallel to the floor. | Inhale and flip your right palm to face upward, then sweep your right arm up and overhead toward the back of the room. | Lower your left hand to rest lightly on the back of your left leg — shin or thigh — without pushing into it for support. | Gently lean your torso back and to the left, creating a long arc through the right side of your body from hip to fingertips. | Keep your right knee bent and pointing toward your right pinky toe throughout the pose. | Hold for 3–5 breaths, feeling the stretch along the right side body and hip flexors. | Inhale to rise back to center, then repeat on the opposite side.

t: Stand with your feet together and arms at your sides. | Bend your knees and lower your hips as if sitting back into a chair, keeping your weight in your heels and your torso upright — this is Chair Pose (Utkatasana). | Bring your palms together at your chest in a prayer position. | On an exhale, rotate your torso to the right, hooking your left elbow outside your right knee. | Press your elbow firmly against your knee to deepen the twist and keep your knees aligned. | Extend through the crown of your head to lengthen your spine, and gently open your chest toward the ceiling. | Hold the position for 5–10 breaths, keeping your hips level and your core engaged. | On an inhale, unwind back to center and return to Chair Pose. | Repeat the twist on the opposite side, rotating to the left with your right elbow outside your left knee.

t: Stand at the top of your mat with your feet together, then step your left foot back about 3–4 feet into a lunge, lowering your back knee toward the floor if needed to find stability. | Align your right knee directly over your right ankle, keeping your front shin vertical and your back leg extended or knee resting gently on the mat. | Place your hands together at your chest in a prayer position (Anjali Mudra) and take a tall breath in to lengthen your spine. | On an exhale, rotate your torso to the right, hooking your left elbow outside your right knee. Repeat on the opposite side, stepping the right foot back.

t: Begin in a high lunge with your right foot forward, knee stacked over the ankle, and your left leg extended straight behind you with the ball of the left foot on the mat. | Square your hips toward the front of the mat and press back through the left heel to straighten the back leg and stabilize the stance. | On an inhale, lengthen through the crown of the head and lift your torso upright, engaging the core. | On an exhale, rotate your torso to the right, bringing your left elbow to the outside of your right knee. Press elbow and knee against each other to deepen the twist. | If the twist allows, lower your left hand to the mat or a block on the outside of the right foot, pressing the palm flat to create a stable foundation. | Extend your right arm overhead and in line with your right ear, reaching the fingertips forward to create a long diagonal line from the back heel through the top hand. | Turn your gaze upward toward the ceiling or, if that strains the neck, look straight ahead. t: Adjust the saddle height so your knee has a slight bend (about 25–35°) at the bottom of the pedal stroke, with your foot flat on the pedal. | Set the handlebar height so you can reach it comfortably without rounding your lower back or locking out your elbows. | Before setting off, do 5 minutes of easy spinning at low resistance to warm up your legs and elevate your heart rate gradually. | Clip in or place the ball of your foot over the center of the pedal, then push off and begin pedaling in smooth, circular strokes. | Sit tall with a neutral spine, a slight forward lean from the hips, and relaxed shoulders — avoid hunching or gripping the bars too tightly. | Maintain a cadence of 70–90 RPM for general fitness; shift to an easier gear to keep your cadence in range rather than grinding a heavy gear. | Ride at a conversational pace for the bulk of your session if you are building base fitness, or follow a structured interval plan for higher-intensity work. | In the final 5 minutes, reduce intensity and spin in an easy gear to cool down and bring your heart rate back toward resting. | Dismount carefully, check your bike is secured, and stretch your quads, hamstrings, and hip flexors after the ride.

t: Stand with your left foot forward and right foot back, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent. | Raise your hands into guard position — left fist near your chin, right fist beside your right cheek, elbows tucked in. | Pivot your right foot, turning the heel outward so your right hip rotates forward. | Drive the rotation through your core and torso, letting your right shoulder follow the hip forward. | Extend your right arm in a straight line toward the target, rotating your fist so the palm faces down at full extension. | Make contact with the first two knuckles of your right hand, keeping your wrist straight and aligned with your forearm. | Exhale sharply as you extend, engaging your core throughout the punch. | Pull your arm back along the same path immediately after contact, returning your fist to guard position. | Reset your stance and weight distribution before throwing another punch or combination.

t: Stand in an orthodox boxing stance: feet shoulder-width apart, left foot forward, knees slightly bent, and weight evenly distributed between both feet. | Raise your hands to guard position — left fist near your left cheekbone, right fist protecting your right cheekbone, elbows angled down toward your ribs. | Shift a small amount of weight onto your right (rear) foot by bending the right knee, loading the hip for rotation. | Initiate the punch by driving your right hip explosively forward and pivoting on the ball of your right foot, letting your heel rise naturally. | As your hips rotate, allow your right shoulder to follow through and bring your right elbow up to roughly shoulder height, forming approximately a 90° bend at the elbow. | Deliver the hook in a tight horizontal arc toward the target, keeping your right fist level with your shoulder at the moment of contact. | Keep your left hand pressed firmly against your left cheekbone throughout the entire movement to maintain your guard. | At the moment of impact, exhale sharply and tighten your core to transfer force through the punch. | Snap your right hand back to guard position by reversing the hip rotation, then reset your balanced stance and prepare for the next combination.

Stand facing away from the anchor point. | Grip one ring in each hand with a neutral (palms facing each other) or slightly turned-out grip, arms extended in front of you. t: Set the rings high enough that your feet stay clear of the floor at the bottom of the dip, with your elbows bent and your upper arms parallel to the ground. | Grip one ring in each hand, then jump or step up and push yourself to the top position with your arms locked out, rings turned slightly outward, and shoulders depressed away from your ears. | Engage your core and keep your legs together, either straight or slightly bent, to maintain a controlled body position throughout the movement. | Begin lowering yourself by bending your elbows and allowing them to flare slightly outward, keeping the rings close to your sides rather than letting them drift wide. | Descend until your upper arms are at least parallel to the floor and your shoulders are at or just below elbow height — a full range of motion. | Pause briefly at the bottom without losing tension in your shoulders, then press firmly through your palms to push yourself back up. | As you rise, squeeze your triceps and chest to straighten your arms fully at the top, returning to the locked-out support position. | Complete your reps, then lower yourself in a controlled manner back to the floor or a step.

t: Set gymnastic rings at roughly knee-to-shin height and place your feet on the floor or an elevated surface behind you. | Grip the rings with a neutral hand position, arms fully extended, and walk your feet in until your hips are directly above your shoulders in a steep pike — aim for a 90° or greater angle at the hips. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and point your toes so your body forms a rigid inverted V. | Allow the rings to rotate naturally to a comfortable wrist angle — avoid forcing them into a fixed position. | Keeping your elbows tracking at roughly 45° from your torso, slowly lower your head down and forward past the level of the rings, maximizing depth without losing spinal alignment. | Pause briefly at the bottom when your head reaches its lowest point under control, feeling a deep stretch through the shoulders. | Press firmly through the rings, pushing the floor away, and drive your head back up through the rings to return to the fully extended starting position. | Reset your core brace and ring stability before beginning the next repetition.

t: Set the rings to approximately face height with your arms extended and the straps even. Ensure the rings hang freely with no twist in the straps. | Stand facing the anchor point and grip one ring in each hand with palms facing each other. Walk your feet forward until your body is at roughly a 45-degree angle to the floor and your arms are fully extended in front of you. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and keep your body in a straight line from heels to head. Maintain this rigid body position throughout every rep. | Begin the pull by driving your elbows wide and upward to shoulder height, keeping them flared out to the sides rather than pointing toward the floor. | Continue pulling until your hands are level with your temples and the rings are beside your ears, with your upper arms forming a T-shape with your torso. | As you reach the top, allow your palms to rotate outward naturally so they face forward or slightly upward, maximizing the range of motion at the shoulder. | Pause briefly at the top with your shoulders fully contracted. | Slowly extend your arms back to the starting position under control, resisting the rings on the way out rather than letting them pull you forward. | Complete all reps, then walk your feet back toward the anchor point and stand upright to exit safely.

t: Adjust the rings so they hang just a few inches above the floor, enough clearance to kneel beneath them comfortably. | Kneel on a mat and grip one ring in each hand with a neutral or pronated grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart. | Brace your core, posteriorly tilt your pelvis, and slowly walk your knees back while extending your arms forward and overhead until your body forms a straight, hollow-body line — hips in line with your torso, arms fully extended. | Hold that extended position: arms straight and pressed down against the rings, ribcage depressed, glutes and abs fully contracted, and hips just above floor level. | Keep your gaze toward the floor and your neck neutral so your spine stays in alignment throughout the hold. | Breathe in controlled nasal inhales and exhale slowly without releasing the abdominal brace — do not hold your breath for the entire set. | Maintain the hollow-body position for the target duration, typically 10–30 seconds, resisting any temptation to let the hips drop or the lower back arch. | To finish, bend your elbows and pull the rings back toward your hips while walking your knees forward, returning to the kneeling start position under control.

t: Set the rings low, roughly 15–30 cm off the floor — high enough to clear your body but low enough that you can hold a straight line from head to heel with your feet on the ground. | Grip a ring in each hand with your palms facing each other and press up into a top push-up position, hands directly under your shoulders. | Brace your core hard, squeeze your glutes, and push through the balls of your feet to make a rigid plank from head to foot. | Keeping your arms straight but not hyperextended, let the rings travel outward away from your midline into a wide fly position until your arms sit roughly 30–45° out from your torso. | Hold there: hands wide, arms straight, hips level, body in one line — do not let the rings drift further out than you can control. | Breathe in short, steady breaths; do not let the hips sag toward the floor or pike upward. | Hold for the prescribed time — start with 5–10 seconds and build toward 20–30 seconds as strength improves. | To finish, pull the rings back in until they are under your shoulders, then lower your knees to the floor and step out of the position.

t: Set the rings at a height that allows a full dead hang with feet off the floor. Grip one ring firmly with your working hand, palm facing toward you or at a neutral angle. | Place the free hand lightly on the wrist or forearm of your working arm for assistance, or let it hang at your side if attempting the unassisted version. | Before initiating the pull, depress and retract the shoulder blade on the working side to create a stable, packed shoulder joint. | Engage your core, squeeze your glutes, and establish a hollow-body position — ribs down, abs braced — to minimize swing. | Drive your elbow forcefully down and back toward your hip to initiate the pull, keeping the ring close to your body rather than letting it drift outward. | Pull continuously until your chin clears the height of the ring on the working side, maintaining as upright a torso as possible. | Lower yourself under full control back to a dead hang, resisting the descent rather than dropping, to maximize back engagement on every rep. | Complete all planned reps on one arm, rest adequately, then repeat on the opposite side.

t: Set the rings at roughly chest height for a standing variation, or suspend them overhead if performing a bodyweight hanging version. | Stand facing away from the anchor point, grasp one ring in each hand with an overhand grip, and step forward until the straps are taut and your arms are extended overhead at roughly a 45-degree angle. | Lean back so your body is at a slight angle, engage your core, and keep your legs straight — your body should form a rigid plank from head to heels. | Inhale, then begin the movement by driving your hands downward and backward in a smooth arc, as if sweeping them from overhead toward your hips. | Keep a slight, consistent bend in your elbows throughout — do not let the elbows fully lock or excessively bend; the arms act as levers, not pullers. | Focus on initiating the arc with your lats rather than your triceps; imagine trying to bring your elbows toward your hip pockets. | Continue the arc until the rings reach roughly hip or thigh level and you feel a strong contraction across the lats and through the teres major. | Exhale at the bottom of the arc, pause briefly, then slowly reverse the motion to return the rings overhead under control. | Complete the target reps, then step back toward the anchor to release tension before letting go of the rings.

t: Set the rings at a height where you can hang freely with your arms fully extended and your feet clear of the floor. | Grip each ring with a neutral or slightly supinated grip, wrapping your thumbs fully around the handles, and let yourself hang at a dead hang to settle your shoulder blades. | Engage your core and squeeze your glutes so your body forms a straight, controlled line from head to heel. | Initiate the pull by drawing your shoulder blades down and together, then drive your elbows toward your hips to bring your chest up toward the rings. | As you rise, allow your wrists to rotate naturally so the rings turn outward at the top of the movement. | Continue pulling until your chin clears the level of the rings and your chest is close to them. | Pause briefly at the top, maintaining tension in your back and keeping your shoulders packed down away from your ears. | Lower yourself under control back to a full dead hang, resisting the urge to drop quickly. | Reset your position at the bottom before beginning the next rep.

t: Set the rings at a height that gives you a complete dead hang with feet clear of the floor. Loop a resistance band through the ring on your working side so it forms a secure foot or knee loop hanging below. | Grip the ring with your working hand, palm facing toward you or in a neutral position. Step one foot or knee into the band loop, then lower yourself into a dead hang, letting the band bear a portion of your bodyweight. | Before pulling, pack the shoulder on your working arm — actively depress and retract the scapula so the shoulder joint is stable rather than elevated and loose. | Brace your core and hold a hollow-body position: ribs down, abs engaged, free leg long or crossed behind the banded leg to minimise swing. | Drive your elbow forcefully down and back toward your hip, keeping the ring close to your torso rather than letting it drift outward. | Pull continuously until your chin clears the height of the ring on the working side, maintaining as upright a torso as you can throughout. | Lower yourself under full control back to a dead hang, resisting gravity the entire way down rather than dropping, to maximise lat and bicep engagement on the eccentric. | Complete all planned reps, then switch sides, matching the band setup and rep count.

t: Set the rings at a height that lets you hang freely with your feet clear of the floor throughout the rotation. | Grip the rings with an overhand grip, palms facing away from you, and hang at full arm extension with your core lightly braced. | Press your shoulders down and away from your ears to establish a stable, active hang — avoid passively dumping into your joints. | Tuck your knees toward your chest, then drive your hips upward, guiding your legs overhead toward an inverted position. | Continue rotating backward, allowing your arms and wrists to turn naturally with your body as your legs pass through and behind you into the German hang — arms extended overhead, body hanging below. | Pause briefly at the bottom of the German hang to allow the shoulder stretch to deepen, keeping your arms straight. | Reverse the movement by tucking your knees and driving your legs back through the way they came, rotating your body forward with the same controlled tempo. | Lower your feet back to the starting hang position to complete one full repetition.

t: Set the rings wider than shoulder-width — roughly 1.5 times shoulder-width is a useful starting point — and adjust them to the same height. | Hang from the rings with a neutral or slightly pronated grip, arms fully extended, and let your shoulder blades rise naturally at the bottom. | Engage your core and squeeze your glutes so your body forms a straight line from shoulders to feet. | Depress and retract your shoulder blades — pull them down and back — before initiating the pull. | Drive your elbows out and down toward your hips, pulling your chest up toward the rings. | Continue pulling until your chest reaches ring level or your chin clears the rings, keeping your torso upright rather than letting it swing. | Pause briefly at the top, then lower yourself under control back to a full hang. | Complete your reps without kipping or swinging, resetting your shoulder position between reps if needed.

t: Sit on the floor with your legs spread wide in a straddle position, as far apart as is comfortable without forcing range. | Sit up tall, place both hands on the floor in front of you for support, and let your feet flex or relax naturally. | Inhale to lengthen your spine, then exhale and slowly rock your weight forward, walking your hands out ahead of you. | Pause at the limit of your comfortable range for one or two breaths, feeling a stretch along the inner thighs and groin. | Slowly rock back to the starting position, keeping your back relatively upright rather than collapsing into a slump. | Continue rocking forward and back in a smooth, controlled rhythm for the desired number of repetitions or time. | To add a lateral component, shift your weight toward one leg, pause briefly, then rock back through center and toward the other leg. | When finished, bring your legs together slowly before standing up.

t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointing slightly outward and arms hanging at your sides. | Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to lower into a squat until your thighs are roughly parallel to the floor, keeping your chest up and your weight through your heels. | As you reach the bottom of the squat, swing your arms back behind your hips to load the movement. | Explode upward by driving through your legs and swinging your arms forcefully overhead, leaving the ground as high as possible. | At the peak of the jump your body should be fully extended — legs straight, arms reaching straight up above your head. | Begin pulling your arms back down as you descend so they help absorb the landing. | Land softly by bending your knees to cushion the impact, allowing your hips to drop back into the bottom of the squat position. | Use the momentum from the landing to flow directly into the next repetition without pausing at the bottom. | Continue for the prescribed number of repetitions or duration, maintaining consistent jump height and soft landings throughout.

t: Kneel on all fours with your hands directly under your shoulders and your knees under your hips, hip-width apart. Keep your spine neutral and your head in line with your back. | Take a slow breath in to prepare, bracing your core lightly without holding your breath. | Exhale as you push your hips back toward your heels, lowering your torso toward the floor in a controlled slide. Allow your arms to extend naturally in front of you as your hips descend. | Pause briefly in the lowered position — your hips should be close to or resting on your heels and your chest near your thighs, resembling child's pose. | Inhale and shift your weight forward, pressing through your hands to return to the starting quadruped position. Keep the movement smooth and continuous rather than jerky. | Continue rocking back and forth at a steady, unhurried pace for the prescribed number of repetitions or time. | To finish, hold the lowered position for two to three breaths before returning to neutral and resting.

t: Kneel on the floor with one foot flat on the ground in front of you, knee bent at roughly 90°, and the other knee resting on the floor behind you for support. | Place your hands on your front knee or the floor for balance. | Keeping your front heel firmly on the floor, slowly rock your body weight forward so your front knee travels over your toes — this is the dorsiflexion (toes-up) end of the movement. | Rock back to the starting position, allowing your ankle to return to neutral. | Continue rocking forward and back in a smooth, controlled rhythm, going a little further into dorsiflexion each time as the joint loosens. | Perform the desired number of reps, then switch legs and repeat on the other side. | To increase intensity, you can perform the exercise standing with one hand on a wall for support, rocking the working knee forward over the toes.

t: Place a foam roller on the floor and kneel behind it, then lower the front of your left shin onto the roller just above the ankle. | Support your upper body with both hands flat on the floor in front of you, arms straight, so you can control how much bodyweight presses into the roller. | Keep your right knee on the floor or extend the right leg out to the side to adjust the load on the working leg. | Brace your core slightly and keep your spine neutral — avoid letting your lower back sag. | Using your arms, slowly push your body forward so the roller travels up the front of the shin toward the knee, moving at roughly one inch per second. | When you reach a tender spot, pause and hold steady pressure on that point for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and letting the tissue relax. | Continue rolling from ankle to just below the knee, covering the full length of the anterior lower leg — never roll directly over the knee joint. | Complete 2–3 slow passes up and down the shin, then switch legs and repeat the same sequence on the other side.

t: Place the foam roller on the floor perpendicular to your spine. Sit in front of it, then lean back so the roller contacts your mid-back at roughly the level of your shoulder blades. | Lower yourself until your upper back rests on the roller with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. | Support your head lightly with your hands or let your arms rest at your sides to start. Engage your core to keep your hips low and your lower back relaxed. | Slowly extend both arms out to your sides, then sweep them up overhead in a wide arc, as if making a snow angel — this is the "around the world" motion. | Continue the sweep, bringing your arms around and back down to your sides, completing a full circle. Move at a slow, controlled pace and breathe steadily throughout. | Pause at any point in the arc where you feel tightness in the upper back, holding for two to three seconds to allow the tissue to release. | Reverse the direction of the arm sweep for the next repetition to work the muscles from both angles. | After completing your reps, shift the roller slightly up or down your spine to address different segments of the thoracic region before repeating.

t: Place a foam roller or cylindrical roll on the floor perpendicular to your body. | Sit on the floor in front of the roller, then lean back so the roller contacts the middle of your upper back, just below the shoulder blades. | Cross your arms over your chest or support the back of your head with both hands to keep your neck neutral. | Plant your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart, and engage your glutes to lift your hips slightly so your body forms a gentle arc over the roller. | Allow gravity to extend your thoracic spine over the roller, breathing out as you relax into the stretch. | Hold the stretched position for one to two seconds, then use your feet and glutes to drive your hips up and roll the foam roller a few centimetres toward your upper back. | Pause again at each new segment, letting the spine extend over the roller before rolling further. | Continue rolling upward until you reach the base of the neck, then reverse direction and work back down toward the lower thoracic area. | Complete the desired number of passes, then roll to one side and press up to a seated position.

t: Place the rollball on the floor and get down onto your forearms, positioning yourself face-down or slightly to one side so you can reach your inner thigh. | Lift one leg out to the side at roughly a 45-degree angle from your body, and position the rollball against the inner thigh just above the knee. | Shift enough bodyweight onto that leg to create firm, tolerable pressure through the ball — support the rest of your weight on your forearms and opposite leg. | Breathe in slowly, then as you exhale, allow your muscles to soften into the pressure rather than tensing against it. | Begin rolling the ball slowly up toward the groin in small increments, pausing for 2–3 seconds on any area that feels noticeably tender or restricted. | When you find a tender spot, hold the ball still there and maintain steady pressure for 20–30 seconds until the discomfort begins to ease. | Continue working the ball along the full length of the inner thigh from just above the knee up to the groin, then reverse direction back down. | Complete 1–2 minutes on one leg, then switch to the other side and repeat the process. | Finish by performing a gentle static stretch of the inner thigh to reinforce the mobility gained from the release.
