t: Place a lacrosse ball or massage ball on the floor in front of you. | Lie face down and position the ball under the front of one upper arm, roughly at the midpoint of the bicep brachii — between the elbow crease and the front of the shoulder. | Extend that arm forward at roughly a 45° angle from your torso with your palm facing down or slightly to the side. | Use your free arm and legs to brace against the floor, controlling how much of your bodyweight presses onto the ball. | Slowly roll your arm so the ball travels along the front of the upper arm, from just above the elbow crease toward the front of the shoulder. | When you find a tender or tight spot, pause and hold light, steady pressure on it for 20–30 seconds while breathing slowly. | Continue rolling for 30–60 seconds total on that arm, then switch to the other side.

t: Sit on the floor with your legs extended in front of you. Place the rollball under your right calf, roughly at the mid-point between the ankle and the back of the knee. | Lift your hips off the floor slightly and prop yourself up on your hands behind you, so your body weight presses the calf down onto the ball. | Slowly roll your calf forward over the ball, moving from just above the ankle toward the base of the knee. Keep the movement controlled — about one inch per second. | When you find a tender or tight spot, pause and hold light pressure on that point for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily, until the tension decreases. | Continue rolling back down toward the ankle, covering the full length of the gastrocnemius (upper calf belly). | Rotate your leg slightly inward and repeat the rolling motion to reach the soleus, which runs deeper and along the inner edge of the lower calf. | Adjust the load by crossing your left ankle over your right leg to add more pressure, or keep both legs down to reduce it. | Spend 60–90 seconds total on each calf, then switch legs and repeat. | Finish with 2–3 slow ankle circles to encourage blood flow through the tissue.

t: Place a rollball against a wall at approximately shoulder height, then position your rear shoulder directly against the ball. | Lean your body weight gently into the ball so it presses into the posterior deltoid — the fleshy area at the back of your shoulder. | Stand with a slight bend in your knees and feet shoulder-width apart to maintain a stable, balanced stance. | Slowly roll the ball upward toward the top of the rear shoulder, pausing on any tender or tight spot you find. | Hold pressure on each tender point for 20–30 seconds, breathing deeply and allowing the muscle to relax into the ball. | Continue rolling the ball downward and outward, exploring the full area of the posterior deltoid. | Rotate your arm slowly inward and outward while maintaining ball pressure to increase the release effect on the muscle fibers. | Work each tight area for 1–2 minutes, then lower your arm and step away from the wall to assess your shoulder mobility.

t: Lie face down on the floor. Place the rollball just below the lower edge of your ribs, slightly to one side of your midline, positioning it against the soft tissue of the upper abdominal and diaphragm region. | Rest your forearms on the floor in front of you and gently lower your torso so that your bodyweight settles onto the ball. Start with minimal pressure — your forearms should bear most of your weight. | Take a slow, deep inhale through the nose, allowing your belly to expand downward into the ball. You should feel the ball press back against the tissue as your diaphragm descends. | Exhale fully and slowly through pursed lips, letting your torso relax further into the ball as you breathe out. The tissue under the ball should soften slightly with each exhale. | Hold this position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily, until you notice a reduction in tension or discomfort at that spot. | Slowly shift your torso a short distance — about one inch — in any direction to move the ball to an adjacent area, then repeat the breathing cycle. | Work across the lower ribcage on that side, covering the area from just left of the sternum to the outer edge of the ribcage, spending 20–30 seconds at each point. | Carefully push yourself up off the ball, reposition it to the opposite side of the midline, and repeat the entire sequence. | Finish by rolling onto your back and taking three to five slow, full diaphragmatic breaths to allow the tissue to settle.

t: Place a rollball on the floor and sit beside it, then carefully lower yourself so the ball sits just to one side of your spine in the lower back, not directly on the vertebrae. | Lean your body weight into the ball by supporting yourself on your hands or forearms and bending your knees with feet flat on the floor. | Breathe out and allow your muscles to relax into the pressure of the ball. | Slowly shift your body up and down a few centimeters to roll the ball along the erector spinae from the top of the hip toward the mid-back. | When you find a tender or tight spot, pause and hold steady pressure on that point for 20–30 seconds until the tension softens. | Continue rolling and pausing on any additional tight areas along the same side of the spine. | When finished with one side, carefully roll off the ball, reposition it to the opposite side of the spine, and repeat. | Finish by moving gently off the ball, resting flat on your back for a moment before standing.

t: Place the rollball on the floor and kneel or sit beside it so the ball sits next to your hip on the side you want to stretch. | Lower your body sideways and position the rollball under your lateral waist, just above the hip bone where the external oblique runs. | Support your upper body with your bottom forearm on the floor, keeping your elbow directly beneath your shoulder. | Extend your legs out so your body forms a straight line from head to feet, stacking your feet or resting the lower knee on the floor for stability. | Relax the side of your waist into the ball and let gravity apply gentle pressure to the tissue. | Breathe slowly and deeply, allowing the muscles to soften with each exhale. | Slowly roll the ball a few centimeters forward and back along the lateral waist to find and dwell on tight spots. | Hold on any tender area for 20–30 seconds until you feel the tissue release. | Repeat on the opposite side, spending equal time on each.

t: Place a rollball on the floor and stand or sit in a stable position near a wall or chair for balance. | Position the ball under the heel of one foot, keeping the opposite foot flat on the floor. | Shift enough weight onto the working foot to create comfortable but firm pressure on the ball. | Slowly roll the ball forward along the arch toward the ball of the foot, moving in a controlled, deliberate pace. | Pause on any tender or tight spots for 5–10 seconds to allow the tissue to release. | Continue rolling back toward the heel, sweeping the full length of the plantar fascia. | Angle the foot slightly inward, then outward, to cover the medial and lateral edges of the arch. | Perform 60–90 seconds of rolling on each foot, then switch sides.

t: Sit at a table or desk with your forearm resting palm-down on the surface. Place the rollball on top of the dorsal (back) side of your forearm, roughly halfway between the wrist and elbow. | Rest your opposite hand on top of the ball to control pressure. Your forearm stays flat and relaxed on the surface throughout. | Apply moderate downward pressure through your top hand so the ball presses into the forearm extensor muscles. You should feel pressure without sharp or radiating pain. | Slowly roll the ball toward your elbow, moving at roughly one inch per second along the extensor muscle belly. Keep the movement controlled and deliberate. | When you find a tender or dense spot, pause and hold steady pressure on that point for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily, until the tension begins to ease. | Continue rolling back toward the wrist, covering the full length of the extensor compartment from just above the wrist crease to just below the lateral epicondyle (the bony point on the outside of the elbow). | Avoid rolling directly over the lateral epicondyle — stop approximately one finger-width before that bony landmark. | Spend 60–90 seconds total on each forearm, then switch sides and repeat. | Finish with 3–5 slow wrist circles in each direction to encourage circulation through the tissue.

t: Sit at a table or bench and place the rollball on the surface in front of you. | Rest your forearm on the table with the palm facing up, so the underside of your forearm (the flexor side) is exposed. | Position the rollball under your forearm, starting just above the wrist crease where the flexor tendons gather. | Apply gentle downward pressure through your forearm onto the ball, using your opposite hand on top of your forearm to add load as needed. | Slowly roll your forearm forward over the ball, moving from the wrist toward the elbow at a rate of roughly one inch per second. | When you encounter a tender or tight spot, pause and hold steady pressure on that point for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly, until the tension begins to ease. | Continue rolling up toward the mid-forearm, covering the full length of the flexor muscle belly. | Rotate your forearm slightly inward or outward to shift the ball onto adjacent flexor muscles and ensure full coverage. | Spend 60–90 seconds on each forearm, then switch arms and repeat.

t: Sit at a table or bench. Place the rollball on the surface and rest your forearm on top of it, palm facing down, so the ball sits against the inner forearm roughly halfway between the wrist and the elbow. | Apply gentle downward pressure through your forearm to compress the tissue against the ball. Use your free hand on top of your forearm to add extra load if needed. | Slowly roll the ball along the length of the inner forearm, moving from just above the wrist toward the elbow crease. Keep the motion controlled — about one inch per second. | When you reach a spot that feels notably tight or tender, pause and hold steady pressure there for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly until the tension softens. | Continue rolling back toward the wrist, covering the full length of the pronator muscle belly. | To increase specificity, rotate your palm slightly upward (supination) while holding on a tight spot. This places a mild active stretch on the pronator fibers under compression. | Spend 60–90 seconds working along the forearm, targeting the area along the medial (inner) edge from the wrist to just below the inner elbow. | Switch arms and repeat the same sequence on the opposite forearm.

t: Place a small, firm ball on a table or flat surface and sit or stand beside it. | Rest your forearm on the ball, positioning it on the lateral (outer) side of the forearm just below the elbow crease where the supinator muscle lies. | Allow your body weight to sink gently into the ball, creating moderate pressure on the tissue. | Slowly rotate your forearm from a palm-down (pronated) to a palm-up (supinated) position while maintaining pressure on the ball. | When you find a tender or tight spot, pause and hold that position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly. | Resume rolling by shifting your forearm slightly toward the wrist or elbow to explore adjacent tissue. | Continue for 60–90 seconds on each arm, adjusting ball position to cover the full supinator region. | Finish by gently shaking out your forearm and performing a light supination stretch to reinforce the release.

t: Sit on the floor and place the rollball on the ground beside your right hip. Lower your outer right hip onto the ball, positioning it just below and behind the bony crest of the ilium — roughly where the side seam of your shorts sits. | Support your upper body by placing your right hand on the floor behind you and your left hand in front for balance. Bend both knees and keep your feet flat on the floor. | Shift enough body weight onto the ball so you feel moderate pressure in the outer hip tissue, but not sharp or shooting pain. | Slowly move your hips in small, controlled circles or inch forward and backward to scan for areas of increased tension in the gluteus medius. | When you find a tender or tight spot, stop moving and hold steady pressure on that point for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and letting the muscle relax into the ball. | After the tension in that spot decreases, continue scanning to find the next area of restriction, working from the posterior edge of the muscle toward the front of the hip. | To reach the anterior portion of the gluteus medius, rotate your hip slightly inward so the ball shifts toward the front of the outer hip. | Spend 60–90 seconds total on the right side, then reposition and repeat on the left hip.

t: Place a rollball on the floor and lie face-down, positioning the ball just inside the front of one hip bone (iliac crest), roughly an inch medial to the ASIS and low on the lower abdomen. | Lower yourself gently onto the ball so it contacts the soft tissue of the lower abdomen where the iliacus lies beneath, keeping most body weight through your forearms and opposite hip. | Breathe slowly and allow your abdomen to relax so the ball can sink progressively deeper toward the iliacus rather than pressing against braced abdominal muscles. | Scan for a tender or tight spot by making small, deliberate shifts of body weight — forward, back, or slightly side-to-side — until you locate a point of significant tension. | Hold sustained pressure on that tender point for 20–30 seconds, breathing deeply and letting the tissue soften under the ball. | Once the initial tenderness eases, slowly flex and extend the same-side hip by sliding the knee out and back, using the movement to further release the iliacus against the ball. | Continue for a total of 60–90 seconds per side, repositioning the ball slightly to address different portions of the muscle. | When finished, press up slowly, rest a moment, then switch to the opposite side.

t: Choose a firm, small ball (lacrosse ball or massage ball) and stand with your back toward a smooth wall. | Reach across your chest with the opposite hand to locate the infraspinatus — the fleshy area below the spine of your shoulder blade and just lateral to the inner edge of the scapula. | Place the ball between the wall and that spot, then shift your body weight gently into the ball to apply comfortable pressure. | Step your feet slightly away from the wall so your body leans back, increasing the load through the ball as needed. | Hold steady pressure on any tender spot for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and letting the muscle relax into the ball. | Make small, controlled movements — shift slightly up, down, or side to side — to explore the tissue and locate additional trigger points. | When you find a sore spot, pause and sustain pressure until the intensity reduces by roughly half before moving on. | Continue for 60–90 seconds on each side, then step away from the wall and gently roll your shoulder in circles to assess any change in mobility. | Switch sides and repeat the process on the opposite infraspinatus.

t: Stand facing away from a wall with a rollball in your hand. Place the ball between your upper back and the wall, positioning it over the infraspinatus — the muscular area on the back of your shoulder blade, below the spine of the scapula. | Lean your body weight back into the ball to create initial contact pressure. This moves the scapula away from the spine and exposes more of the infraspinatus to the ball. | Using your legs to drive movement, slowly shift your body up, down, and in small lateral arcs so the ball rolls across the infraspinatus. Breathe slowly and allow the tissue to soften under the sustained load. | Continue exploring the infraspinatus by adjusting the height and lateral position of the ball, covering from just below the scapular spine down toward the inferior angle of the shoulder blade. | To increase pressure, bend your knees slightly and lean more of your body weight into the wall. To reduce it, stand more upright and bear less load. | Spend 60–90 seconds total on each side, then switch arms and repeat on the opposite shoulder.

Breathe slowly through the hold and allow the tissue to relax under the compression. | After each hold, continue rolling — either continuing upward toward the ribs or shifting slightly toward the midline — to cover the full surface of the rectus abdominis on that side. | Adjust the amount of pressure by shifting more or less body weight through your forearms. Never press down sharply or bounce into the tissue. | Spend 60–90 seconds working one side, then reposition the ball to the opposite side of the midline and repeat. | Finish by rolling gently off the ball, pressing into a hands-and-knees position, and taking two or three slow, full breaths to let the abdomen fully release.

t: Place the rollball on the floor and position yourself face down (prone) with the ball under the front of one thigh, roughly in the center of the quadriceps just below the hip crease. | Support your upper body with your forearms flat on the floor, elbows directly beneath your shoulders, keeping your spine neutral. | Extend the working leg straight so the front of the thigh rests on the rollball. Keep the opposite leg either extended alongside or bent out to the side for stability. | Shift enough bodyweight onto the thigh to create moderate pressure on the rectus femoris — a sensation of 4–6 out of 10 discomfort is appropriate. | Slowly roll the ball in one direction, moving from just below the hip crease down toward the knee, taking approximately five seconds to cover each inch of tissue. | When you reach a tender or tight spot, pause and hold steady pressure on that point for 20–30 seconds. Breathe slowly and allow the muscle to relax. | After the hold, continue rolling distally toward the knee, working through the full length of the rectus femoris from hip to just above the kneecap. | Spend 60–90 seconds working through the muscle on one side, then switch legs and repeat on the opposite thigh. | Finish by standing and performing a gentle standing quad stretch on each side to reinforce the tissue length gained from rolling.

t: Lie on your back on a firm surface with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor. | Place the massage ball beneath your upper back, positioning it between your spine and one shoulder blade to target the rhomboid area — not directly on the spine. | Cross both arms over your chest, or reach one arm across your body, to retract the shoulder blade and expose the rhomboid muscle beneath it. | Press through your feet to lift your hips slightly, loading your body weight onto the ball. | Slowly shift your body up and down, or side to side, rolling the ball across the rhomboid area in small, controlled movements. | When you find a tender spot, pause and hold steady pressure there for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and allowing the tissue to soften. | Continue rolling across the full rhomboid region — from the upper border near the base of your neck down to the lower border near the mid-back — for 60–90 seconds per side. | Lower your hips, reposition the ball to the opposite side of your spine, and repeat on the other shoulder.

t: Stand with your back facing a wall and place the rollball between the wall and the upper back, just beside the base of your neck at the top of the shoulder blade. | Lean your body weight into the wall to compress the ball against the target area — the levator scapulae attachment near the superior angle of the scapula. | Adjust your feet a few inches away from the wall so you can control the amount of pressure applied through your bodyweight. | Tilt and rotate your head gently away from the side being worked to lengthen the levator scapulae and increase the stretch on the tissue. | Hold still on any tender point for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing slowly and allowing the muscle to relax into the pressure. | Make small, controlled movements — shifting slightly up, down, or sideways — to locate additional areas of tension along the muscle. | Reduce pressure by standing more upright if the sensation becomes too intense; increase pressure by leaning further into the wall. | Once the area feels released, move the ball to an adjacent tender spot and repeat the process. | Complete the work on one side before repositioning the ball to mirror the same area on the opposite side.

t: Sit or stand beside a wall and hold the rollball in the hand on the side you intend to work. | Place the rollball between the wall and the upper back, positioning it just above the top inner corner of the shoulder blade where the levator scapulae attaches. | Lean gently into the wall so the ball takes on a comfortable amount of your body weight — you should feel noticeable pressure without sharp pain. | Drop that shoulder slightly downward to lengthen the levator scapulae and allow the ball to sink into the muscle. | Slowly rotate your head away from the side being worked and tuck your chin slightly toward the opposite collar bone to deepen the stretch. | Hold this position and breathe deeply, allowing the muscle to relax and soften into the ball for 20–40 seconds. | To explore the tissue further, make small, slow head rotations or gently nod your chin up and down while maintaining contact with the ball. | Release the pressure gradually, reposition the ball slightly higher or lower if needed, and repeat on the same spot or move to an adjacent area. | Switch sides and repeat the full sequence on the opposite levator scapulae.

t: Sit on the floor with both legs extended loosely in front of you, or bend one knee slightly outward to open the inner thigh of the leg you will work on. | Place the rollball on the floor against your inner thigh, positioning it high near the groin crease where the pectineus runs between the pubic bone and the upper femur. | Shift your body weight gently toward that side so the rollball makes firm contact with the pectineus — use your hands on the floor behind you for support and balance. | Allow the weight of your thigh to sink into the ball rather than forcing pressure downward; the target sensation is a tolerable, deep ache rather than sharp pain. | Breathe slowly and hold the initial position for 20–30 seconds to let the surrounding tissue begin to relax. | Make small, deliberate movements — gently rolling the ball a centimeter or two in any direction — to scan for areas of increased tenderness within the pectineus. | When you find a sensitive spot, stop moving and hold sustained pressure there, breathing deeply until you feel the tension soften — typically 20–45 seconds per point. | Reposition the ball to cover any remaining tight areas along the upper inner thigh, repeating the hold-and-breathe approach at each location. | To finish, shift your weight off the ball, remove it from beneath your thigh, and gently bring the leg back to a neutral position before switching sides if needed.

nE: Roll Ball Side Lying Scalene Muscles Activation
nR: Roll Ball Side Lying Scalene Muscles Activation
nH: Roll Ball Side Lying Scalene Muscles Activation
t: Place a rollball on an exercise mat and lie on your side, keeping your body in a straight line from head to hips. | Stack your knees and bend them slightly for stability; rest your bottom arm extended along the floor or use it to lightly support your head. | Lift your head and slide the rollball beneath the lateral side of your neck, positioning it roughly midway between your ear and the top of your shoulder. | Lower your head gently onto the ball so its weight alone provides the pressure — do not push down actively. | Breathe slowly and allow the scalene muscles to soften under the sustained contact for 20–30 seconds. | Make small adjustments — tilt your chin slightly toward the ceiling or let it drop toward your chest — to shift pressure across the anterior, middle, and posterior scalene fibers. | When you find a tender spot, hold steady and breathe through the discomfort until it softens, typically 20–45 seconds. | Reposition the ball slightly higher or lower along the lateral neck to address additional areas of tightness. | To finish, support your head with your top hand, lift it clear of the ball, then roll onto your back and rest for a moment before repeating on the opposite side.

nR: Roll Ball Side Lying Scalene Muscles Activation (side POV)
nH: Roll Ball Side Lying Scalene Muscles Activation (side POV)
t: Place the rollball on the floor or a firm, non-slip surface. Lie on your side and position the rollball under the lateral side of your neck, roughly between your ear and the top of your shoulder. | Allow your head to rest gently onto the rollball, using only the natural weight of your head to create pressure. Rest your top arm along your hip or on the floor in front of you for stability. | Take a slow breath in and exhale fully, letting your neck muscles relax around the ball. Avoid pressing your head down with any additional force. | Begin a slow scan by making very small movements with your head — shifting slightly forward toward your collarbone, then slightly back toward your spine — to work across the scalene muscle group. | When you find a tender or tight spot, pause and hold still. Breathe slowly and steadily for 20–30 seconds, allowing the pressure to gradually release the tissue. | Adjust the height of the ball contact by gently tucking or extending your chin slightly to access different portions of the scalene muscles along the lateral neck. | Continue scanning the lateral neck for 60–90 seconds total. If you feel any pain, tingling, or numbness at any point, lift your head immediately and remove the ball. | Carefully lift your head, remove the rollball, and rest for a moment before repeating on the opposite side if needed.

t: Place a rollball on the floor and kneel or sit on the ground with one leg extended or bent in front of you. | Position the rollball under the front of your lower leg, just below the knee, against the tibialis anterior muscle on the outer edge of the shin bone. | Support your upper body with your hands on the floor behind you or to the sides to control how much bodyweight you apply. | Press your shin gently down onto the rollball so you feel moderate pressure on the tibialis anterior — not sharp pain. | Slowly roll the ball down toward your ankle in small, deliberate movements, pausing on any tender or tight spots for 5–10 seconds. | Continue rolling from just below the knee to just above the ankle, covering the full length of the muscle belly. | When you find a particularly tight spot, flex and point your foot slowly to encourage the tissue to release. | After completing one pass, roll back up to the starting position and repeat for the desired duration, then switch legs.

t: Step onto the treadmill and place both feet on the side rails before starting the machine. | Set your target speed — begin at a comfortable walking pace (3–4 mph) and increase gradually to your intended running speed. | Step onto the moving belt and walk briefly to establish your balance and stride rhythm before accelerating. | Accelerate to your running pace, aiming for a midfoot strike that lands beneath your center of mass rather than far out in front of your heel. | Maintain an upright torso with a slight forward lean originating from the ankles, not the waist; keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. | Drive your elbows back at roughly 90° and swing your arms naturally in line with your direction of travel — do not let them cross the midline of your body. | Breathe rhythmically — inhale for two to three strides and exhale for two to three strides — to sustain effort and manage pace. | At the end of your session, reduce speed gradually to a walking pace and complete 2–3 minutes of cool-down walking before stopping. | Step off to the side rails before the belt comes to a full stop, or wait for it to stop completely before dismounting.

t: Set the safety squat bar in a rack at approximately shoulder height and duck under it so the padded yoke sits across your upper traps, just below the base of your neck. | Grip the forward-facing handles firmly and stand upright to unrack the bar, then take two controlled steps back. | Set your feet shoulder-width apart with toes turned out slightly, brace your core hard, and take a deep breath into your belly. | Push your hips back first, maintaining a neutral or very slightly arched spine, and allow your torso to hinge forward under the bar. | Continue hinging until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor or until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings — whichever limit you reach first. | Hold the bottom position for one count without rounding your lower back or letting your knees collapse inward. | Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return your torso to upright, exhaling on the way up. | Stand fully tall with hips locked out at the top before beginning the next rep. | After completing all reps, step forward and re-rack the bar under control.

t: Sit on the floor with both legs extended straight in front of you in Dandasana (Staff Pose). Keep your spine tall and your hands flat on the floor beside your hips. | Bend your right knee and draw the right foot flat to the floor, placing it close to your right sitting bone with the shin roughly vertical. | Root both sitting bones evenly into the floor. If your lower back rounds immediately, sit on a folded blanket to tilt the pelvis forward. | On an inhale, lengthen your spine upward. Wrap your right arm around the inside of your right shin, then reach behind your back with your right hand while sweeping your left arm behind you to clasp both hands — or use a strap if the hands do not yet reach. | On an exhale, hinge forward from the hips — not the waist — over the extended left leg, keeping the spine as long as possible rather than rounding. | Allow your torso to descend toward your left thigh. t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, holding a medicine ball at chest height with both hands and your elbows pointing down. | Brace your core and keep your chest up as you step one foot forward into a long stride. | Lower your back knee toward the floor, descending into a full lunge so your front thigh is roughly parallel to the ground. | At the bottom of the lunge, press the medicine ball directly overhead until your arms are fully extended, keeping your torso upright. | Pause briefly with the ball locked out overhead and your front knee tracking over your toes. | Lower the medicine ball back to chest height with control as you begin to rise. | Push through your front heel to return to the starting position, stepping your front foot back beside the other so your feet are hip-width apart again. | Alternate legs for the desired number of reps, or complete all reps on one side before switching.

t: Sit tall on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you and spread apart to a comfortable V-shape, roughly shoulder-width or slightly wider. | Flex your feet so your toes point toward the ceiling, and press through your heels to keep your legs grounded. | Sit up as tall as possible, lengthening through the crown of your head and keeping your spine neutral. | Extend both arms out to your sides at shoulder height, palms facing down. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale as you rotate your torso to the right, bringing your left hand toward the outside of your right foot in a reaching, 'sawing' motion. | Pulse your left little finger gently past your right pinky toe three times, reaching a little further with each exhale to deepen the stretch through the left waist and obliques. | Inhale as you unwind and return to the upright, centered position with arms extended to the sides. | Exhale and repeat the rotation to the left side, reaching your right hand toward the outside of your left foot. | Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions, then sit tall to finish the set.

t: Stand or sit tall with your arms relaxed at your sides, spine neutral, and feet hip-width apart. | Let your shoulders hang in their natural resting position — this is your starting point. | Inhale and shrug both shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can, keeping your neck long and your head still. | Hold the elevated position for one to two seconds, feeling the upper trapezius contract. | Exhale and pull your shoulders down deliberately, drawing the shoulder blades away from your ears and toward your back pockets. | Hold the depressed position for one to two seconds, feeling the lower trapezius and serratus anterior engage. | Return to the neutral resting position in a controlled manner. | Repeat for the target number of repetitions, maintaining a slow, deliberate tempo throughout.

t: Start in a quadruped position with your hands directly under your shoulders and knees under your hips, spine neutral. | Keep your elbows straight and your head in line with your torso throughout the movement. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale and let your shoulder blades slide apart — push the floor away so your upper back rises slightly toward the ceiling (protraction). | Hold the protracted position for one to two seconds, feeling the stretch between the shoulder blades. | Inhale and draw your shoulder blades toward each other, allowing your chest to drop gently toward the floor (retraction). | Hold the retracted position for one to two seconds, feeling the squeeze in the mid-back. | Continue alternating between protraction and retraction in a slow, controlled rhythm for the prescribed number of repetitions.

t: Grip a pull-up bar with both hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, using an overhand (pronated) grip. | Hang at full arm extension — this is the dead-hang starting position. Let your shoulders rise naturally toward your ears and allow your body to relax. | Keep your elbows completely straight and locked throughout the entire movement. This is a scapular drill, not a pull-up. | Exhale and depress your shoulder blades — think of pulling your shoulders away from your ears and driving them straight down toward your hips. | Simultaneously retract your scapulae by squeezing them together slightly, 'packing' your shoulders down and back. | Pause for a full second at the top of the movement. Your body will visibly rise an inch or two without any elbow bend. | Inhale and slowly release, letting your shoulders rise back up to the fully elevated dead-hang position. | Repeat for the target number of reps, maintaining control throughout each rep without swinging or kipping.

t: Grip a pull-up bar with an overhand (pronated) grip slightly wider than shoulder-width, wrapping your thumbs fully around the bar. | Hang at full arm extension with your legs straight or slightly crossed, allowing your shoulder blades to rise naturally into a passive shrug — this is your starting dead-hang position. | Without bending your elbows, depress and retract your shoulder blades: pull them down toward your back pockets and squeeze them gently together. | Your body will rise a few centimeters and your chest will lift slightly — this is the scapular pull. t: Stand with your back, head, and glutes fully against a wall, feet a few inches away from the base and shoulder-width apart. | Press your lower back into the wall as much as possible to reduce the lumbar arch — a slight gap is acceptable, but minimize it. | Raise your arms to a 90/90 position: upper arms out to the sides at shoulder height, elbows bent to 90°, and forearms vertical with the backs of your hands touching the wall. | Brace your core lightly and retract your shoulder blades to establish contact between your entire forearms, wrists, and the backs of your hands and the wall. | Exhale and slowly slide both forearms upward along the wall, straightening your elbows as your arms reach overhead — keep every part of your arms in contact with the wall throughout. | Continue until your arms are fully extended overhead, or until you can no longer maintain wall contact without compensating. | Pause briefly at the top, then inhale and reverse the motion, sliding your arms back down to the starting 90/90 position under control. | Complete the target number of repetitions, maintaining wall contact and scapular control on every rep.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your core braced. | Step your right foot forward and your left foot back into a split stance, as if you were at the bottom of a lunge — front knee bent to roughly 90°, back knee lowered toward the floor. | Swing your arms back to load for the jump. | Drive explosively through both feet, pressing the floor away to launch yourself into the air. | While airborne, scissor your legs by swinging your left foot forward and your right foot back, simultaneously switching your arm swing to the opposite side. | Land softly with your left foot now forward and your right foot back, absorbing impact through your heel-to-toe and bending both knees to cushion the landing. | Without pausing, immediately load for the next jump and repeat the switch — each landing counts as one rep. | Continue alternating legs for the target number of reps or time.

nR: Seated Toe Extensor And Foot Everter Stretch
nH: Seated Toe Extensor And Foot Everter Stretch

t: Stand facing a smooth wall with your feet hip-width apart and about 15–20 cm away from the wall. | Place both forearms flat against the wall at roughly shoulder height, elbows bent to 90°, with your forearms vertical and hands pointing toward the ceiling. | Gently brace your core and tuck your chin slightly so your neck is long and neutral. | Reach your arms upward by sliding your forearms along the wall, actively pushing your chest away from the wall as you raise your arms. | Continue sliding until your arms are nearly fully extended overhead, keeping both forearms in contact with the wall throughout. | At the top, consciously protract and elevate your shoulder blades — think of pushing the wall away and reaching tall through your fingertips. | Slowly slide your forearms back down to the starting 90° position under control, resisting the urge to let your lower back arch. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, maintaining steady contact between your forearms and the wall on every repetition.

t: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and your feet roughly hip-width apart. Rotate both knees to the left so your left shin is in front of you and your right shin is behind you, each forming a 90-degree angle — this is the 90-90 position. | Place your hands lightly on the floor behind you for initial support, keeping your torso upright. | Press the outer edge of your front shin and the inner edge of your rear shin gently into the floor to feel the hip stretch on both sides. | To switch, lift both knees off the floor simultaneously, rotating your hips so your knees pass through center and drop to the opposite side. | Land with your right shin now in front and your left shin behind, re-establishing the 90-90 position on the other side. | Sit tall, minimize leaning on your hands as your mobility improves, and feel the stretch settle into your hips. | Continue alternating sides in a slow, controlled rhythm for the desired number of repetitions.

t: Stand tall or sit upright on a bench with your spine neutral and your feet flat on the floor. | Raise your right arm to the side so your upper arm is parallel to the floor and your elbow is bent to 90°, forearm pointing straight up. | Keep your upper arm fixed and stationary throughout the test — it should not drift forward, backward, or drop. | Slowly rotate your forearm backward and downward, as if trying to lay the back of your hand on a surface behind you. | Stop rotating when you feel resistance, tension, or discomfort — do not force past that point. | Note the angle your forearm makes relative to vertical. t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms resting at your sides, and your core lightly braced. | Relax the shoulder you are about to move — let it sit in its natural, neutral position before you begin. | Keeping your elbow straight but not locked, begin raising your arm forward with the palm facing down or inward. | Move the arm slowly and smoothly, tracing a straight path upward in front of your body. | Continue lifting until you reach the end of your comfortable range — ideally overhead with the arm alongside your ear. | Pause briefly at the top, allowing the anterior deltoid and upper chest to feel a gentle lengthening. | Lower the arm back down at the same controlled pace, resisting gravity the entire way. | Complete all repetitions on one side before switching, or alternate arms for the prescribed number of reps. | Aim for fluid, continuous motion — treat each repetition as an exploration of your range rather than a race.

t: Stand with your back, head, and hips pressed firmly against a wall, feet roughly 15 to 30 centimetres away from the base. | Begin with your arms at your sides, palms facing forward, elbows straight. | Press the entire length of your spine and the back of your head into the wall and maintain that contact throughout the movement. | Slowly raise both arms forward and upward, keeping the elbows straight and palms facing the ceiling as your arms travel overhead. | Continue lifting until your arms are fully overhead, reaching as high as possible while your back and head remain in contact with the wall. | Hold the end position for one to two seconds, feeling the stretch across the posterior shoulder area and the engagement through the upper back. | Lower your arms back to the starting position in a slow, controlled manner. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining wall contact on every rep.

t: Lie on your back on a firm, flat surface with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor. | Raise your right arm out to the side until it is level with your shoulder — 90° of abduction — and bend your elbow to 90° so your forearm points straight up toward the ceiling. | Allow your upper arm to rest fully on the floor; your elbow should stay in contact with the surface throughout the test. | Keeping your elbow fixed and your upper arm pinned to the floor, slowly rotate your forearm forward and downward toward the floor — this is internal rotation. | Stop when you feel resistance or when your elbow begins to lift off the surface, noting the angle your forearm makes with the floor. | Hold the end-range position for 2–3 seconds to confirm this is your true limit, not muscular guarding. | Return your forearm to the starting vertical position under control. | Repeat the assessment on the left side and compare the range of motion between arms. | Record any asymmetry greater than 10–15° or any reproduction of familiar pain as a positive finding warranting follow-up.

t: Stand or sit tall with your spine neutral and your feet hip-width apart if standing. | Bring your right arm out to the side at shoulder height, elbow bent to 90 degrees so your forearm points straight up toward the ceiling. | Keep your upper arm parallel to the floor and your elbow fixed at shoulder height throughout the movement. | Slowly rotate your forearm downward and backward — externally rotating the upper arm — until your forearm is parallel to the floor or until you reach a comfortable end range. | Pause briefly at the end range, feeling a gentle stretch across the posterior shoulder and rotator cuff. | Slowly reverse the motion, rotating the forearm back up to the starting vertical position in a controlled, deliberate arc. | Perform 8–12 slow, controlled rotations on one side, pausing at the end range of each rep. | Switch to the opposite arm and repeat for the same number of repetitions. | Complete 2–3 sets per side, focusing on smooth movement and increasing range of motion with each repetition.

t: Stand upright in a relaxed, natural posture with your feet hip-width apart and your arms hanging loosely at your sides. | Look straight ahead at a fixed point on the wall or in a mirror at eye level to avoid tilting your head. | Relax your shoulders completely — do not shrug, pull them back, or force them into any particular position. | Have an observer stand directly in front of you, or position yourself in front of a full-length mirror so both shoulders are visible simultaneously. | Observe the height of the bony tip of each shoulder (the acromion) and note whether one side sits higher, lower, or level with the other. | Take a deep breath, relax, and repeat the observation two or three times to confirm the finding is consistent rather than a momentary postural shift. | Record which shoulder appears elevated or depressed, and note whether the difference is subtle or pronounced, to guide any follow-up assessment or corrective work.

t: Stand with both feet hip-width apart and centered on the middle of the band, or loop the band under one foot for a narrower stance. | Grasp one end of the band in each hand and bring your hands up to shoulder height with your palms facing forward and elbows pointed out to the sides. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and maintain a neutral spine — avoid arching your lower back. | Press both hands directly overhead in a straight vertical path until your arms are fully extended without locking the elbows forcefully. | Pause briefly at the top, ensuring the band does not pull you forward or to one side. | Lower your hands in a controlled manner back to shoulder height, resisting the pull of the band on the way down. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, keeping tension in the band throughout the entire set.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your arms alongside your body, palms facing down and legs fully extended. | Press your palms and arms firmly into the mat, then engage your core and swing your legs up overhead, bringing your hips off the floor. | Bend your elbows and place your hands on your lower back, fingers pointing upward, to form a supportive shelf for your spine. | Walk your hands higher up your back toward the shoulder blades to straighten your torso as vertical as possible. | Extend your legs straight up toward the ceiling, squeezing your thighs and pointing your toes so your body forms a single vertical line from shoulders to feet. | Keep your weight distributed evenly across both shoulders and your upper back — not your neck — and gaze softly at your toes or the ceiling. | Hold the position for the desired duration while breathing steadily through your nose. | To exit, lower your legs slowly back overhead, release your hands to the mat, and unroll your spine back down to the floor one vertebra at a time.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and hold one end of a towel in your right hand. | Raise your right arm overhead, bend the elbow so your right hand drops behind your head, and let the towel hang down your back. | Reach your left arm behind your lower back and bend the elbow upward so your left hand can grasp the lower end of the towel. | Gently walk your hands closer together along the towel until you feel a moderate stretch in both shoulders — stop before any pain. | Hold the position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and letting the shoulders relax deeper into the stretch with each exhale. | Release the towel, lower both arms, and shake them out briefly. | Switch sides: raise your left arm overhead and reach your right arm up from below, then repeat the same hold.

t: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, core lightly braced, and your spine in a neutral position. | Extend your working arm out to your side at shoulder height, palm facing forward or down, so it is roughly parallel to the floor. | Begin the movement by driving your arm forward and across your body in a smooth horizontal arc, keeping it at shoulder height throughout. | Continue sweeping the arm past the midline of your chest until it reaches the opposite side of your body — as far as your shoulder mobility comfortably allows. | Pause briefly at the end range to let the pectoralis major fully shorten. | Reverse the arc in a controlled manner, returning the arm back out to the starting position at your side. | Allow a small, natural rotation of the torso if your mobility requires it, but keep the movement led by the shoulder rather than the trunk. | Complete all reps on one side, then repeat with the opposite arm. | Perform 10–15 smooth repetitions per side, treating each swing as an active articulation rather than a ballistic throw.

t: Lie on your side on a flat surface with your body in a straight line from head to feet, stacking your hips directly on top of each other. | Rest your head on your lower arm or prop it up with your hand for support, and place your top hand lightly on the floor in front of your torso to help maintain balance. | Point your top foot slightly downward or keep it neutral, and ensure your toes face forward rather than toward the ceiling. | Brace your core to keep your torso stable and prevent your hips from rocking backward as you lift. | Exhale and raise your top leg upward in a controlled arc, leading with your heel, until it reaches roughly 45 degrees from the floor — or as high as you can go without your hips tilting. | Pause briefly at the top of the movement, feeling the contraction along the outer hip. | Inhale and lower your leg back down slowly until it is just above the bottom leg, maintaining tension rather than letting it drop. | Complete all reps on this side, then roll over and repeat on the opposite side.

t: Lie on your side on a mat with your hips stacked, your bottom arm extended under your head for support, and your top hand resting on the floor in front of your chest for balance. | Bend both knees to roughly 45–90°, keeping your feet together and your spine in a neutral position. | Brace your core lightly and press your feet firmly together throughout the movement. | Keeping your feet touching, rotate your top knee upward and outward as far as comfortable — like a clamshell — by contracting your glutes and outer hip. | At the top of the range, extend the top leg outward with a kicking motion, straightening the knee while maintaining the hip's outward rotation. | Pause briefly at the fully extended position, feeling the squeeze in your gluteus maximus and gluteus medius. | Reverse the movement by bending the knee back in and lowering it to meet the bottom leg in a controlled manner. | Complete all reps on one side, then roll over and repeat on the opposite side.

t: Set up in a high plank with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms fully extended, and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Spread your fingers slightly and press firmly through your palms to stabilize your wrists and shoulders. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and keep your hips level — they should not rise or sag. | Drive your right knee out to the right side toward your right elbow, keeping your foot close to the floor and your hips square. | Return your right foot to the starting position with control before initiating the next rep. | Drive your left knee out to the left side toward your left elbow using the same controlled lateral path. | Return your left foot to the starting position to complete one full rep. | Continue alternating sides at a steady pace, breathing rhythmically and maintaining your plank alignment throughout the set.

t: Sit or stand tall with your spine neutral, shoulders relaxed, and feet flat on the floor. | Let both arms hang at your sides or rest your hands on your thighs — keep your shoulders down and away from your ears. | Slowly tilt your head to the right, bringing your right ear toward your right shoulder. t: Lie on your side on a flat surface. Stack your feet on top of each other and place your bottom forearm on the floor with your elbow directly beneath your shoulder. | WRONG — Let your hips sag toward the floor so your body forms a downward curve. Notice how this collapses the waist and removes tension from the lateral core. This is the position to avoid. | WRONG (alternative) — Raise your hips too high so your body forms an inverted V (piked). This also misaligns the spine and shifts load away from the target area. | RIGHT — Brace your core and lift your hips off the floor until your body forms a single straight line from your head through your hips to your feet. | Keep your top hand on your hip or extend it toward the ceiling to help with balance. Your neck should remain neutral, aligned with your spine. | Press your bottom forearm into the floor to create a stable base, and squeeze your glutes and lateral core to maintain the rigid plank position. | Hold the correct position for the prescribed duration, breathing steadily. Resist any tendency for the hips to drift down or spike upward. | Lower your hips back to the floor with control to complete the hold, then switch sides.

t: Set a decline bench to your desired angle, typically between 30 and 45 degrees, and secure your feet under the foot pads. | Sit at the top of the bench and hold a single dumbbell with both hands, gripping each end of the weight (a diamond grip on the handle also works). | Lower yourself back until your torso is fully reclined, allowing your arms to extend overhead so the dumbbell is behind your head and nearly parallel to the bench. | Keep your arms relatively straight and your lower back in light contact with the bench pad at the bottom of each rep. | Brace your core and begin the sit-up by contracting your abdominals, curling your chin slightly toward your chest. | Continue raising your torso in a controlled arc, keeping the dumbbell extended overhead throughout the ascent. | Sit all the way up until your torso is upright or slightly past vertical, maintaining control of the dumbbell. | Reverse the motion slowly, lowering your torso back to the starting position under control. | Complete all reps for the set, then carefully bring the dumbbell to your chest before unclipping your feet.

t: Stand facing a wall or sturdy railing near a step or stair for balance support. | Place the ball of one foot on the edge of the step so your heel hangs freely off the back. | Keep your other foot off the step or lightly resting on it for stability. | Hold the railing or wall lightly with one or both hands. | Keep the working leg straight and your core engaged. | Slowly lower your heel downward below the level of the step, allowing gravity to deepen the stretch through the Achilles tendon and calf. | Hold the stretched position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily throughout. | Slowly raise your heel back to the starting position. | Complete all reps on one side before switching to the other foot.

t: Stand on a step, curb, or raised platform with the balls of both feet on the edge and your heels hanging free off the back. | Shift your weight onto one foot, placing the other foot lightly behind your working ankle for balance support if needed. | Hold a wall, railing, or doorframe with one or both hands to keep yourself steady throughout the stretch. | Slowly lower the heel of your working foot downward as far as comfortable, allowing gravity to deepen the stretch through your calf. | Keep your working knee straight to emphasize the gastrocnemius (the larger, outer calf muscle). | Hold the bottom position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and relaxing into the stretch rather than forcing it. | To target the deeper soleus, slightly bend the knee of the working leg and hold the lowered-heel position for another 20–30 seconds. | Raise your heel back to the starting position, then switch feet and repeat on the other side.

t: Kneel on a soft surface with both knees on the floor and your torso upright. | Bring your right foot forward so it is flat on the floor directly under your right knee, creating a half-kneeling position. | Tuck your pelvis slightly under to neutralize your lower back and engage your core. | Slowly lean your torso backward, shifting your weight toward your left heel while keeping your hips square and your left knee pointing down. | Lower your hands toward the floor behind you for support, or place them on your front knee if balance allows. | Continue leaning back until you feel a strong but comfortable stretch along the front of your left thigh and hip. | Hold the position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily. | Press through your hands to return to the upright half-kneeling position. | Switch legs and repeat the stretch on the opposite side.

t: Stand with feet hip-width apart on a flat, open surface. t: Stand facing away from a bench with your feet hip-width apart and the bench roughly one shin-length behind you. | Shift your weight onto your right foot and extend your left leg slightly forward off the floor, keeping it straight or lightly bent. | Brace your core, set your shoulders back, and hinge forward slightly at the hip to keep your torso from collapsing as you descend. | Bend your right knee and slowly lower your hips toward the bench, tracking your knee over your second toe throughout the descent. | Descend in a controlled manner until your glutes make light contact with the bench — do not relax or sit down fully. | Pause briefly at the bottom, maintaining tension in the glute and quad of the working leg. | Drive through your right heel to press the floor away and extend your hip and knee back to the starting position. | Complete all reps on the right leg, then switch sides and repeat with your left leg as the working leg.

t: Stand on one foot roughly 30–60 cm behind a low, stable board or step, keeping your standing knee soft and your core braced. | Hinge slightly at the hip and bend your standing knee to load your leg, swinging your arms back to prepare for the jump. | Drive your arms forward and upward explosively while pushing through the ball of your foot to launch yourself onto the board. | Land on the same single leg on the center of the board, absorbing the impact by bending your hip, knee, and ankle simultaneously — aim for a soft, quiet landing. | Stabilize briefly on top of the board, keeping your knee tracking over your second toe and your torso upright. | Drive off the board with the same leg, jumping back to the starting position and landing softly on that foot. | Reset your balance for a moment, then immediately repeat for the next rep. | Complete all reps on one leg before switching sides.

t: Stand facing a box or bench, feet hip-width apart and roughly one foot away from the surface. | Place the entire working foot flat on the top of the box so your knee is bent at approximately 90°. | Brace your core and keep your torso upright with a neutral spine throughout the movement. | Press firmly through the heel of the working foot to drive your body upward, avoiding any push-off from the trailing foot. | As you rise, bring the trailing leg up and forward, stopping with the hip and knee at roughly 90° at the top. | Pause briefly at the top with hips fully extended and the working glute contracted. | Slowly lower the trailing foot back to the floor under control, landing softly with the ball of the foot first. | Complete all reps on the same side, then switch legs.

Load the weight and stand facing the bar with your feet hip-width apart. | Grip the bar with a narrow, supinated (underhand/palms-up) grip, hands about 6–8 inches apart and directly below your shoulders. | Unhook the bar and hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly 30–45° above horizontal, keeping your back flat and your knees slightly bent. | Brace your core and retract your shoulder blades to create a stable base before initiating the pull. | Drive your elbows straight back close to your sides, pulling the bar toward your lower abdomen or belly button. | Squeeze your lats and mid-back at the top of the movement, holding for a brief pause. | Lower the bar in a controlled manner back to full arm extension, allowing your shoulder blades to protract slightly to stretch the lats. | Complete your reps, then stand up to raise the bar back to hook height and rotate it onto the rails before letting go.

t: Set the Smith machine bar to approximately hip height and stand facing it with your feet shoulder-width apart. | Hinge at the hips until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor, maintaining a neutral spine and soft bend in your knees. | Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip, letting it hang at arm's length. | Retract your shoulder blades and brace your core before initiating the pull. | Row the bar toward your upper chest, flaring your elbows out to roughly 90° from your torso to emphasize the rear delts. | Squeeze your posterior deltoids and upper back at the top of the movement for a brief pause. | Lower the bar in a controlled path back to the starting position, allowing your shoulder blades to protract fully. | Complete your reps, then re-rack the bar by rotating the safety hooks into place.

t: Set the Smith machine bar to upper-back height and load it with your desired weight. | Step under the bar and position it across your upper traps, away from your neck; unrack it by rotating the bar forward. | Stand with your feet hip-width apart and flat on the floor, toes pointing straight ahead or angled slightly outward. | Brace your core and stand tall with a soft, unlocked bend in your knees. | Drive through the balls of your feet and raise your heels as high as possible, squeezing your calves hard at the top. | Hold the peak contraction for one to two seconds, then lower your heels slowly until they rest flat on the floor again before starting the next rep. | After completing your set, rotate the bar to re-rack it safely.

t: Position a sturdy block or weight plate on the floor directly under the Smith machine bar. | Step onto the block with the balls of your feet, allowing your heels to hang off the edge freely. | Unrack the bar by rotating it and rest it across your upper traps, keeping your torso upright and your core braced. | Stand with feet hip-width apart and toes pointing straight ahead or slightly outward. | Lower your heels as far as comfortably possible toward the floor to achieve a deep stretch in your calves. | Press through the balls of your feet to raise your heels as high as possible, fully contracting the gastrocnemius at the top. | Pause briefly at the top of the movement before lowering with control. | Complete all reps, then rotate the bar to re-rack it safely.

t: Set the bar on the Smith machine at upper-chest height. Step under it and position the bar across your traps and upper back, not on your neck. Place your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width and unrack the bar. | Stand with your feet hip-width apart, facing forward. This is your starting position. | Shift your weight onto your right foot (the front leg). Cross your left foot behind and to the right of your right foot, stepping diagonally so your left toes land roughly one to two feet behind and outside your right heel. | Keep your torso upright and your front knee tracking over your front toes. Begin lowering your hips by bending the front knee and allowing the rear knee to drop toward the floor. | Descend until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor or your rear knee is just above the ground — whichever limit comes first. | Hold the bottom position for one count, then drive through your front heel to press back up to the starting stance. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch legs and repeat the crossover step with the opposite foot.

t: Set the Smith machine bar to its lowest position, just a few inches off the floor. | Place an exercise mat in front of the bar and kneel down on all fours — hands directly under your shoulders, knees under your hips. | Position yourself so that one foot can hook under the bar with the sole of that foot facing upward toward the bar. | Brace your core and keep your spine neutral — avoid letting your lower back arch or round. | Inhale, then drive the working heel upward and backward, pressing into the bar and extending the hip fully at the top. | Pause briefly at the top, squeezing the glute of the working leg. | Lower the leg slowly under control until the knee is back near the floor, resisting the weight on the way down. | Complete all reps on one side before switching legs.

t: Set the Smith machine bar to approximately mid-thigh height and load it with your working weight. | Stand facing the bar with your feet hip-width apart, unhook the bar, and hold it with a shoulder-width underhand (supinated) grip. | Let the bar hang at arm's length against the front of your thighs, keeping your torso upright and your shoulders pulled back. | Initiate the curl by driving your elbows back behind your torso rather than forward, allowing the bar to travel up along your body — brushing the abdomen, then the chest — as your elbows travel rearward. | Continue dragging the bar up until your elbows are fully bent and the bar is at upper-chest or shoulder level. | Squeeze your biceps hard at the top for a one-count, keeping the bar close to your body throughout. | Lower the bar under control by reversing the path — letting it slide down your torso as your elbows drift forward — until your arms are fully extended. | Complete your reps, then re-hook the bar safely.

t: Set the Smith machine bar to shoulder height and load it with your working weight. | Position a flat bench or sturdy box about two feet behind the bar. | Step under the bar, rest it across your upper traps, and unrack it by rotating the safeties. | Walk forward until there is enough space for a full lunge stride, then place the top of your rear foot on the bench behind you. | Position your front foot far enough forward so that when you squat down your shin stays roughly vertical and your knee does not travel far past your toes. | Lower your hips straight down by bending the front knee and hip, keeping your torso upright and your core braced. | Descend until your rear knee approaches but does not touch the floor, or until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the ground. | Drive through your front heel and mid-foot to extend the knee and hip and return to the starting position. | Complete all reps on that leg, then re-rack the bar, switch legs, and repeat.

t: Set the Smith machine bar to roughly shoulder height and step under it so the bar rests across the front of your shoulders on your anterior deltoids. | Extend both arms straight out in front of you, parallel to the floor, with palms facing down — the classic 'Frankenstein' position. | Step your feet roughly shoulder-width apart with toes turned out slightly, far enough forward that your torso can stay upright during the descent. | Unrack the bar by rotating the hooks and stand tall with your chest up, core braced, and your upper back tight to hold the bar in place. | Begin the descent by bending your hips and knees together and sitting straight down rather than pushing your hips back, keeping the bar stable on your shoulders without gripping it. | Squat down until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor or slightly below, maintaining an upright torso and keeping your knees tracking over your toes. | Drive through your full foot to press the floor away, extending your hips and knees at the same rate to return to the starting position. | Lock out at the top without hyperextending your lower back, then immediately begin the next rep or re-rack safely by rotating the hooks.

t: Position a flat bench perpendicular to a Smith machine and sit on the floor with your upper back resting against the long edge of the bench. | Set the Smith bar to a height that allows it to sit comfortably across your hip crease when you are seated on the floor. t: Set the Smith machine bar to roughly shoulder height and load it with an appropriate weight. | Place a stable platform or weight plate — 2–4 inches high — on the floor directly in front of the bar. | Step under the bar, position it across your upper traps, and unrack it. | Step one foot forward and place it flat on the platform, keeping the heel fully in contact with the surface. | Step the rear foot straight back until you are in a long split stance — far enough that your rear knee can reach near the floor at the bottom. | Stand tall with your torso upright, core braced, and hips square to the front. | Inhale and lower your body by bending both knees, letting the front knee track over your toes as you descend. | Stop when your rear knee is just above or lightly grazing the floor and your front thigh is at or below parallel. | Drive through your front foot to press back up to the starting position, complete all reps on one leg, then switch sides.

t: Set the Smith machine bar to upper-chest height and load it with the desired weight. | Step under the bar and position it across the front of your shoulders, resting on your front deltoids with your elbows raised high and upper arms roughly parallel to the floor. | Grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder width, using either a clean grip with fingers under the bar or a cross-arm grip for comfort. | Unrack the bar by rotating the hooks and step your feet to hip-width, toes pointed out 15 to 30 degrees, positioned slightly in front of the bar. | Brace your core, take a breath, and initiate the descent by pushing your knees out in line with your toes while sitting your hips back and down. | Lower until your thighs reach parallel to the floor or as deep as your mobility allows while keeping your torso upright and elbows high. | Drive through your full foot to press the floor away and return to the standing position, exhaling as you rise. | Rack the bar by rotating the hooks back into the catches once you have completed all reps.

t: Set the Smith machine safety pins at the height the bar reaches when it is resting on your upper traps and your torso is hinged to roughly parallel with the floor — around hip height for most lifters. Test the height with an empty bar first. | Load the bar and rest it on the pins, then step under it so it sits across your upper traps, not on your neck. Set your feet hip- to shoulder-width apart with toes turned out slightly. | Push your hips back to settle into the hinged start position with the bar loaded on your traps, a soft bend in the knees, and a neutral (not rounded) spine from tailbone to skull. | Brace your core hard, set your shoulder blades back and down, and take the bar's weight off the pins. | Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to stand tall, keeping your spine neutral the whole way up. Do not turn the rep into a squat by leading with the knees. | Pause briefly at the top with hips fully extended, then push your hips back and lower under control over 2–3 seconds along the same path. | Let the bar settle onto the pins and release the tension for a beat, then re-brace and drive the next rep from the dead stop. | After your final rep, stand tall, rotate the bar into the Smith machine hooks at standing height, and step out from under it.

t: Stand with the barbell over your mid-foot, feet hip-width apart. Take a wide snatch grip — much wider than shoulder-width, far enough out that the bar rests at your hip crease when you stand upright. Wrap your thumbs around the bar using a hook grip. | Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to reach the bar: set your hips above your knees but below your shoulders, back flat and neutral, chest up. Your hips and shoulders must rise at the same rate — if the hips rise faster than the shoulders the bar will swing forward. | As the bar passes your knees, shift it back slightly toward your hips and transition into the second pull. Maintain your back angle until the bar reaches mid-to-upper thigh. | Explode into the second pull by simultaneously extending your hips, knees, and ankles — triple extension — driving maximum upward force into the bar. This is the most powerful phase of the lift. | At the peak of the extension, shrug your shoulders forcefully straight up toward your ears with your arms still extended. Rise onto the balls of your feet as the bar reaches its highest point. | Lower the bar under control back to the floor by reversing the movement — hips back, knees forward — then reset your starting position before beginning the next rep.

t: Start on all fours with your hands directly under your shoulders and your knees under your hips. Keep your spine in a neutral position. | Take a slow breath in to prepare. On the exhale, begin the movement at the tailbone by gently tilting your pelvis into anterior tilt, allowing the lumbar curve to deepen. | Progressively extend the movement upward through each lumbar vertebra in sequence — think of stacking each segment into extension one at a time from the base of the spine toward the mid-back. | Continue until you reach a comfortable end range of lumbar extension, keeping your neck long and gaze forward rather than cranking your head back. | Pause briefly at the top of the extension arc, feeling a gentle lengthening through the front of the lumbar spine. | Reverse the motion by slowly returning each segment back to neutral, again moving sequentially from the lower lumbar upward. | Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, maintaining smooth, controlled articulation throughout each cycle.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides or crossed over your chest, and your gaze forward. | Take a slow breath in, then exhale as you begin to tuck your chin gently toward your chest. | Continue the exhale while rounding your upper back, then your mid-back, and finally your lower back, curling the spine forward one segment at a time from top to bottom. | Allow your torso to fold until you reach a comfortable end range — your hands can hang toward the floor or rest on your thighs if needed. | Pause briefly at the bottom, feeling a gentle stretch through the lumbar region and along the sides of the torso. | On your next exhale, slowly begin to rebuild the spine from the bottom up — stack the lumbar vertebrae first, then the mid-back, then the upper back, and finally lift your head to return to a tall, upright position. | Reset your breath and repeat for the prescribed number of articulations, keeping each repetition slow and deliberate.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides or hands resting lightly on your hips. | Engage your core gently and ensure your pelvis is level and neutral — avoid letting one hip hike before you begin. | Inhale to prepare, then on the exhale slowly side-bend your torso to the right, letting your right hand slide down the outside of your right thigh. | Move vertebra by vertebra, articulating through the lumbar spine rather than collapsing at a single segment. | Stop when you feel a lengthening stretch through the left side of your waist and hip — do not rotate or lean forward. | Hold the end position for one breath, actively reaching through the top of your head to maintain length. | Slowly return to upright on an inhale, stacking each vertebra back into neutral. | Repeat on the left side, then continue alternating for the prescribed number of repetitions.

t: Lie face-up on a firm, flat surface with your legs extended and your arms out to your sides at roughly shoulder height, palms facing down. | Bend your knees to roughly 90° and plant your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. | Brace your core lightly so your lower back maintains a neutral contact with the floor before you begin moving. | On an exhale, let both knees drop slowly toward the floor on your right side. Move only as far as your hips and pelvis will allow without your left shoulder lifting off the surface. | Pause at the end of your comfortable range for 2–3 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the obliques and iliopsoas to release. | On an inhale, engage your core and draw both knees back to the center starting position. | On the next exhale, let both knees drop slowly toward the floor on your left side, again keeping your opposite shoulder flat on the surface. | Pause for 2–3 seconds, then return to center on an inhale. | Continue alternating sides for the prescribed number of repetitions, moving at a deliberate, controlled pace throughout.

t: Sit upright on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you, feet flexed and hip-width apart. | Raise both arms to shoulder height, reaching forward with palms facing down. | Inhale to prepare, sitting as tall as possible and lengthening through the crown of your head. | Exhale and begin to curl forward, starting from the crown of your head, then rounding through your upper back and lower back one vertebra at a time. | Reach your fingertips forward past your feet, hollowing the abdominals inward and upward as you deepen the stretch. | Hold the stretched position briefly, feeling the lengthening through your spine, hamstrings, and calves. | Inhale and slowly stack your vertebrae back to the upright starting position, rebuilding the spine from the base to the top. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining smooth, controlled breathing throughout.

t: Sit tall on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you, feet flexed and hip-width apart. | Place your hands lightly behind your head or extend your arms out to the sides at shoulder height, whichever feels more comfortable. | Inhale to lengthen your spine, sitting as tall as possible and engaging your core. | Exhale and slowly rotate your upper body to the right, leading with your chest and keeping your hips and legs completely still. | Pause at the end of your comfortable range of motion for 1–2 seconds, feeling the stretch through your waist and obliques. | Inhale and return your torso back to the center with control. | Exhale and rotate to the left in the same controlled manner, again keeping the hips anchored to the floor. | Return to center, then repeat the sequence for the desired number of repetitions on each side.

t: Stand in your fighting stance with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and hands raised to guard position. | Shift your weight onto your rear foot and begin rotating your hips and shoulders away from your target, initiating the spin. | Pivot on the ball of your rear foot, allowing your body to rotate 180 degrees so your back momentarily faces the target. | As your body continues rotating toward the target, lift the knee of your kicking leg to chamber height — roughly hip to mid-chest level. | Drive your hips through by extending the kicking leg outward in a sweeping hook motion, making contact with the heel or sole of the foot at the target. | Keep your standing knee slightly bent throughout to absorb force and maintain stability. | Pull the kicking leg back sharply after contact, reversing the hook motion to chamber the knee again. | Land in a controlled stance with your weight centered and your guard back up, ready to follow with the next technique.

t: Stand tall with your feet together and your arms at your sides. | Jump and simultaneously split your legs so your right foot lands forward and your left foot lands behind you, landing in a staggered stance roughly shoulder-width apart. | At the same time, swing your arms in opposition — right arm forward and left arm back — to mirror your leg movement. | Keep your torso upright, core braced, and land with soft knees to absorb the impact. | Jump again and switch legs and arms in a single fluid motion, so your left foot moves forward and your right foot moves back. | Continue alternating the split position at a controlled, rhythmic pace. | To finish, bring your feet together on a jump and return your arms to your sides.
