t: Stand facing a sturdy box (6–18 inches tall) and step one foot forward into a split stance, with your front foot roughly two feet from the base of the box. | Sink into a lunge position — front knee bent to approximately 90 degrees, rear knee hovering just above the floor — with your torso upright and core braced. | Load your hips by driving them slightly back and keeping your front heel planted. | Swing your arms back to generate momentum, then explosively drive both arms upward as you push off both feet simultaneously. | Leave the ground with maximum power, extending fully through your hips, knees, and ankles at the peak of the jump. | While airborne, bring both feet together and position them to land simultaneously on top of the box with feet roughly hip-width apart. | Land softly with knees slightly bent, hips back, and weight distributed evenly across both feet to absorb impact. | Step back down to the floor one foot at a time, reset into the split stance, and repeat for the target number of repetitions before switching your lead leg.

t: Stand with your feet roughly two to three shoulder-widths apart and your toes turned out slightly, hands clasped in front of your chest or extended forward for balance. | Shift your weight to the right, pushing your hips back and bending your right knee as you descend into a lateral squat on that side. | Lower until your right thigh is roughly parallel to the floor (or as deep as your mobility allows), keeping your left leg straight and your left foot fully planted. | At the bottom of the squat, roll onto the outer edge of your left foot, allowing the sole to tilt slightly as your hips sink deeper and your torso leans forward with a neutral spine. | Pause briefly, feeling the stretch across your left inner thigh and groin. | Roll your left foot back to flat, then drive through your right heel to push yourself back up to the starting position. | Repeat for the desired reps on the right side before switching to the left.

t: Stand with feet hip-width apart, then step one foot forward roughly two to three feet, placing the ball of your back foot on the floor with your heel raised. | Align your front foot so the knee tracks directly over the second toe, and keep your back leg nearly straight with a soft bend at the knee. | Lift your torso to a tall, upright position — chest up, shoulders back, core braced — avoiding any forward lean. | Rest your hands on your hips or extend them alongside your body for balance. | Inhale, then lower your hips straight down by bending the front knee until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor or as low as control allows. | Keep your back knee hovering just above the floor without touching it, and maintain an upright torso throughout the descent. | Exhale and drive through your front heel to press the floor away, extending the front hip and knee to return to the starting high position. | Complete all repetitions on one side before switching legs, or alternate sides each rep depending on your training goal.

t: Start standing with your feet together and your hands relaxed at your sides. | Step your right foot forward roughly two to three feet and plant it flat on the floor, toes pointing straight ahead. | Lower your left knee toward the floor, keeping the left toes tucked under so you are in a low lunge position with the back knee close to — or resting lightly on — the ground. | Sink your hips down and forward until your right thigh is roughly parallel to the floor and your right shin is vertical. This is the low lunge base position. | Drive your right knee forward slightly over the toes to deepen the stretch in the left hip flexor while simultaneously pressing your right foot into the floor to engage the glutes and quadriceps. | To add the sprinter element, lean your torso slightly forward over the front thigh and drive both arms into a sprint-arm position — right arm back, left arm bent forward at roughly 90° — mimicking the upper-body mechanics of a running stride. | Hold the position for the prescribed duration or pulse gently through a small range of motion to increase hip-flexor release and glute activation. | Press through the right heel to stand back up, step your feet together, and repeat on the left side.

t: Stand in a split squat position: step one foot forward and the other back so your feet are roughly hip-width apart and staggered about two to three feet in length. | Raise the heel of your front foot off the floor so you are balancing on the ball of that foot. Keep the rear foot flat on the floor with the heel down. | Stand tall with your torso upright, core braced, and hands on your hips or extended in front for balance. | Inhale and slowly lower your body straight down by bending both knees simultaneously. t: Stand in a split stance with one foot roughly two to three feet in front of the other, both feet pointing forward and your torso upright. | Place your hands on your hips or extend them in front of you for balance. | Engage your core and lower your back knee toward the floor, keeping your front shin close to vertical and your front heel flat on the ground. | Once your back knee is just above or lightly touching the floor, initiate the roll by shifting your hips backward, letting the back knee travel slightly further back while your torso hinges forward from the hips. | Hold the rolled position for a brief pause, feeling a deep stretch through the hip flexor of the back leg and the glute of the front leg. | Reverse the roll by shifting your hips forward and returning to the bottom split squat position. | Drive through the heel of your front foot and the ball of your back foot to press back up to the starting position. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch legs and repeat.

t: Sit on the floor with your legs extended in front of you, then open them out to the sides as wide as is comfortable — typically 70–90° to start. | Flex both feet so your toes point straight up toward the ceiling, actively engaging your leg muscles to keep your knees tracking upward. | Sit up tall on your sit bones, lengthening your spine and lifting through the crown of your head. | Inhale and extend your arms forward along the floor between your legs, beginning to walk your fingertips away from your hips. | On an exhale, hinge from your hips — not your waist — and fold your torso forward, keeping your back as flat as possible. | Lower your chest toward the floor, resting your forearms, hands, or chin on the ground depending on your flexibility. | Hold the pose for 5–10 slow, deep breaths, allowing your hips and inner thighs to release a little deeper with each exhale. | To come out, walk your hands back toward your hips, inhale, and slowly lift your torso upright before drawing your legs together.

t: Stand facing a wall at arm's length and lean into it, placing both palms flat on the surface at roughly shoulder height. t: Set up four corners of a square on the floor, either by placing small markers (cones, tape strips, or water bottles) roughly 30–60 cm apart, or by visualizing the corners of an imaginary square. | Stand on both feet at the back-left corner of the square with a slight bend in your knees and your weight distributed evenly across the balls of your feet. | Brace your core, keep your chest up, and drop your hips slightly — this is your ready position between every hop. | Hop forward to the front-left corner, landing softly on the balls of both feet with your knees tracking over your toes. | Immediately hop to the right, landing at the front-right corner. | Hop backward to the back-right corner, controlling the landing and absorbing force through your ankles, knees, and hips. | Complete the square by hopping left, returning to the back-left starting corner — this counts as one full circuit. | Continue for the prescribed number of circuits or time (typically 20–40 seconds), maintaining consistent foot speed and the same square pattern throughout. | Finish by stepping out of the square and standing tall on both feet, letting your breathing settle before the next round.

t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and toes turned out slightly, arms relaxed at your sides. | WRONG — intentionally round your lower and upper back, letting your chest cave forward and your tailbone tuck under as you begin to descend. t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and toes turned out 15–30°. Let your arms hang at your sides or hold them in front for balance. | Look down at your feet and identify the line of each toe. t: Stand upright with your feet hip-width apart and toes pointing straight ahead or turned out slightly — either flat on the floor or with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step so the heels can drop below toe level. t: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointing forward, and your core lightly braced. | Bring both hands behind your head, interlacing your fingers loosely, or bend your elbows and rest your fingertips on your temples — keep your elbows wide and your chest open. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale as you slowly bend directly to the right, sliding your torso laterally without rotating or pitching forward. | Lower only as far as you can while keeping both feet flat on the floor and your hips level — you should feel a gentle stretch along the left side of your waist. | Hold the end position for one to two seconds, consciously relaxing into the stretch. | Inhale and use your obliques to draw your torso back to the upright starting position. | Exhale and repeat the movement to the left side, matching the range of motion you used on the right. | Continue alternating sides in a controlled, rhythmic manner for the prescribed number of repetitions on each side. | When finished, lower your arms and shake out your torso gently before moving on.

nR: Standing Wall Serratus Slide with Towel

t: Stand facing a smooth wall, roughly one arm's length away, with feet hip-width apart and a slight bend in your knees. | Fold a towel so it lies flat and place it against the wall at chest-to-shoulder height, holding one end in each hand with a comfortable overhand grip. | Lean gently into the wall so your palms press the towel firmly against the surface; transfer just enough weight forward to keep the towel in place. | Brace your core and align your body so your ears, shoulders, and hips form a straight line — avoid arching the lower back. | Before moving, actively push the wall away by protracting your shoulder blades: think of rounding the upper back slightly and spreading the shoulder blades wide apart. | Maintaining that protracted position, exhale and slide both hands upward along the wall in a controlled arc until your arms approach full overhead extension. | At the top, pause for a moment and reinforce the protraction by pushing harder into the towel, feeling the muscles along the sides of your ribcage engage. | Inhale and slide your hands back down to the starting position in a controlled manner, keeping light pressure on the towel throughout. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining active scapular protraction on every rep.

t: Place the wheel roller on the floor in front of you. Stand with your feet hip-width apart, a few inches behind the wheel. | Hinge at the hips and bend forward until you can place both hands on the wheel handles while keeping your legs as straight as your hamstring flexibility allows — a slight knee bend is acceptable. | Brace your core hard, squeeze your glutes, and create full-body tension before initiating the movement. | Inhale and slowly roll the wheel forward, allowing your hips to lower and your arms to extend overhead. Keep your spine in a neutral position — do not let your lower back arch excessively. | Continue rolling out until your body is nearly parallel to the floor or until you reach the maximum range you can control without your hips dropping or your back collapsing. | Pause briefly in the extended position while maintaining full tension throughout your core and hips. | Exhale and drive through your latissimus dorsi and teres major to pull the wheel back toward your feet, simultaneously lifting your hips and returning to the starting hinged position. | Reset your brace fully before beginning the next repetition.

t: Stand with your feet significantly wider than shoulder-width apart, toes turned outward at roughly 30–45°. | Place your hands on your thighs or hold them together at chest height for balance. | Slowly bend your knees outward, tracking them in line with your toes, and sink into a wide-stance squat position. | Keep your torso upright and your chest tall — avoid rounding your lower back. | Lower until you feel a comfortable pull along your inner thighs and groin, stopping before any sharp discomfort. | Hold the position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the adductors to relax into the stretch. | To deepen the stretch on one side, shift your hips slightly toward that leg and hold for an additional 10–15 seconds. | Press through your feet to return to standing, then repeat for the desired number of rounds.

t: Stand with your feet significantly wider than shoulder-width apart, toes pointed forward or angled slightly outward. | Place your hands on your hips or rest them on your thighs for support. | Keeping your back straight and chest tall, hinge slightly at the hips and push them back as you sink your weight downward. | Shift your bodyweight to one side, bending that knee while keeping the opposite leg straight, feeling a stretch along the inner thigh of the straight leg. | Hold the stretch for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and relaxing deeper into the position on each exhale. | Slowly return to the center, then shift to the other side and repeat for the same duration. | Alternate sides for the desired number of repetitions or hold the center position symmetrically if targeting both adductors equally. | To finish, walk your feet back toward center and stand upright.

t: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, chest up, and shoulders relaxed away from your ears. | Raise both elbows to shoulder height and bend them to 90°, so your forearms hang straight down with palms facing behind you — this is the starting position. | From this position, rotate both forearms upward and outward simultaneously, as if trying to press the backs of your hands toward the ceiling, until your forearms are parallel to the floor or slightly above. | Your arms should now form a "W" shape when viewed from the front — elbows at shoulder height and bent to 90°, forearms angled upward and out to each side. | Hold the end position for 2–3 seconds, consciously squeezing the shoulder blades together and feeling the stretch across the front and inner shoulder where the subscapularis and teres major are engaged. | Slowly rotate the forearms back down to the starting position in a controlled manner — do not let them drop passively. | Repeat for the desired number of reps or hold duration, keeping the movement smooth and deliberate throughout.

t: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and your arms extended straight out in front of you at shoulder height, palms facing down. | Interlace your fingers so both hands are clasped together. | Begin rotating your clasped hands to the right as if wringing water out of a towel, allowing your forearms to twist and your right arm to roll over the left. | Continue the rotation until you feel a stretch through your forearms, upper arms, and into your shoulders and neck. | Hold the end position for 2–3 seconds, keeping your elbows as straight as you comfortably can. | Slowly reverse the motion, returning your hands to the starting position with palms facing down. | Repeat the twist in the opposite direction, rolling your left arm over the right, and hold for 2–3 seconds. | Alternate sides for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining an upright posture throughout.

t: Stand with your feet roughly two to three times hip-width apart, toes pointing forward or turned out slightly. | Place your hands on your hips and stand tall, lengthening through your spine before you begin the fold. | Inhale to create length, then exhale and hinge at the hips — not the waist — folding your torso forward while keeping your back as flat as possible. | Lower your hands toward the floor, resting them on your shins, the floor between your feet, or blocks if you cannot comfortably reach the ground. | Allow your head and neck to relax downward without straining to look forward. | Press evenly through the entire foot — especially the outer edges — to keep your knees from collapsing inward. | Hold the position for five to ten slow, steady breaths, deepening the fold slightly on each exhale if your range allows. | To exit, bend your knees slightly, place your hands on your hips, and use your core to slowly hinge back upright on an inhale.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your arms extended overhead and your legs extended outward, forming a wide X-shape — like a starfish. | Press your lower back gently into the mat to engage your core before the first rep. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale forcefully as you crunch upward: simultaneously lift your shoulders off the mat and raise your legs, drawing your arms and legs toward each other at the centre. | At the top of the crunch, your body should form a shallow V-shape, with arms and legs hovering above the mat. | Hold the contracted position for one count, feeling your abdominals fully engaged. | Inhale as you slowly lower your arms and legs back to the full starfish position, keeping the movement controlled rather than dropping. | Allow your core to remain lightly braced even in the extended position — do not fully relax between reps. | Complete all reps, then lower fully to the mat to rest.

t: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, then step one foot forward roughly 2–3 feet so you are in a split stance with your front foot flat and your back heel raised. | Engage your core and keep your torso upright, shoulders stacked over your hips throughout the entire set. | Inhale and slowly lower your back knee toward the floor by bending both knees simultaneously, aiming for a 90-degree angle at each joint. | Stop when your back knee hovers 1–2 inches above the floor without letting it touch down. | Ensure your front knee tracks over your second toe and does not cave inward or shoot past your toes. | Exhale and press through the heel of your front foot to drive both legs back to the starting split-stance position. | Complete all reps on one side before switching legs, or alternate legs each rep as preferred. | Maintain the same foot position for the entire set — do not shuffle or reposition between repetitions.

t: Place a foam roller, folded towel, or firm pad on the floor perpendicular to your body. | Sit on the floor in front of the pad with your knees bent and feet flat. | Carefully lean back so the pad sits beneath your mid-back, roughly level with your shoulder blades. | Lower your upper back and head toward the floor, letting your spine gently drape over the pad. | Extend your arms out to the sides or rest them on your abdomen, whichever feels more relaxed. | Breathe slowly and steadily, allowing gravity to gradually increase the extension of your thoracic spine with each exhale. | Hold the position for 30 to 60 seconds, or as long as comfortable without pain. | To exit, engage your core, roll to one side, and use your arms to press yourself back up to seated.

t: Lie face-down on a flat, comfortable surface with your legs extended straight behind you and the tops of your feet resting on the floor. | Place your palms flat on the floor beside your chest, fingers pointing forward, elbows bent and close to your sides. | Gently press through your palms and forearms to lift your chest slightly off the floor, keeping your hips and pelvis grounded. | Find a comfortable degree of extension — a low sphinx position or a slightly higher prop — where you feel a mild stretch across your abdomen and hip flexors without pain. | Relax your glutes and lower back rather than actively squeezing them, allowing gravity and your body weight to deepen the stretch naturally. | Breathe slowly and evenly, letting your torso sink a little further into the stretch with each exhale. | Hold the position for 20–60 seconds, then gently lower your chest back to the floor to release.

t: Stand on a step, box, or raised surface with one foot near the edge and the other foot hanging free off the side, hip-width apart. t: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and hold a stick, dowel, or broom handle vertically in front of you with both hands stacked on top, resting the bottom end on the floor for support. | Engage your core lightly, keep your chest lifted, and distribute your weight evenly through both feet. | Begin the movement by reaching your torso laterally to one side, allowing the same-side hip to shift slightly outward while the opposite arm and shoulder rise; use the stick for balance rather than support. | Hold the lateral bend briefly at the end of your comfortable range, feeling the stretch along the obliques and the side of your waist. | From the lateral position, begin to rotate and hinge forward at the hips, transitioning smoothly toward a forward bend while maintaining a long spine. | Continue into the forward bend, allowing your hands to slide or walk down the stick as needed, until you feel a deep stretch across the iliopsoas, rectus abdominis, and front of the hips. | Hold the end position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and allowing your muscles to relax further with each exhale. | To exit, press through your feet, engage your core, and return to standing in the reverse order — front bend back to side bend, then upright. | Repeat on the opposite side for the same duration.

t: Lie on your back on the floor with your arms extended to your sides, palms flat for support. | Place your right heel on top of the stability ball, with your right leg nearly straight. | Raise your left leg off the ground, keeping it in line with or slightly above your right leg. | Press your right heel into the ball and engage your core to lift your hips just enough to keep them level — do not bridge high, maintain a neutral hip position close to the floor. | Curl the ball toward your glutes by bending your right knee, pulling the ball with your heel in a controlled arc. | Stop when your right knee reaches roughly a 90-degree angle and you feel a strong contraction in the back of your thigh. | Slowly extend your right leg to roll the ball back to the starting position, maintaining hip level throughout. | Complete all reps on the right leg, then switch legs and repeat.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs fully extended and feet together, toes pointing toward the ceiling. | Extend your arms overhead or cross them over your chest, depending on your preferred starting position. | Brace your core and press your lower back toward the mat before initiating the movement. | Exhale and curl your torso upward, leading with your chest rather than your chin, until your torso is roughly perpendicular to the floor. | Keep your legs flat on the mat throughout — do not let your heels rise. | Pause briefly at the top, feeling the contraction in your abs and hip flexors. | Inhale and slowly lower your torso back to the mat under control, resisting the urge to drop quickly. | Reset your brace and repeat for the desired number of reps.

t: Load the axle bar and set it on the floor; approach and position your mid-foot directly under the bar, feet hip-width apart. | Apply chalk generously to both hands, covering the fingers and palm — chalk is essential with a thick-axle handle. | Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to reach the bar; grip it with a double-overhand (pronated) grip, hands just outside your legs, fingers wrapped fully around the bar with no hook grip. | Flatten your back, lift your chest, and pull your shoulder blades down and back to create a rigid torso. | Take a deep breath into your belly, brace your core as hard as possible, and build tension through your lats by trying to 'bend the bar' around your shins. | Drive your feet through the floor to initiate the pull; keep the bar in contact with your shins as your hips and shoulders rise together. | As the bar passes your knees, drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to finish the lockout — stand fully upright with hips through and knees straight. | Hold the lockout position for a moment if required by the event, then hinge at the hips and lower the bar under control back to the floor. | Release your grip, reset your stance and bracing, and repeat for the required number of repetitions.

t: Sit on the floor with your legs extended in front of you and the rope running straight ahead, with the sled or load positioned at the far end. | Lean your torso slightly back into a braced, upright position; grip the rope firmly with both hands as far up the rope as you can comfortably reach. | Pull the rope toward you with your first hand, driving your elbow back and down to your hip to complete the stroke. | As your first hand reaches your hip, immediately reach forward with your other hand and take a new grip as high up the rope as possible. | Continue in a smooth, alternating hand-over-hand rhythm — each reach as long as you can manage without losing grip pressure. | Keep your torso braced and upright throughout; avoid rounding your lower back or falling backward between strokes. | Continue pulling until the sled reaches you or the set distance is covered, then release the rope and rest.

t: Stand with your feet roughly hip-width apart, toes pointed out slightly, with the atlas stone resting on the ground between your legs. | Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to lower yourself until you can wrap both arms around the stone, getting your forearms underneath it as low as possible. | Pull the stone tight into your lap by driving your elbows under it — your torso should be nearly vertical at this point, with the stone resting against your thighs. | Take a deep breath, brace your core hard, and keep your chest tall and back as straight as possible throughout the lift. | Drive through your legs by extending your hips and knees to raise the stone up your body, using your thighs as a shelf to re-grip as needed. | Continue extending your hips and leaning slightly back to load the stone onto the top of your thighs at roughly hip height. | From the hip position, explosively extend your hips forward and shrug upward, driving the stone up your torso toward chest height. | As the stone reaches chest height, use your arms and chest to guide it up and over the lip of the platform or barrel, extending fully to deposit it on top. | Step back under control once the stone is secured on the platform, reset your stance, and repeat for the required number of lifts.

t: Place two barbells parallel to each other on the floor, spaced roughly hip-width apart, and load each with equal weight. | Stand between the barbells with your feet hip-width apart, hinge at the hips, and grip each bar with a firm overhand grip just outside your legs. | Brace your core, retract your shoulder blades, and take a deep breath into your abdomen before initiating the lift. | Drive through your heels to stand tall, extending your hips and knees simultaneously as if performing a deadlift, until you are fully upright with the barbells hanging at your sides. | Hold the barbells with straight arms and tightly packed shoulders — avoid shrugging or letting the shoulders roll forward. | Begin walking with controlled, deliberate steps, maintaining an upright torso and keeping your gaze forward throughout. | Keep your core braced and your breathing rhythmic for the entire distance; avoid leaning to either side or letting the bars sway. | At the end of the distance, hinge at the hips and lower both barbells to the floor under control, following the same mechanics used to pick them up.

t: Position yourself at one end of the vehicle with your feet roughly hip-width apart and your toes pointing slightly outward. | Squat down and slide your hands under the bumper or chassis edge, gripping as wide and securely as possible with both palms facing up. | Brace your core tightly, keep your chest up, and set a neutral spine before you begin to lift. | Drive through your legs explosively, extending your hips and knees together to break the vehicle off the ground. | As the vehicle rises past knee height, shift your hips forward and begin pushing with your upper body, transitioning from a pulling to a pressing motion. | Continue driving with your chest and upper arms, pushing the vehicle upright until it tips past its balance point. | Step back quickly and under control as the vehicle falls forward and lands on its far end. | Reset your stance, walk around to the new end, and repeat for the desired number of flips.

t: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and the dumbbell on the floor just outside your right foot. Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to reach down and grip the dumbbell with a neutral grip, keeping your back flat and chest up. | Brace your core and set your lats. Your hips should be below your shoulders and your shoulder should be directly over or slightly in front of the dumbbell. | Initiate the clean by driving through your heels to extend your hips and knees explosively, pulling the dumbbell up close to your body. As the dumbbell reaches hip height, shrug your shoulder hard. | Continue pulling by driving your elbow high and fast. As the dumbbell reaches chest level, rotate your elbow under the dumbbell and drop into a quarter-squat to catch it at shoulder height in the rack position — dumbbell resting on your shoulder with your elbow pointing forward. | Stand tall from the quarter-squat to reach the fully upright rack position. Pause briefly to establish balance and a firm base. | Dip straight down by bending your knees 4–6 inches, keeping your torso vertical. Drive forcefully back up through your legs to load the dumbbell upward. | As the dumbbell leaves your shoulder, punch your arm overhead while splitting your feet front-to-back or pushing straight up into a slight squat. Lock your elbow out fully at the top. | Recover your feet to parallel and stand tall with the dumbbell pressed firmly overhead, arm fully extended and shoulder packed. | Lower the dumbbell under control back to the shoulder, then to the floor to complete one rep. Complete all reps on one side before switching arms.

t: Set the barbell in a squat rack at approximately upper-chest height, then step up and position the bar across your front deltoids and upper chest — the bar should sit in the groove between your shoulders and throat. | Cross your arms over the bar (each hand gripping the opposite shoulder) or cup your hands beneath the bar with elbows raised high, whichever allows you to keep the bar stable; elbows should be parallel to the floor or slightly above. | Unrack the bar by standing tall, take two small steps back, and set your feet shoulder- to hip-width apart with toes turned out 15–30 degrees. | Take a deep breath into your belly, brace your core hard as if bracing for a punch, and keep your chest tall and elbows up throughout the entire movement. | Begin the descent by pushing your knees out in line with your toes while hinging slightly at the hips, lowering under control until your thighs are parallel to the floor or deeper if mobility allows. | At the bottom, maintain an upright torso — do not let the elbows drop or the upper back round, as this will cause the bar to roll off the chest. | Drive through the full foot, push your knees out, and stand back up with a controlled, powerful extension of the hips and knees simultaneously. | Exhale at the top of the rep, reset your brace, then perform the next repetition. | After completing your set, step forward to re-rack the bar safely — never drop the elbows to attempt a forward dump.

t: Set up two weighted sleds or implements at equal distances from a centre point, arranged so they form a cross (plus-sign) pattern with the starting position at the intersection. | Step into the pulling harness and adjust the straps so they sit firmly across your hips and chest with the attachment point centred on your back, then take up the slack in the cables or chains. | Adopt a strong pulling stance: feet hip-width apart, knees slightly bent, hips pushed back, chest tall, and core braced as if preparing to absorb a heavy load. | Drive through your thighs and glutes to initiate forward movement, leaning into the harness at roughly a 45-degree angle to keep tension on the implement throughout each step. | Take short, powerful strides — pushing aggressively through the full length of each step — until you reach the first marker. | Come to a controlled stop at the marker, pivot to face the next arm of the cross, and re-establish your pulling stance before driving again. | Repeat the loaded pull in each direction of the cross, completing all required arms in sequence as fast and powerfully as possible. | Maintain an upright torso and active core on every arm of the cross — avoid excessive forward lean from the waist, which shifts stress from the thighs to the lower back. | After completing all arms, walk back to the centre point and remove the harness safely once the implement comes to a full stop.

t: Sit on the board facing your opponent with your feet firmly planted against the footboards, knees bent and positioned outside your arms. | Grip the wooden stick with both hands using a full overhand grip, hands approximately shoulder-width apart, placed between your opponent's grip points. | Brace your core, set your back into a rigid, slightly forward-leaning position, and press your feet hard into the footboards before the pull begins. | At the start signal, drive through your legs into the footboards and pull the stick toward your hips, engaging your back, arms, and entire posterior chain simultaneously. | Keep your elbows close to your torso and use your bodyweight as leverage by leaning back into the pull while maintaining a flat, braced spine. | If your opponent surges, resist by reinforcing your grip, pushing harder through your feet, and maintaining your position on the board without lifting your hips. | Continue pulling and countering your opponent's force until you extract the stick from their hands or pull them off the board, then release in a controlled manner. | When training solo, sit on the floor with your feet braced against a wall or anchor point, grip a resistance band or rope at the same height, and practice both explosive burst pulls and sustained isometric holds. | Rest fully between sets to allow grip and full-body recovery before repeating.

t: Stand the sandbag upright on the floor in front of you, centered between your feet, which are set roughly hip-width apart. | Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to reach around the bag, wrapping both arms as low around its girth as possible — aim to clasp your hands or forearms together behind it. | Brace your core hard, take a deep breath, and drive through your legs to stand up, pulling the bag tight to your chest and upper abdomen in a bear-hug position. | Once upright, squeeze the bag firmly against your torso, keep your elbows tucked, and pull your shoulder blades back and down to prevent the weight from rounding your upper back. | Maintain a neutral spine — chest tall, slight arch in the lower back — and avoid letting the bag's shifting load pull you forward. | Begin walking with controlled, deliberate steps, keeping your gaze forward and your breathing rhythmic; exhale on each step rather than holding your breath. | Walk the prescribed distance or time without setting the bag down, fighting any tendency to lean backward excessively to counterbalance the load. | To set the bag down, reverse the pick-up: hinge at the hips and bend the knees, lower the bag under control until it rests on the floor, then release.

t: Set the yoke uprights so the crossbar sits at approximately upper-trap height — you should be able to walk under it with a slight bend, not duck fully under. | Step under the yoke and centre the crossbar across your upper traps and rear deltoids, exactly as you would position a low-bar squat. | Take a tight grip on the uprights to help lock the yoke against your back, then brace your core hard and take a big breath into your belly (Valsalva). | Drive through your legs to stand the yoke up, keeping your chest tall and eyes fixed on a point at the far end of the course. | Begin walking with short, quick, controlled strides — keep your feet close to directly under your hips to minimise lateral sway of the yoke. | Maintain constant abdominal and glute tension throughout the walk; do not allow your lower back to hyperextend or your torso to lean excessively forward. | At the turnaround, plant both feet, pivot in place, and re-establish your brace before continuing — do not rush the turn. | At the finish, walk the yoke over the designated set-down point, hinge at the hips under control, and lower it to the ground — never drop it uncontrolled unless safety demands it.

t: Lie flat on your back with your legs extended and your arms resting at your sides. | Draw your right knee into your chest, wrapping both hands around your shin briefly to create a light compression through the hip. | Extend your right arm out to the side at shoulder height, palm facing up, to anchor that shoulder to the floor. | Use your left hand to gently guide your right knee across your body toward the floor on the left side, stacking the right knee roughly at hip height. | Turn your head to the right, away from the direction your knees are pointing, to extend the rotational stretch through the cervical spine. | Press your right knee gently downward with your left hand if it does not reach the floor, without allowing your right shoulder to lift. | Hold the position for 20–60 seconds, breathing slowly and letting your torso release further into the twist with each exhale. | Return your knee to center and lower your leg back to the floor, then repeat on the opposite side.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your arms extended out to your sides at shoulder height, palms facing down. | Bend your knees to roughly 90 degrees and lift your feet off the floor so your thighs are vertical and your shins are parallel to the ground. | Brace your core lightly and keep your shoulders pressed flat against the mat throughout the movement. | Slowly lower both knees together to the right, letting them travel toward the floor while keeping your left shoulder from lifting. | Lower only as far as your range of motion allows without discomfort, pausing briefly at the end of the range. | Reverse the movement and sweep both knees back through center and over to the left side in a controlled arc. | Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions, moving at a slow, steady tempo.

t: Kneel on the floor and interlace your fingers, placing your forearms flat on the mat shoulder-width apart to form a stable triangular base. | Set the crown of your head — not your forehead or the back of your skull — on the mat inside your cupped hands, so your hands cradle the back of your head. | Tuck your toes, lift your knees, and walk your feet in toward your elbows until your hips stack above your shoulders as much as possible. | Engage your shoulder blades by pressing your forearms firmly into the mat and lifting your shoulders away from your ears; this protects the neck throughout the pose. | If you are a beginner, position yourself facing a wall about one foot away so the wall can catch your feet if you go too far. | Draw your core in and up, then slowly lift one foot off the floor, bending the knee and bringing it toward your chest. | When you feel balanced, lift the second foot and bring both knees to your chest before gradually straightening the legs toward the ceiling. | Hold the inverted position for 5–30 seconds while breathing steadily, keeping your core firm and your shoulder blades active. | To come down, bend your knees back to your chest, lower your feet to the floor one at a time, and rest in Child's Pose for several breaths.

t: Stand facing a sturdy support — a wall, squat rack upright, or TRX straps held at arm's length — with your feet shoulder-width apart and toes turned out slightly. | Grip or lightly rest your hands on the support at chest height so it can assist balance without bearing significant load. | Brace your core and keep your chest tall before you begin the descent. | Push your hips back and bend your knees simultaneously, lowering your body as if sitting toward a chair behind you. | Continue descending until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, or as deep as your mobility comfortably allows. | Pause briefly at the bottom, keeping your heels flat on the floor and knees tracking over your toes. | Drive through your entire foot to press the floor away, extending your hips and knees together to return to standing. | Squeeze your thighs and glutes at the top and reset your brace before beginning the next repetition.

t: Set the suspension straps to a height where, when you grip the handles and extend your arms, your body forms a straight line from head to heels at roughly a 20–45 degree angle to the floor — the more horizontal your body, the harder the exercise. | Face away from the anchor point, grip one handle in each hand with a neutral or slightly outward-facing grip, and walk your feet back until your arms are fully extended in front of you. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and align your head, hips, and heels in a straight plank position before you begin. | Inhale and lower your chest toward the level of the handles by bending your elbows, allowing them to flare out to roughly 45 degrees from your torso. | Continue lowering until your chest passes the line of your hands and you feel a full stretch across your chest — handles should be near the outside of your chest. | Press your hands firmly into the handles and exhale as you push your body back up to the starting position, fully extending your arms without locking the elbows aggressively. | Keep the straps as still as possible throughout — resisting the natural sway of the handles is what drives the additional muscle demand. | Complete all reps, then step your feet forward to return to an upright position before releasing the handles.

t: Anchor the suspension trainer overhead, at or above head height, and hold one handle in each hand with an overhand grip, palms facing down. | Walk your feet forward until the straps are taut and your body is angled back — begin with a moderate lean of around 45 degrees and make the exercise harder by walking your feet closer to directly below the anchor. | Extend your arms fully in front of you so the straps take your weight; your body should form a straight line from head to heels with your core engaged. | Retract your shoulder blades and begin the pull by driving your elbows out to the sides and slightly back, leading with the elbows rather than the hands. | Pull yourself up until your hands are level with your ears and your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor, keeping your elbows flared wide rather than tucking them toward your torso. | Pause briefly at the top with your shoulder blades fully retracted and depressed, feeling the posterior deltoids and upper-back muscles contract. | Slowly lower yourself back to the start under control, allowing your arms to extend fully before beginning the next repetition. | Complete all reps, then step your feet back to release tension from the straps.

t: Stand facing the anchor point and hold one suspension handle in each hand with your palms facing each other, arms extended in front of you at roughly chest height. | Shift your weight onto your left foot and step your right foot back, placing the ball of your right foot on the floor about two to three feet behind you. | Keep your chest tall and your core braced as you bend both knees, lowering your right knee toward the floor in a controlled descent. | Lower until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor and your rear knee hovers just above the ground, or as deep as your mobility allows. | Drive through your left heel to stand back up, fully extending the hip and knee of your front leg. | Return your right foot to the starting position beside your left foot to complete one rep. | Complete all reps on one side before switching, or alternate legs each rep depending on your training goal.

t: Grip both suspension strap handles with your palms facing down and step back until your body forms a straight line from head to heels at roughly a 45° angle or lower to the floor — the more horizontal you are, the harder the movement. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and align your head, hips, and heels in a rigid plank position before beginning. | Inhale and begin lowering your chest toward the handles by bending your elbows, keeping them at roughly a 45° angle from your torso rather than flaring them straight out. | As you descend, simultaneously drive one knee out to the side and up toward the same-side elbow in a wide arc — this is the Spiderman knee drive. | Lower until your chest is level with the handles and your knee is as close to the elbow as your hip mobility allows. | Exhale and press back up explosively through the handles while returning the leg to its starting position. | Maintain a locked plank through the hips — do not let them sag or pike during the press. | Alternate the knee drive each rep, or complete all reps on one side before switching. | Rerack by walking your feet toward the anchor point and releasing the straps under control.

t: Stand facing the suspension anchor point and hold one handle in each hand with a neutral grip, arms extended at roughly shoulder height. | Set your feet together or slightly staggered, then walk them toward the anchor to the distance you want — the closer your feet, the steeper the lean and the greater the resistance. | Lean back so your bodyweight is supported by the straps, and brace your core so your body forms a straight line from heels to head. | Simultaneously sweep one arm forward and upward (anterior arc) while the other arm sweeps backward and to the side (posterior arc), keeping both elbows softly extended throughout. | Continue until your front hand is at or just above shoulder height in front of you and your rear hand is at shoulder height behind your hip — this is the split position. | Pause briefly at the end range, feeling the stretch and contraction across both deltoid heads. | Slowly reverse the motion, bringing both arms back to the starting position under control. | Complete all reps on this arm configuration, then switch the forward and rear arms to train symmetrically on both sides.

t: Set the suspension straps to a length where the handles hang at approximately waist height when you stand facing the anchor point. | Stand facing the anchor, feet shoulder-width apart or slightly wider, toes angled out 15–30 degrees. | Grasp both handles with a firm overhand grip and extend your arms so there is light tension in the straps. | Brace your core, keep your chest tall, and shift your weight back slightly into your heels. | Begin the descent by pushing your hips back and bending your knees, allowing them to track over your toes. | Lower yourself until your thighs reach parallel to the floor or as deep as your mobility allows, using the strap tension to counterbalance and maintain an upright torso. | Pause briefly at the bottom with your weight distributed across the full foot. | Drive through your heels and midfoot to extend your hips and knees simultaneously, rising back to the starting position. | Stand tall, fully extend your hips, and reset your brace before starting the next rep.

t: Set the suspension straps to a length that positions the handles roughly 12–18 inches above the floor when you are in a push-up position. | Place one hand in each strap handle and walk your feet back until your body forms a straight line from head to heels, arms fully extended beneath your shoulders. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and position your feet together so your body is rigid before beginning. | Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows out to roughly 45 degrees, keeping your hips level and your spine neutral. | At the same time as you descend, step or slide one foot laterally out to the side, spreading your stance into a star shape. | Pause briefly at the bottom with your chest level with the handles and your abducted leg fully extended to the side. | Press through both hands to extend your arms and return to the starting plank position, drawing the abducted leg back in line with the other. | Alternate the abducting leg each rep, or complete all reps on one side before switching, then walk your feet forward and step out of the handles to finish.

t: Stand tall with your feet together or hip-width apart, arms resting at your sides and weight evenly distributed through both feet. | Inhale and raise both arms overhead, interlacing your fingers and turning the palms to face the ceiling. | Root down through both feet and engage your core lightly to protect the lower back. | On your next exhale, slowly lean your entire torso to the right, keeping both arms straight and both feet planted firmly on the floor. | Hold the position for 2–3 breaths, feeling the stretch along the left side of your body from hip to fingertip. | Inhale to return to center with both arms still extended overhead. | Exhale and lean to the left, holding for 2–3 breaths to stretch the right side equally. | Return to center on an inhale, then lower your arms back to your sides to complete one full repetition.

t: Push off the wall or step into the water and extend your body into a horizontal, face-down position with your head in line with your spine. | Begin the arm cycle: reach one arm fully forward, enter the hand thumb-first into the water, and extend through the shoulder. | Pull that arm through the water in a high-elbow catch, sweeping it back along your centerline and finishing the stroke at your hip. | As one arm finishes the pull, recover it above the water with a high elbow and swing it forward to re-enter while the opposite arm begins its catch. | Keep a continuous flutter kick throughout — alternating small, quick up-and-down kicks driven from the hips, with relaxed ankles and feet just breaking the surface. | Rotate your body 30–45° toward the recovering arm on each stroke cycle; use that rotation to drive power into the pull rather than swimming flat. | To breathe, rotate your head with your body roll to the side — not upward — inhale quickly as your mouth clears the water, then return your face to the water and exhale steadily. | Maintain a streamlined body position throughout: hips near the surface, core engaged, and head neutral so water meets your forehead at the hairline.

t: Set up four cones in a T shape: place cone A at the starting line, cone B 10 yards directly ahead, and cones C and D each 5 yards to the left and right of cone B. | Stand behind cone A in an athletic stance — feet shoulder-width apart, knees bent, weight forward over the balls of your feet. | On your signal, sprint forward from cone A to cone B and touch the base of the cone with your right hand. | From cone B, shuffle laterally to your left toward cone C, keeping your hips square to the front and your feet from crossing. | Touch cone C with your left hand, then immediately shuffle to your right all the way past cone B to cone D. | Touch cone D with your right hand, then shuffle back to your left until you reach cone B. | Touch cone B, then backpedal in a straight line — staying low and facing forward — back to cone A. | Drive your arms actively throughout every phase to maintain stride rate and generate power through the cuts. | Stop the clock when you cross cone A and record your time; rest fully for 60–90 seconds before the next repetition.

t: Sit on the very edge of a firm table or plinth so your hips are at the table's border. | Lie back slowly while holding both knees to your chest to flatten your lower back against the table. | Keep one knee hugged firmly to your chest throughout the test to stabilize the pelvis and eliminate lumbar lordosis. | Lower the opposite (test) leg off the edge of the table, allowing gravity to pull it toward the floor. | Observe whether the test-side thigh rests flat and parallel to the table; a thigh that stays elevated indicates iliopsoas tightness. | Check whether the knee of the test leg bends to approximately 90 degrees; reduced knee flexion suggests rectus femoris tightness. | Note whether the test leg abducts (drifts outward) away from the midline; lateral drift indicates IT band or TFL tightness. | Return the test leg to the chest, sit up carefully, and repeat the assessment on the opposite side. | Record the angle and any compensations observed for each hip to guide stretching or rehabilitation priorities.

t: Sit at the very edge of a flat bench or table so that your hips are at the edge and you can safely lie back. | Bring both knees toward your chest as you lower your back down onto the surface, using your hands behind your thighs for support. | Once lying flat, pull one knee firmly into your chest and hold it there with both hands — keep this position throughout the test. | Let the other leg lower toward the floor in a relaxed, passive manner, releasing any muscular effort in that leg. | Observe or have a partner observe the position of the lowered leg: the thigh should be roughly parallel to the table and the knee should flex to approximately 90 degrees if hip flexor length is adequate. | Note any deviation: if the thigh rises above horizontal, the iliopsoas is likely shortened; if the knee fails to reach 90 degrees of flexion, the rectus femoris may be restricted. | Return the lowered leg to your chest, sit up carefully, and repeat the assessment on the opposite side.

t: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, arms resting at your sides. | Cross your right ankle over your left knee so that your right knee points out to the side in a figure-4 position. | Press through your left foot and drive your hips up into a single-leg glute bridge, squeezing the gluteus maximus and engaging the hamstrings to hold the position. | Once your hips are lifted and stable, reach your right arm up toward the ceiling, keeping the elbow straight. | Slowly rotate through your thoracic spine, lowering the right arm across your body and toward the floor on the left side while your hips remain elevated. | Follow the movement with your head and eyes, allowing the upper back to rotate as far as comfortable without letting the hips drop. | Pause for 2–3 seconds at the end range, feeling the stretch across the latissimus dorsi, obliques, and posterior shoulder. | Reverse the rotation to return the arm to the ceiling, then lower your hips to the floor to complete one repetition. | Complete all reps on this side, then switch — cross the left ankle over the right knee and repeat with the left arm sweeping.

t: Start on all fours with your hands directly under your shoulders and your knees under your hips, spine in a neutral position. | Inhale to prepare, then on the exhale slide your right arm along the floor underneath your left arm, palm facing up. | Continue threading the arm through until your right shoulder and right side of your head rest on the floor. | Allow your right shoulder to sink toward the ground while your left arm remains extended in front of you for support. | Keep your hips level and stacked over your knees — do not let them shift to one side or rotate along with your upper body. | Hold the stretch for 20–45 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the thoracic spine to rotate further with each exhale. | To release, press through your left hand and slowly return your right arm back to the starting position. | Reset to the all-fours position, then repeat on the opposite side by threading your left arm under your right arm.

t: Stand or sit tall with your spine neutral and one arm extended in front of you at shoulder height, palm facing down. | Curl your thumb across your palm toward the base of your little finger. | Wrap your remaining four fingers over your thumb to hold it gently in place. | Slowly bend your wrist downward, toward the floor, until you feel a moderate stretch along the top of your thumb and the outer forearm. | Hold the stretch for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and keeping your shoulder relaxed. | Slowly release your wrist and uncurl your thumb. | Repeat on the same hand for the prescribed number of holds, then switch to the opposite hand.

nR: Tibial Flexion Stretch On Wall Bar
nH: Tibial Flexion Stretch On Wall Bar
t: Stand facing the wall bar and grip it at roughly hip to waist height with both hands, feet hip-width apart. | Step one foot forward and place it flat on the floor, approximately 15–20 cm from the base of the wall. | Keep your back foot on the floor with toes pointing straight ahead, maintaining a slight bend in the back knee for balance. | Keeping the front heel firmly pressed into the floor, slowly shift your weight forward and drive the front knee toward the wall, allowing the ankle to dorsiflex. | Use the bar for support — do not pull yourself forward with your arms; let your body weight create the stretch organically. | Continue pushing the knee forward until you feel a distinct stretch along the back of the lower leg, Achilles tendon, and calf. | For a deeper stretch targeting the soleus and Achilles, allow a slight bend in the front knee; for more gastrocnemius emphasis, keep the front leg straighter. | Hold the stretched position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and relaxing further into the stretch with each exhale. | Slowly return to the starting position and repeat on the opposite leg. Perform 2–3 holds per side.

t: Begin on all fours in a tabletop position with your wrists directly under your shoulders, your knees under your hips, and your spine neutral. | Brace your core lightly and keep your neck in line with your spine — avoid looking up or letting your chin drop to your chest. | On an inhale, simultaneously extend your right leg straight back and reach your left arm forward, raising both limbs until they are parallel to the floor. | Pause for one breath in the extended position, creating length from your fingertips to your heel while keeping your hips level. | On an exhale, round your spine toward the ceiling and draw your right knee and left elbow together underneath your torso. | Hold the curled position briefly, bringing your knee and elbow as close together as your range of motion allows, with your spine fully rounded. | Return slowly to the extended position on your next inhale, then repeat the curl for your target number of reps before switching sides. | After completing the same number of repetitions with your left leg and right arm, lower both limbs and return to a neutral tabletop to rest.

t: Sit or stand in a comfortable position with the arm you plan to treat resting on your thigh or a flat surface, palm facing up. | Form a loose fist or extend the fingers of your opposite hand, and position your thumb or knuckles at the wrist end of the forearm. | Apply moderate downward pressure with your thumb or knuckles into the soft tissue of the forearm. | Slowly glide your pressing hand up the forearm toward the elbow, maintaining consistent pressure throughout the stroke. | When you encounter a tender or tight spot, pause and hold steady pressure on that point for five to ten seconds before continuing the stroke. | Return your pressing hand to the starting position at the wrist and repeat the stroke, adjusting the angle slightly to cover different areas of the forearm. | After three to five passes along the inner forearm, rotate the arm so the palm faces down and repeat the process on the outer forearm. | Complete three to five minutes of work on each forearm, then gently shake out the hand and wrist to encourage circulation.

t: Sit tall on a chair or stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, spine neutral, and shoulders relaxed away from your ears. | Let your chin drop gently toward your chest, feeling a mild stretch along the back of your neck. | Slowly roll your right ear toward your right shoulder, pausing for one to two seconds when you feel a gentle pull on the left side of the neck. | Continue the arc by tilting your head back slightly, looking up at the ceiling without compressing the back of the neck. | Roll your left ear toward your left shoulder, pausing again for one to two seconds. | Return your chin back toward your chest to complete one full circle. | Reverse direction and perform the same slow circular sweep the opposite way. | Complete three to five slow circles in each direction, then return your head to a neutral upright position.

t: Sit on the floor or on a bench with your legs extended in front of you and your torso upright. | Place the Tiger Tail roller horizontally across the outer lower leg, positioning it just below the head of the fibula — the bony prominence on the outside of the knee. | Rest your opposite hand on top of the roller to apply additional downward pressure and control the amount of force you use. | Slowly roll the tool down the outer lower leg toward the lateral ankle, taking 2–3 seconds per pass to cover the full length of the peroneals. | When you find a tender spot, pause over it and hold steady pressure for 20–30 seconds until you feel the tension begin to release before continuing. | Work back up toward the fibula head and repeat, completing 2–3 passes over the entire length of the muscle group. | Between passes, rotate your foot slightly inward and then outward to expose different fibers of the peroneal group to the roller. | Complete 2–3 minutes of rolling on each leg, then switch sides.

t: Stand or sit tall with your spine neutral and your feet roughly hip-width apart. | Raise your right arm straight overhead, then bend your elbow so your right hand drops behind your head toward the center of your upper back. | Bring your left hand up and place it on your right elbow, just above the joint. | Gently pull your right elbow toward the midline and slightly backward to deepen the stretch along the back of your upper arm. | Hold the position while breathing steadily, keeping your neck relaxed and your chin level — do not let your head jut forward. | Maintain an upright torso; avoid leaning to the side or letting your lower back arch excessively. | Hold for 20–40 seconds, or as long as instructed, feeling a comfortable stretch along the triceps and into the shoulder. | Release the pull, lower both arms, and shake them out gently. | Repeat on the opposite side, raising your left arm overhead and assisting with your right hand.

t: Stand tall at one end of a clear, flat surface with your feet together and arms extended out to your sides at shoulder height. | Fix your gaze on a point directly ahead at eye level to anchor your balance throughout the movement. | Step forward with one foot, placing the heel directly in front of the toes of the standing foot so the feet form a continuous line. | Shift your weight smoothly onto the front foot as you bring it fully down, keeping your hips level and avoiding sideways sway. | Bring the back foot forward and again place the heel directly against the toes of the foot now in front, continuing the heel-to-toe chain. | Maintain a slight bend in the knee of the standing leg to engage the stabilising muscles and absorb any balance corrections. | Keep your core braced and your arms gently active — make small, controlled adjustments with your hands rather than large swinging motions. | Continue walking in a straight line for the target distance or rep count, then pause, turn carefully, and walk back. | Perform the prescribed number of lengths and finish by returning to a neutral standing position.

t: Stand facing the tire with your feet hip-width apart and your toes close to its base. | Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to squat down, sliding your fingers under the tire's lower edge with your palms facing up and your spine in a neutral position. | Brace your core, take a breath into your belly, and grip the tire firmly with both hands. | Drive explosively through your heels, extending your hips and knees to lift the tire off the ground — keep it close to your body throughout the pull. | As the tire rises past hip height, step forward to close the gap and shift your hands from underneath to a pushing position on the side of the tire. | Drive through your palms, pressing the tire forward and over until it falls flat on the ground. | Walk to the opposite side of the tire, reset your stance and grip, and begin the next rep.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides or held lightly in front of you for balance. | Shift your weight forward onto the balls of your feet, lifting your heels slightly off the ground. | Spring upward by quickly extending through your ankles and pushing off with your toes, leaving the ground with a small, controlled jump. | Keep the jump compact — focus on height generated by ankle extension rather than by bending your knees deeply. | As you rise, keep your core braced and your torso upright with a neutral spine. | Land softly on the balls of your feet, absorbing impact through your ankles and allowing your heels to lightly kiss the ground. | Rebound immediately into the next jump, maintaining a continuous, rhythmic cadence with minimal ground contact time. | Complete the target number of reps or duration, then lower both heels fully to the floor to rest.

t: Kneel on the floor on a mat or soft surface with your knees together and feet pointing straight back. | Tuck all ten toes under so the balls of your feet press into the floor and your toes are dorsiflexed. | Slowly sit back toward your heels, shifting your bodyweight onto your tucked toes. | Place your hands on your thighs or the floor for balance as needed. | Keep your spine upright and your torso relaxed — avoid hunching forward. | Hold the position for 30–60 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the stretch to deepen gradually. | To release, lean forward slightly, lift your hips, and untuck your toes before returning to a neutral kneeling position.

t: Sit on the floor with your back flat against a wall and your legs extended straight out in front of you, feet together and toes pointing up. | Press your lower back gently into the wall and sit tall, engaging your core before you begin. | Extend both arms straight out in front of you at shoulder height, parallel to the floor. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale as you rotate your torso to one side, reaching both hands toward the toes on that side. | Keep your legs pressed firmly into the floor and your quadriceps contracted so your knees remain straight throughout the movement. | Hold the rotated position for one second, feeling the obliques engage on the working side. | Inhale as you return to the centered starting position with your back against the wall. | Repeat the reach on the opposite side to complete one full repetition. | Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.

t: Grip an overhead bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip, thumbs wrapped fully around the bar. | Jump or step up so that your chin clears the bar and your chest is close to it — this is your starting position. | Pull your shoulder blades down and together, keeping your chest open and your torso from swinging. | Hold your elbows at full flexion with your chin above the bar, maintaining a slight forward lean of the torso. | Breathe steadily throughout the hold without letting your shoulders shrug up toward your ears. | Aim to hold the position for the target duration — typically 5 to 30 seconds depending on your strength level. | Lower yourself under control until your arms are fully extended, then release the bar.

t: Stand tall with your feet together, arms relaxed at your sides, and your core lightly braced. | Take a step forward with your right foot to create a short walking stride. | As you shift your weight onto the right foot, swing your left leg straight forward and upward, keeping the knee fully extended. | Simultaneously reach your right arm forward and down toward the toes of your rising left foot. | Aim to bring your hand and foot as close together as possible without rounding your lower back or bending the raised knee. | Lower the left foot to the ground in front of you to take a step, then repeat the movement on the opposite side. | Swing the right leg up while reaching the left arm toward the right foot. | Continue walking forward in this alternating pattern, maintaining an upright torso and a controlled, deliberate kick on each rep. | Complete 10–20 total reps (5–10 per leg) or cover the prescribed distance before moving on to the next warm-up drill.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand with your arms hanging at your sides. | Brace your core and keep your chest up to establish a neutral spine before you move. | Step one foot out at roughly a 45° diagonal angle (forward-lateral) or a rear-lateral angle, depending on the variation you are using. | Sink into the lunge by bending both knees, lowering your hips toward the floor until your front thigh approaches parallel to the ground. | Keep your front knee tracking over your second toe and avoid letting it cave inward. | Drive through the heel of your stepping foot to push the floor away and return to the starting position. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch legs, or alternate legs each rep.

t: Stand with a sturdy box or step at roughly a 45° diagonal to your front-right, feet hip-width apart. | Shift your weight onto your left foot, then pivot on your right hip and place your right foot fully on the step, toes pointing along the diagonal. | Let your torso and hips rotate to face the step as the foot lands, keeping your chest up and core braced. | Drive through your right heel to press yourself up onto the step, straightening your right leg at the top. | Bring your left foot up beside your right foot so you are standing tall on the step. | Step your left foot back down to the floor with control, rotating back to your start position, then follow with your right foot. | Complete all reps on one side, then set the step at a 45° diagonal to your front-left and repeat with the left leg leading.

t: Sit upright in a chair or stand with your feet hip-width apart, shoulders relaxed and arms resting at your sides. | Slowly tilt your head to the right, bringing your right ear toward your right shoulder until you feel a gentle pull along the left side of your neck and upper trapezius. | Reach your right hand over the top of your head and rest it lightly on the left side of your head, just above the ear — do not pull; allow the weight of your relaxed hand alone to deepen the stretch gradually. | Actively press your left shoulder downward, away from your ear, to increase the stretch through the upper trapezius and the side of the neck. | Hold this position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and allowing the muscles to lengthen with each exhale. | Gently lift your head back to center, remove your hand, and pause for a few seconds before switching sides. | Tilt your head to the left, place your left hand lightly on the right side of your head, and hold for another 20–30 seconds. | Return to the starting position and repeat for 2–3 sets per side.

t: Load the trap bar and step inside it, positioning your feet hip-width apart with the bar centered over your mid-foot. | Hinge at the hips and push them back until your torso is roughly 45° to the floor — or closer to parallel for a stricter row — then grip the neutral handles firmly with both hands. | Slightly bend your knees, brace your core, and pull your shoulder blades back and down to set a flat, neutral spine before the first rep. | Take a breath in, brace hard, and drive your elbows straight back and slightly flared — keeping them close to your body — until the handles reach your lower ribcage. | Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the movement for a brief pause to maximize mid-trap and rhomboid recruitment. | Lower the handles under control along the same path, fully extending your arms and allowing your shoulder blades to protract slightly at the bottom. | Reset your brace at the bottom of each rep without losing the hip-hinge position, then initiate the next pull. | After completing your set, lower the bar to the floor in a controlled manner by pushing your hips back and bending your knees — do not let it drop from a bent-over position.

nR: Two Legged Inverted Staff Pose Dwi Pada Viparita Dandasana

nE: Two Legs Hammer Curl with Towel (VERSION 2)
nR: Two Legs Hammer Curl with Towel (VERSION 2)
nH: Two Legs Hammer Curl with Towel (VERSION 2)
t: Sit on the floor or on the edge of a firm, flat surface and fold a bath towel lengthwise into a long strip. | Loop the center of the towel around the arches of both feet, then hold one end of the towel in each hand with a neutral grip — palms facing each other as in a hammer curl. | Extend your arms straight and raise both legs off the floor so the towel is taut between your hands and feet before the movement begins. | Sit tall with your spine upright, shoulders pulled back and down, and core braced to prevent your torso from rocking. | Begin the curl by bending both elbows simultaneously, driving your knuckles upward toward your shoulders while keeping your palms facing each other throughout. | Hold your legs steady — your feet and legs are the anchor providing resistance, so any unintended movement of the feet reduces the load. | Continue curling until your hands are at or near shoulder level and you feel a strong contraction in your brachioradialis and upper arms. | Slowly extend your elbows back to the starting position over two to three seconds, maintaining towel tension and keeping your legs elevated. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions without allowing the towel to go slack between reps.

t: Loop a towel around a sturdy overhead anchor point — a door frame, pull-up bar, or structural beam — and let both ends hang down within reach. | Lie on your back on the floor directly beneath the anchor, with your arms extended overhead and your hands gripping one end of the towel each, palms facing down (pronated grip). | Raise both legs off the floor and hold them at a comfortable angle, keeping your core braced so your body forms a rigid plank from shoulders to feet. | Exhale and pull your torso upward by driving your elbows toward your hips, keeping the pronated grip throughout the movement. | Continue curling until your hands reach the sides of your chest or your elbows are fully flexed — whichever your range of motion allows. | Hold the top position for a brief pause, squeezing the elbow flexors. | Inhale and lower yourself back to the starting position under full control until your arms are fully extended. | Repeat for the target number of reps without letting your hips sag or your legs drop.

t: Stand between two vertical ropes hanging parallel and close together. Reach up and grasp one rope in each hand at roughly the same height, slightly above your head. | Pull your shoulder blades down and back to engage your lats before you begin climbing. | Simultaneously pull both ropes downward by driving your elbows toward your hips, lifting your body off the ground. | As your hands reach chest or chin level, re-grip higher up each rope — right hand then left hand (or both together if the ropes are close enough) — before your arms extend fully. | Keep your core braced and your body as vertical and controlled as possible throughout the climb; avoid excessive swinging or kipping. | Continue alternating pulls and re-grips, maintaining tension in your lats and a firm grip, until you reach your target height. | To descend, lower yourself hand-over-hand in a controlled manner, resisting the urge to slide or drop quickly.

t: Stand with your feet hip-width apart on a firm, flat surface with enough clear space in front of and around you. | Bend your knees and hips into a quarter-squat, swinging your arms back to load the jump. | Drive your arms forward and upward as you extend through your hips, knees, and ankles to jump as high as you comfortably can. | While in the air, identify your landing foot and draw the opposite knee up slightly to prepare for a single-leg landing. | Land softly on the ball of your chosen foot first, then let your heel settle as you absorb the impact by bending your knee and hip — aim for a 45–60° knee bend at the bottom. | Keep your landing knee tracking over your second toe and your torso upright; avoid letting the knee cave inward. | Hold the single-leg landing position for one to two seconds to confirm balance and control before resetting. | Return both feet to the ground, reset your stance, and repeat for the desired number of reps, alternating the landing leg each set or each rep.

t: Grip a pull-up bar with one hand in a standard overhand position and place your other hand several inches lower — either by gripping a looped towel, a gymnastics ring, or a lower rung — so the two hands are at noticeably different heights. | Hang at full arm extension with both arms, letting your shoulders depress naturally into a passive hang. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and cross your ankles to keep your lower body still throughout the set. | Initiate the pull by actively depressing and retracting the shoulder blade on the higher-hand side. | Drive your higher elbow down and back while allowing your lower arm to assist with reduced force. | Pull until your chin clears the bar or until the higher-side elbow reaches full flexion. | Lower yourself under control to full arm extension, maintaining tension rather than dropping passively. | Complete all target reps on one side, then switch hand positions and perform the same number of reps on the opposite side.

t: Step onto the vibration plate and set the frequency to a low-to-moderate level (25–40 Hz is a common starting range for stretching work). | Stand upright at the center of the plate with your feet hip-width apart, core lightly braced, and hands on your hips or at your sides for balance. | Step your right foot forward roughly two to three feet, placing it flat on the plate and keeping your left foot in place behind you. | Lower your back (left) knee toward the plate by bending both knees simultaneously, descending until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the plate and your rear knee hovers just above it. | Keep your torso upright and your front knee tracking directly over your second toe — do not let it cave inward or drive past your toes. | Hold the lowered position for 2–3 seconds, allowing the vibration to work through your hips, thighs, and calves. | Push through your front heel to drive yourself back to the standing position. | Complete all reps on the right side, then switch legs and repeat the sequence with the left foot forward.
