t: Begin in a high plank position with your hands shoulder-width apart, wrists directly under your shoulders, body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Engage your core and keep your elbows close to your sides as you lower your body toward the floor in a slow, controlled descent — this is chaturanga dandasana. | Lower until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor, elbows at a 90-degree angle, and pause briefly without letting your hips sag or rise. | Press through your palms and roll over your toes to shift into upward-facing dog: straighten your arms, lift your chest, draw your shoulders back and down, and let only your hands and the tops of your feet contact the floor. | Hold the upward-facing dog position for one breath, keeping your thighs lifted off the floor and your neck long. | Exhale, tuck your toes, and press your hips up and back to transition into downward-facing dog, forming an inverted V-shape. | In downward-facing dog, straighten your arms, press your heels toward the floor, and lengthen your spine away from your hands. | Hold for one to three breaths before stepping or jumping your feet toward your hands to return to the top of the sequence or to a standing position.

t: Place your hands shoulder-width apart on the floor about 30–45 cm from a wall, fingers spread wide and pointing forward. | Kick up into a handstand with your heels lightly resting against the wall, arms fully locked out and body vertical. | Squeeze your glutes, brace your core hard, and protract (push away) your shoulder blades to establish full body tension. | Tuck both knees toward your chest simultaneously, shifting your center of mass forward and away from the wall. | Begin leaning forward through your shoulders, letting your hips drop slowly by increasing the forward tilt of your torso. | Maintain straight, locked arms throughout — resist the descent using shoulder flexion strength and core tension, not by bending your elbows. | Lower your body as slowly as possible, aiming to hold the tucked horizontal position (tuck planche) for a beat before continuing. | Either hold the lowest position you can control for 1–3 seconds, or continue descending until your knees or feet touch the floor in a controlled manner. | Rest fully before the next repetition — this is a high-neurological-demand movement; 2–3 minutes between sets is appropriate.

t: Stand facing a wall with your feet shoulder-width apart and a target mark on the wall roughly 10 feet (3 m) high; hold a medicine ball at chest height with both hands. | Brace your core, keep your chest tall, and push your hips back to begin the squat descent. | Lower until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, keeping your knees tracking over your toes and the ball at chest level. | Drive explosively through your heels to stand, extending your hips and knees simultaneously. | As you reach full hip extension, use the momentum to press and throw the medicine ball upward toward the target on the wall. | Watch the ball as it hits the target and rebounds off the wall. | Catch the ball with both hands at chest height, absorbing the impact by softening your elbows. | Immediately use the catch momentum to flow into the next squat descent without pausing. | Repeat for the prescribed number of reps or time, maintaining a smooth, rhythmic squat-throw-catch cycle throughout.

t: Set up in a plank with your feet against the base of the wall and your palms flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart with fingers spread wide. | Walk your feet up the wall while stepping your hands back toward the baseboard until your palms are about 6–10 inches from it, your chest is close to the wall, and both legs are together. | Establish a solid base: lock out your elbows, press through your fingertips, push the floor away so your shoulders elevate and protract, and engage your core. | Slowly peel one leg off the wall and reach it away from the wall behind you while keeping the other leg in contact with the wall. | Press the wall leg straight up along the wall so it stays in line with your torso, and simultaneously reach the free leg as far back as your hip flexibility allows. | Square your hips as much as possible — avoid rotating the pelvis toward either leg; aim to keep both hip points level. | Hold the split position for the target duration, breathing steadily through your nose. | To exit, bring both legs back together against the wall, then walk your feet down or lower in a controlled tucked descent.

Keep your torso upright and directly over your hips, not leaning toward the bent knee. | Hold the pose for 5 to 10 steady breaths, maintaining length through the crown of your head and relaxed shoulders. | To release, straighten your right leg on an inhale, lower your arms, and return your feet to parallel. Repeat the full pose on the opposite side.

t: Stand at the top of your mat, then step your feet wide apart — roughly 3.5 to 4 feet — so your stance is stable but not strained. | Turn your right foot out 90 degrees so the toes point toward the short edge of the mat, then angle your left foot in about 15 degrees so the heel is grounded and the arch lifts slightly. | Align your right heel with the arch of your left foot, pressing all four corners of each foot evenly into the floor. | Inhale and extend both arms out to the sides at shoulder height, palms facing down, reaching actively through the fingertips without shrugging the shoulders. | Exhale and bend your right knee until it tracks directly over your right ankle, aiming for the shin to be vertical and the thigh parallel to the floor — do not allow the knee to cave inward. | Keep your torso upright and centered between both legs, neither leaning over the front thigh nor tilting back. | Turn your head to gaze over your right (front) hand with a soft but focused look — this is the traditional drishti for the pose. | Hold for 5 to 10 steady breaths, maintaining even pressure through both feet and an active reach through both arms. | To release, straighten the front leg on an inhale, lower the arms, and either pause in a wide-leg stance before switching sides or step back to the center of the mat.

t: Begin standing tall at the top of your mat in Mountain Pose (Tadasana) with your feet together and arms at your sides. | Step your left foot back approximately 3–4 feet, angling it out 45–60 degrees. Repeat on the opposite side.

t: Load a sturdy backpack with the target weight, positioning the weight high and close to your back to keep the load centered over your hips. | Adjust the shoulder straps so the pack sits snugly against your upper back without any swaying, then fasten the chest strap if one is available. | Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, take a few deep breaths, and establish an upright posture before you begin. | Start at a brisk walk for one to two minutes to let your body acclimate to the load and warm up your hips and ankles. | Transition to a jog or run at a controlled pace, keeping your torso upright and your gaze forward rather than looking at the ground. | Drive your arms naturally at your sides and maintain a slight forward lean from your ankles, not your waist, to stay balanced under the pack. | Land with each foot roughly under your hips, using a mid-foot strike to reduce impact forces on your knees and lower back. | Keep your core braced throughout to prevent the pack from pulling your spine into excessive extension. | Slow to a walk during the final one to two minutes to cool down, then remove the pack before stretching your hip flexors, calves, and upper back.

t: Pack a backpack with a load appropriate for your fitness level — beginners can start with 10–15 lb and progress over time. | Position the backpack high on your back so the load sits close to your shoulder blades rather than hanging low toward your hips. | Fasten the sternum strap and hip belt if available to distribute the weight and prevent the pack from shifting side to side. | Stand tall with your shoulders back and your head in a neutral position — avoid rounding forward under the load. | Begin walking at a brisk, deliberate pace, striking the ground with your heel and rolling through to push off with your toes. | Keep your arms relaxed and swinging naturally at your sides, bending at the elbows to help maintain your walking rhythm. | Maintain an upright posture throughout the walk — check in regularly and pull the shoulders back if you feel them rounding. | Continue for the planned distance or duration, then remove the pack and allow your spine and shoulders to decompress before any additional training.

t: Stand with feet hip- to shoulder-width apart and drape the weighted bag across your upper back, gripping the sides to keep it secure. | Brace your core, pull your shoulder blades down and back, and establish a neutral spine from your tailbone to the crown of your head. | Soft-bend your knees slightly — about 10–15 degrees — and maintain that angle throughout the movement. | Push your hips back, hinging at the hip joint rather than bending at the waist, while keeping your chest up and your back flat. | Lower your torso until it is roughly parallel to the floor, or until you feel a firm stretch through your hamstrings and cannot maintain a neutral spine. | Pause briefly at the bottom, keeping tension in your hamstrings and glutes. | Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return to the upright starting position. | Reset your brace between reps if needed before beginning the next repetition.

t: Set the GHD so the hip pad sits just below your hip bones, giving your legs full clearance to swing. Place a weighted ball on the floor near the foot end of the machine. | Lie face-down on the GHD, draping your hips over the pad edge. Grip the handles firmly and let your legs hang straight down toward the floor. | Reach down with your feet and secure the weighted ball between your ankles, squeezing to hold it in place before you begin. | Brace your core and squeeze your glutes, then drive your heels upward in a controlled arc until your body forms a straight line from head to heels — or just slightly above parallel with the floor. | Hold the top position for a brief pause, actively contracting your glutes and posterior chain at full hip extension. | Lower your legs back down in a slow, controlled manner, resisting gravity until you return to the starting hang position. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, maintaining a steady grip on the handles and keeping the ball secured throughout each rep. | When the set is complete, carefully lower your legs, release the ball to the floor, and dismount the GHD safely.

t: Sit on the edge of a flat bench with your hands gripping the bench just outside your hips, fingers pointing forward. | Place a weight plate or dumbbell across your lap just above your knees, and use your forearms to hold it steady. | Slide your hips off the bench and extend your legs in front of you with your heels resting on the floor, or place your feet on a second bench to increase the range of motion. | Pull your shoulders down and back, brace your core, and keep your hips close to the bench. | Inhale and lower your body by bending your elbows, tracking them straight back rather than flaring them out, until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor. | Exhale and press through the heel of your palms to extend your elbows and return to the starting position. | Pause briefly at the top with your arms nearly extended to maintain tension in the triceps brachii. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, then return your hips to the bench before removing the weight.

t: Select a dumbbell of appropriate weight and place it near the captain's chair before you mount the station. | Step into the captain's chair, press your back firmly against the pad, and grip the handles securely with both hands. | Carefully pick up the dumbbell by squeezing it between the arches of both feet, holding it horizontally and securely before lifting off the ground. | Start in the hanging position with your legs straight and core braced — this is your starting position. | Exhale and raise your legs by driving your knees toward your chest or lifting your legs to parallel (or higher), initiating the movement from your hip flexors and lower abs. | Pause briefly at the top, maintaining control of the dumbbell and avoiding any swinging. | Inhale and slowly lower your legs back to the starting position under full muscular control — do not let them drop. | Complete all reps, then carefully lower the dumbbell to the floor before stepping out of the captain's chair.

t: Drape the chains evenly over the barbell so each end hangs to the floor on both sides and the links pool on the ground at the start position. | Stand with your feet wider than shoulder-width, toes angled out 30–45°, and the barbell positioned over your mid-foot. | Hinge at the hips and grip the bar with both hands inside your knees using either a double-overhand or mixed grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart. | Pull your hips down until your shins are near-vertical, lift your chest, and set a neutral spine from head to tailbone. | Take a deep breath, brace your core firmly, and create full-body tension before the bar leaves the floor. | Drive through the floor with both feet, keeping the bar close to your legs as your hips and shoulders rise together. | Lock out at the top by driving your hips fully forward and standing tall — avoid hyperextending the lower back. | Lower the bar under control by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees as the bar passes them, letting the chains settle back to the floor. | Reset your brace fully between each rep before initiating the next pull.

t: Select a very light weight plate to start — even experienced lifters should begin with 2.5–5 lb until the movement pattern is well established. | Sit on the end of a flat bench, then carefully lie back so the back of your head hangs just off the edge; your shoulders should remain fully supported on the bench. | Fit the head harness snugly over your skull and attach the chain or strap to your loaded weight plate, allowing the plate to hang toward the floor. | Let the weight pull your head into full flexion — chin moving toward your chest — so you reach a comfortable starting stretch at the bottom of the range of motion. | Brace your core lightly and keep your shoulders pressed flat against the bench throughout the set. | Using only your neck extensors, slowly lift your head by pushing the back of your skull upward and backward, extending the neck until your head is roughly level with or just above the bench surface. | Pause briefly at the top, consciously squeezing the posterior neck musculature. | Lower your head back down in a slow, controlled manner — take at least 2–3 seconds on the descent — returning to the stretched starting position. | Complete the desired number of reps, then carefully remove the harness and sit up slowly before standing.

t: Lie face-up on a flat bench with your head extended just beyond the edge so it hangs freely; keep your shoulders flat and your spine neutral. | Place a small weight plate (2.5–5 lb) on the side of your head just above the temple, or attach a weighted head harness and adjust it to sit comfortably. | Support the weight lightly with one hand to prevent it from sliding during the first few reps. | Begin with your head in a neutral position — ears aligned over shoulders, chin neither tucked nor raised. | Slowly tilt your head toward the weighted side, allowing gravity and the weight to guide a controlled lateral flexion until you feel a mild stretch on the opposite side. | Pause briefly at the end range, then contract the muscles on the weighted side to bring your head back to neutral. | Without stopping, continue in one fluid arc to the opposite side, tilting your head away from where the weight now rests. | Return to neutral to complete one full side-to-side repetition. | Complete all reps, then carefully remove the weight before sitting up slowly to avoid dizziness.

t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and hold a weight plate with both hands at chest height, elbows slightly bent and close to your body. | Brace your core, keep your chest tall, and push your hips back to begin the descent. | Lower into a squat until your thighs are roughly parallel to the floor, keeping your knees tracking over your toes and your heels flat on the ground. | Without pausing at the bottom, drive explosively through both feet to launch yourself off the floor. | Keep the plate controlled at chest level throughout the jump — do not let it swing forward or overhead. | Land softly on the balls of your feet first, then roll back to your heels, allowing your knees and hips to absorb the impact by bending immediately into the next squat. | Use the momentum of the landing to transition directly into the next rep, or pause briefly to reset before repeating.

t: Sit on a stability ball and walk your feet forward until the ball sits in the curve of your lower back, with your feet flat on the floor hip-width apart and your knees bent at roughly 90°. | Hold a weight plate or dumbbell at your chest with both hands, or position it behind your head with your fingertips lightly supporting it. | Allow your torso to drape back over the ball so your lower back is supported and your upper back is below your hips — this is the stretched starting position. | Brace your core and exhale as you curl your upper back off the ball, bringing your chest toward your hips and fully contracting your rectus abdominis at the top. | Pause briefly at the peak of the contraction, keeping the weight close to your body. | Inhale and slowly lower your torso back over the ball, allowing your abs to fully stretch before beginning the next rep. | Keep your feet pressed firmly into the floor and your hips stationary throughout — avoid letting the ball roll.

t: Attach a weight plate or chain to the head harness loop and adjust the harness straps so it sits snugly on your skull without pinching or shifting during movement. | Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, a slight bend in your knees, and your torso upright. t: Stand with your feet roughly shoulder-width apart and your core braced. Hold a dumbbell in each hand (or a weight plate) at shoulder height, palms facing forward and elbows pointing slightly in front of your body. | Pull your shoulder blades down and together, and tuck your chin slightly to keep a neutral spine from head to tailbone. | Brace your glutes and abdomen firmly before you begin pressing — this prevents your lower back from arching under load. | Press the weights directly overhead in a straight vertical path, extending your elbows fully at the top without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears. | At lockout, the weights should be directly over your mid-foot, not drifted forward, with your arms fully extended and biceps near your ears. | Lower the weights under control back to shoulder height, maintaining the same slight elbow-forward position, and reset your brace before the next rep. | Complete your target reps, then bring the weights down to your sides in a controlled manner.

t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, and core braced. Hold a weight plate, dumbbell, or medicine ball at chest height with both hands and arms slightly extended. | Engage your core and set your shoulders back and down. Keep your hips square and facing forward throughout the movement. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale as you rotate your torso to the right, driving the movement from your obliques rather than your arms or hips. | Rotate until your torso faces roughly 45–90 degrees to the right, or until you feel full tension through the obliques — do not let the hips swing or the lower back round. | Pause briefly at the end range to increase time under tension, then control the weight back to the centre. | Immediately rotate to the left with the same controlled tempo, keeping the pelvis stable throughout. | Continue alternating sides for the prescribed number of repetitions per side, maintaining upright posture and steady breathing.

t: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, core braced and glutes lightly engaged. | Hold the steel mace (or weight) at chest height with both hands gripping the handle close together, mace head pointing upward. | Tilt the mace to one side and begin guiding it backward and upward, initiating the circular path around your head. | Keep your head still and chin slightly tucked as the mace passes behind your head — do not duck or crane the neck. | Continue the arc smoothly so the mace travels around the back of the skull, staying as close to the head as control allows. | Guide the mace forward and back to the starting position in front of your chest to complete one full circle. | Perform the prescribed number of reps in one direction, then reverse the direction for the same count. | Maintain an upright torso throughout — avoid leaning or rotating the trunk to compensate for the weight.

t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out slightly, and the steel mace held vertically in front of your body at chest height with both hands gripping the handle. | Brace your core, pull your shoulder blades back and down, and keep your chest tall throughout the movement. | Inhale and initiate the squat by pushing your hips back and bending your knees simultaneously, keeping the mace close to your body. | Descend until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, or as low as your mobility comfortably allows, while maintaining an upright torso. | Keep your knees tracking in line with your toes and prevent them from caving inward as you lower. | Pause briefly at the bottom of the squat with your weight distributed evenly through both feet. | Exhale and drive through your heels to press the floor away, extending your hips and knees simultaneously to return to the starting position. | Fully extend at the top without hyperextending your lower back, then reset your brace before the next repetition. | Complete the desired number of repetitions, then carefully lower the mace before setting it down.

t: Lie flat on your back on the floor or a mat with your legs extended straight up toward the ceiling, perpendicular to your torso. | Hold a weight plate or dumbbell with both hands, arms extended overhead or resting on your chest — for maximum load, keep the weight extended directly above your chest as you prepare to crunch. | Press your lower back firmly into the floor and brace your core before initiating any movement. | Exhale and contract your abdominals, curling your upper back off the floor and reaching the weight upward toward your toes. | Drive the crunch from your abs — avoid pulling with your neck or jerking the weight to create momentum. | At the top, aim to bring the weight as close to your feet as your flexibility allows while keeping your legs fully straight and your lower back on the floor. | Pause briefly at the peak contraction, then slowly lower your upper back back to the floor under control. | Inhale as you descend and return to the starting position with your arms extended and upper back just touching the mat. | Repeat for the desired number of reps without losing tension in the abdominals between repetitions.

t: Lie flat on a bench and select a light weight plate (5–10 lb to start). Hold it between both palms with your fingers pointing away, arms extended toward the ceiling directly over your chest. | Squeeze your palms forcefully into the plate before the set begins and commit to maintaining that inward pressure for every rep — the constant squeeze is the defining technique of this exercise. | Retract and depress your shoulder blades against the bench, plant your feet firmly on the floor, and take a full breath to brace your core. | Lower the plate in a controlled arc toward the middle of your chest, keeping your elbows slightly soft and the squeeze unbroken the entire way down. | Stop when the plate is just above your chest — do not let the squeeze relax or rest the plate on your sternum. | Press upward and very slightly inward, driving through your chest while continuing to squeeze the plate together, until your arms return to full extension above your chest. | Pause briefly at the top to feel peak contraction in the sternal pec, then begin the next controlled descent. | After completing all reps, lower the plate to your chest and sit up carefully before releasing the squeeze.

t: Sit on the end of a flat bench and secure your feet — hook them under a foot pad if the bench has one, or have a partner hold them down — with your knees bent at roughly 90°. | Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against your chest or behind your head, keeping your arms in that position throughout the set. | Lean back until your torso is at approximately 45° to the bench — this is your starting position. | Brace your core and begin curling your ribcage toward your hips, initiating the movement with your abs rather than pulling with your neck or shoulders. | As you reach the midpoint of the crunch, rotate your right shoulder toward your left knee, adding the twist on top of the flexion. | Hold the top position for one count, feeling the contraction in your obliques and rectus abdominis. | Slowly lower back to the starting 45° position in a controlled manner — do not let the weight pull you all the way down to the bench. | On the next rep, rotate your left shoulder toward your right knee, and continue alternating sides for the desired number of reps.

t: Place the bosu ball dome-side up on the floor and sit on the dome, centering your hips on its highest point. | Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against your chest with both hands. | Lean your torso back to roughly 45 degrees while extending your legs straight out in front of you, keeping your feet just off the floor — this is your starting position. | Brace your core firmly to stabilize your balance on the dome before beginning each rep. | Simultaneously draw your knees toward your chest while lifting your torso forward to meet them, compressing your midsection into a tight V shape at the top. | Pause briefly at the top and squeeze your rectus abdominis and hip flexors. | Slowly lower your torso and legs back to the starting position under control, resisting the descent rather than letting gravity drop them. | Keep your feet from touching the floor between reps to maintain continuous tension through the rectus abdominis and iliopsoas. | Repeat for the target number of reps, maintaining a stable, centered position on the dome throughout.
